writtenQuestions.text:
A lunar mission has recently brought samples from the Moon. The following experiments were then carried out on it. Point out the branch of chemistry these experiments are related to. 1. Determining its composition
2. Studying the physical properties of materials it contains
3. Carrying out chemical reactions with usual inorganic reagents
modelAnswer: 1. Determining the sample's composition involves analysis of its components, so it is analytical chemistry.
2. Studying physical properties of materials is related to physical chemistry.
3. Reactions with usual inorganic reagents are related to inorganic chemistry.
Therefore, the branches are analytical chemistry, physical chemistry and inorganic chemistry, respectively.

solution: Organic chemistry deals with carbon compounds, including their structure, formation, properties, composition and reactions.

It gives insights into the structure and function of molecules such as proteins, carbohydrates, lipids and nucleic acids.
So organic chemistry focuses on carbon compounds, while biochemistry focuses on chemical processes and molecules in living organisms.

explain.title: What chemistry studies
explain.body: Chemistry is the branch of science which deals with the properties, composition and the structure of substances. It also deals with the physical and chemical changes in matter and the laws or principles which govern these changes.

explain.title: Why chemistry has branches
explain.body: Chemistry is a widely spread, complex subject. Its branches give scientists distinct areas to focus on, making it possible to study specific aspects and achieve breakthroughs and advancements.

explain.title: Physical and analytical chemistry
explain.body: Physical chemistry investigates how substances behave at atomic and molecular levels. Analytical chemistry deals with the analysis of substances through separation, identification and determination of component concentrations.

explain.title: Organic, inorganic and nuclear chemistry
explain.body: Organic chemistry deals with carbon compounds other than simple salts such as carbonates, bicarbonates, oxides and carbides. Inorganic chemistry studies elements and compounds that contain little or no carbon. Nuclear chemistry deals with reactions taking place in an atom's nucleus.

explain.title: Chemistry in living things, the environment and space
explain.body: Biochemistry studies chemical substances and vital processes in living organisms. Environmental chemistry studies chemical phenomena and species in air, soil and water. Astrochemistry studies molecules and ions in space and interstellar space.

mistakes: Mixing up analytical chemistry (analyzing components) with a branch that studies what substances do or how they behave.
Calling every study of a carbon-containing molecule biochemistry: organic chemistry studies carbon compounds, while biochemistry focuses on living organisms and their chemical processes.
Confusing inorganic chemistry with nuclear chemistry: inorganic chemistry concerns elements and compounds with little or no carbon; nuclear chemistry concerns reactions in atomic nuclei.
Giving only one reason when asked for three reasons chemistry is divided into branches.
Writing a branch name without linking it to the topic in a branch-identification question.

explain.title: What matter and a state of matter mean
explain.body: Your textbook defines matter as: “Anything other than energy which carries weight and occupies volume is called matter.” It defines a state of matter as: “A state of matter is one of the many distinct forms in which matter can exist.” The four states observed in everyday life are solid, liquid, gas and plasma.

explain.title: Solids, liquids and gases
explain.body: Solids have a definite shape and fixed volume; their particles are closely packed and can oscillate about their mean positions. Liquid molecules are closely attached but move randomly. Gas molecules are very widely apart, have no order whatsoever and have very weak intermolecular forces, so gases are easily compressible and have very low densities.

explain.title: Plasma and other states
explain.body: Your textbook defines plasma as: “Plasma can be considered as a partially ionized gas containing electrons, ions, photons, etc.” It gives fluorescent tubes, lightning and welding arcs as examples. Supercritical fluids show properties of both gases and liquids. Liquid crystals have properties between conventional liquids and crystalline solids.

explain.title: Graphene and exotic states
explain.body: Graphene is a two-dimensional crystal: a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal pattern. The section describes it as tough, flexible and light, with a high resistance. States not commonly encountered are called exotic states of matter; examples include dark matter and Bose-Einstein condensate.

mistakes: Do not say gas molecules are close together; the text says they are very widely apart.
Do not say solid particles are completely motionless: they can oscillate about their mean positions.
Do not confuse plasma with an ordinary gas; plasma is described as a partially ionized gas.
Do not confuse graphene with liquid crystal: graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms, while liquid crystal properties are between those of conventional liquids and crystalline solids.
When describing supercritical fluids, include both gas and liquid properties, not just one of them.

explain.title: Element
explain.body: Element is the simplest form of matter. It is a pure substance containing the same kind of atoms. It cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical reactions.

explain.title: Compound
explain.body: Compound is also a pure substance. It is made up of two or more different chemically elements combined in a fixed ratio. When elements come together, they react with each other and form chemical bonds that are not easy to break.

explain.title: Mixture
explain.body: A mixture is formed when more than one types of elements or compounds are mixed together in any ratio. A mixture may be homogeneous or heterogeneous.

explain.title: Homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures
explain.body: A homogeneous mixture has uniform concentration throughout, as in salt water. A heterogeneous mixture has different concentrations of its constituents in different parts, as in a sample of rock.

mistakes: Do not call a compound a mixture: elements in a compound are chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
Do not say a mixture has to have a fixed ratio; its substances may be mixed in any ratio.
Do not classify a sample as homogeneous just because it contains several substances; check whether its composition is uniform throughout.
Do not say an element can be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical reactions.

writtenQuestions.text: What are allotropic forms? Explain the allotropic forms of carbon and sulphur. How does coal differ from diamond?
modelAnswer: Allotropic forms are different structural forms of the same element.
Carbon has three main allotropic forms: diamond, graphite and Buckminster fullerene (C₆₀).
Diamond has a giant macromolecular structure.
Graphite has a layered structure of hexagonal rings of carbon.
Buckminster fullerene (C₆₀) consists of a cage-like sphere of atoms arranged in pentagons and hexagons.
Sulphur exists in two crystalline allotropic forms: rhombic and monoclinic sulphur.
Rhombic sulphur is more stable than monoclinic sulphur.
Coal is an impure, non-crystalline form of carbon, whereas diamond is a crystalline form of carbon with a giant macromolecular structure.

explain.title: What allotropy means

explain.title: Elements
explain.body: An element is the simplest form of matter. It is a pure substance containing the same kind of atoms. It is not possible to break down an element into simpler particles by ordinary chemical reactions.

explain.title: Compounds
explain.body: A compound is a pure substance. It is formed by the chemical combination of two or more atoms of different elements. In a compound, the atoms of elements must combine together by a fixed ratio by weight. A compound can be broken into its constituent elements by a chemical reaction.

explain.title: Mixtures
explain.body: Mixture is an impure compound. A sample of matter having more than one type of elements or compounds mixed together in any ratio, is called a mixture. Its components are not chemically bound together, retain their identities and specific properties, and can be separated by physical methods.

explain.title: Examples and forms
explain.body: Water (H₂O) and ammonia (NH₃) are compounds. A salt solution in water is a homogeneous mixture, while a sample of rock is a heterogeneous mixture. Mixtures have the combined properties of their components.

mistakes: Do not call a mixture a compound: mixtures are not chemically bound together, while compounds are chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
Do not say that components of a mixture lose their properties; each component retains its identity and specific properties.
Do not confuse homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures: salt solution is homogeneous, while a sample of rock is heterogeneous.
Do not say a compound can be separated by physical methods; breaking it into its constituent elements requires a chemical reaction.

Its solute particles are completely homogenized in the solvent.
The particles cannot be seen with the naked eye.
On filtration, the particles pass through the filter paper, leaving no residue.
yourTurn.answer: Sodium chloride forms a true solution in water; its particles are completely homogenized, cannot be seen with the naked eye and pass through filter paper leaving no residue.

example.question: No worked example is included in the supplied section.
example.answer: No worked example is provided.

explain.title: True solution
explain.body: A solution is such a mixture in which solute particles are completely homogenized in the solvent e.g. dissolution of sodium chloride or copper sulphate in water. The solute particles in such a solution cannot be seen by the naked eye. If solution is filtered, these particles pass through the pores of filter paper leaving no residue. Such a solution is called a true solution.

explain.title: Suspension
explain.body: A suspension, on the other hand, is a mixture in which solute particles do not dissolve in the solvent. We can actually see these particles. If a suspension is kept for some time, these particles settle down. Again, if this suspension is filtered, the particles in it cannot pass through the pores of filter paper and can be collected as a residue. A mixture of chalk in water is an example of suspension.

explain.title: Colloidal solution
explain.body: Besides a true solution and a suspension, there is a third form of solution called colloidal solution. In this type, the solute particles do not homogenize with solvent. These particles are a little bit bigger than the solute particles present in the true solution but not big enough to be seen with a naked eye like the particles present in a suspension. If kept for some time, the particles of a colloidal solution do not settle down. On filtration, these particles pass through the filter paper like the particles of a true solution. Starch solution and white of an egg are the common examples of colloidal solutions.

mistakes: Do not say that colloidal particles settle; the section says they do not settle on standing.
Do not say colloidal particles are caught by filter paper; they pass through it.
Do not confuse a true solution with a colloid: both pass through filter paper, but colloidal particles are bigger than true-solution particles.
Do not use chalk in water as an example of a true solution; it is a suspension.

modelAnswer: The increase in the solubility of solids in liquids with increase in temperature may be used to purify them.
Pure solids commonly appear as beautifully shaped crystals.

Soda water bottles are stored in the refrigerator to keep carbon dioxide gas dissolved in water for a longer period of time.
Therefore, variation of solubility with temperature is useful for purification by crystallization and for keeping gases dissolved.

explain.title: What solubility means
explain.body: The solubility of a solute is the amount of solute which can dissolve in 100g of a solvent at a particular temperature. Always include the amount of solvent and the temperature when you give the definition.

explain.title: Temperature does not affect every substance in the same way
explain.body: Many solids, including potassium nitrate (KNO₃), silver nitrate (AgNO₃) and potassium chloride (KCl), become more soluble as temperature rises. But this is not a general rule. Sodium chloride changes very little, while lithium carbonate (Li₂CO₃), calcium chromate (CaCrO₄) and calcium hydroxide become less soluble.

explain.title: Gases and useful applications
explain.body: The solubility of gases in water generally decreases as temperature increases. Carbon dioxide is more soluble in cold water, so soda water bottles are stored in a refrigerator to keep the gas dissolved longer. The increase in solubility of many solids when heated can also be used to purify them by crystallization.

mistakes: Defining solubility without saying “in 100g of a solvent” or “at a particular temperature.”
Writing that the solubility of every solid increases with temperature; the textbook says this is not a general rule.
Mixing up the examples: NaCl changes little, while Li₂CO₃ and CaCrO₄ become less soluble as temperature rises.
Claiming that gases become more soluble in warm water; gases generally become less soluble.
Describing crystallization without explaining that the hot solution is cooled so crystals form.

example.answer: Polar water molecules attract and surround Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, overcoming the forces in the NaCl crystal and dispersing the hydrated ions through the water.

explain.title: Chemistry has branches
explain.body: Chemistry covers many substances, properties and reactions. Dividing it into branches makes its study organised and allows people to specialise. Each branch focuses on a different kind of question or material.

explain.title: Matter has different states and structures
explain.body: Matter includes solids, liquids and gases, as well as states such as plasma, liquid crystals and supercritical fluids. Elements can also occur in different structural forms called allotropes, such as diamond and graphite, which are both forms of carbon.

explain.title: Mixtures and solutions are different
explain.body: A true solution is uniform, while colloids and suspensions contain dispersed particles. A saturated solution contains as much solute as can dissolve under the stated conditions.

explain.title: Solubility depends on the substance and temperature
explain.body: Different compounds dissolve to different extents because their particles interact differently with water. The solubility of most solids increases as temperature rises; the solubility of gases generally decreases.

explain.title: Crystallization can purify a solid
explain.body: A substance such as potassium nitrate can be dissolved in hot water, and the solution can be cooled to form crystals. Filtering, washing and drying the crystals separates the purified solid from soluble impurities.

explain.title: Structure explains useful properties
explain.body: Graphite feels slippery because its layers slide over one another, while a diamond's high refractive index contributes to its brilliance. Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms and is useful in electronics because of its electrical properties.

mistakes: Do not confuse plasma with an ordinary gas: plasma contains ionized particles.
Do not call every mixture a solution; suspensions and colloids have dispersed particles.
When defining solubility, include the temperature and the saturated-solution condition.
Do not say all solutes respond to heating in the same way: most solids become more soluble, while gases generally become less soluble.
For crystallization, do not cool before dissolving the impure solid in hot water and filtering the solution.
Do not describe graphene as many layers; it is a single layer, while graphite consists of stacked layers.
When comparing coal with diamond, distinguish impure amorphous coal from crystalline diamond.
In branch questions, choose the branch by the focus of the topic, not just by the name of a substance.

solutions.question: Why is there a need to divide Chemistry into many branches? Give three reasons.
steps: Chemistry is a vast subject and includes a large number of facts, concepts and processes.
Its branches make the subject easier to study and understand by grouping related topics together.
Each branch allows specialised study of a particular area and its applications.
solutions.answer: Chemistry is divided into branches because it is vast, the division makes it easier to study, and it enables specialised study of its different areas.

solutions.question: Reactions may take place due to electrons present outside the nucleus or they may take place inside the nucleus. Which branches of Chemistry cover these two types of reactions?
steps: Reactions involving electrons outside the nucleus are studied in ordinary chemistry.
Reactions taking place inside the nucleus are studied in nuclear chemistry.
solutions.answer: Ordinary chemistry studies reactions involving electrons outside the nucleus; nuclear chemistry studies reactions inside the nucleus.

solutions.question: What types of problems are solved in analytical chemistry?
steps: Analytical chemistry deals with the identification of substances and the determination of their composition.
It solves qualitative problems (what substances are present) and quantitative problems (how much of each substance is present).
solutions.answer: Analytical chemistry identifies the substances present in a sample and determines their amounts.

solutions.question: Both graphite and graphene have hexagonal layered structures. What is the difference?
steps: Graphite consists of many layers of carbon atoms arranged in hexagonal patterns.
Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal pattern.
solutions.answer: Graphite has many hexagonal layers, whereas graphene is a single hexagonal layer of carbon atoms.

solutions.question: Why are supercritical fluids important?
steps: A supercritical fluid forms above a substance's critical temperature and critical pressure.
It has properties of both liquids and gases, so it can act as an effective solvent.
Supercritical fluids are important for processes such as extracting substances and can be used as alternatives to conventional solvents.
solutions.answer: Supercritical fluids are useful solvents for extraction and other processes because they combine properties of liquids and gases.

solutions.question: In which state does matter exist in the Sun?
steps: Matter in the Sun exists in the plasma state.
solutions.answer: Plasma.

solutions.question: What is the importance of graphene?
steps: Graphene is a very strong, lightweight and flexible form of carbon.
It conducts electricity and heat very well.
These properties make it useful in electronic devices and other advanced materials.
solutions.answer: Graphene is important because it is strong, light, flexible and an excellent conductor, making it useful in advanced materials and electronics.

solutions.question: Which form of matter do most of the material things in this world belong to?
steps: Most material things in the world belong to the solid state of matter.
solutions.answer: The solid state.

solutions.question: How does a supercritical state look like?
steps: In a supercritical state, a substance is above its critical temperature and critical pressure.
The liquid and gas states become indistinguishable; there is no clear boundary or meniscus between them.
The substance exists as a supercritical fluid.
solutions.answer: A supercritical state is a fluid state in which liquid and gas are indistinguishable.

solutions.question: In what way is plasma created in a fluorescent tube?
steps: An electric current passes through the gas inside a fluorescent tube.
The gas atoms become ionized, producing ions and free electrons; this ionized gas is plasma.
The plasma excites mercury vapour atoms, which emit ultraviolet radiation.
The fluorescent coating on the inside of the tube absorbs the ultraviolet radiation and emits visible light.
solutions.answer: Plasma is created when the electric current ionizes the gas inside the fluorescent tube.

solutions.question: Most of the molecules we study in biochemistry are organic in nature. Where does the difference exist in organic and biochemistry branches of Chemistry?
steps: Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with carbon compounds.
Biochemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the chemical substances and reactions occurring in living organisms.
Thus, organic chemistry studies carbon compounds generally, while biochemistry studies chemical processes in living organisms.
solutions.answer: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds, whereas biochemistry studies the substances and reactions in living organisms.

solutions.question: Give the reason of brilliance shown by diamond. Can you improve it?
steps: Diamond has a very high refractive index, so its critical angle is small.
Light entering a properly cut diamond undergoes repeated total internal reflection before emerging, producing brilliance.
The brilliance can be improved by cutting and polishing the diamond into properly arranged facets, which increase internal reflection.
solutions.answer: Diamond’s high refractive index gives it brilliance through repeated total internal reflection; proper cutting and polishing can improve it.

solutions.question: Explain the dissolution of sodium chloride in water.
steps: Water is a polar solvent: the oxygen end of a water molecule is partially negative, while its hydrogen ends are partially positive.
The oxygen ends attract Na⁺ ions, and the hydrogen ends attract Cl⁻ ions.
These attractions pull the ions away from the sodium chloride crystal and surround them with water molecules.
The hydrated ions disperse throughout the water, forming a sodium chloride solution: NaCl(s) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq).
solutions.answer: Polar water molecules attract, separate and hydrate the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, dissolving sodium chloride.

solutions.question: Why do different compounds have different solubilities in water at a particular temperature?
steps: Solubility depends on the nature of the solute and the solvent and on the strength of the attractive forces between their particles.
Different compounds interact with water to different extents, so different amounts dissolve at the same temperature.
In general, a substance dissolves better when the attractions between its particles and water molecules are strong enough to separate its particles.
solutions.answer: Different compounds have different solubilities because their particles interact with water with different strengths.

solutions.question: Why NaCl can not be crystallized from water just like KNO₃?
steps: The solubility of KNO₃ increases greatly as temperature rises, so much more KNO₃ dissolves in hot water than in cold water.
When a hot saturated KNO₃ solution cools, the excess KNO₃ crystallizes out.
The solubility of NaCl changes very little with temperature.
Therefore, cooling a saturated NaCl solution does not produce much crystallization; NaCl is commonly obtained by evaporating the water.
solutions.answer: NaCl cannot be crystallized from water by cooling as readily as KNO₃ because its solubility changes very little with temperature.

solutions.question: Why graphite is slippery to touch? Which property of graphite enables it to be used as lubricant?
steps: Graphite consists of layers of carbon atoms.
The forces between these layers are weak, so the layers can slide over one another easily.
This easy sliding makes graphite slippery to touch and enables it to be used as a lubricant.
solutions.answer: Graphite is slippery because its layers slide over one another easily, making it useful as a lubricant.

solutions.question: What are allotropic forms? Explain the allotropic forms of carbon and sulphur. How does coal differ from diamond?
What are supercritical fluids. How are they different from ordinary liquids?
steps: A supercritical fluid is a substance at a temperature and pressure above its critical temperature and critical pressure.
In this state, the distinction between the liquid and gaseous states disappears.
Unlike an ordinary liquid, a supercritical fluid has no definite surface separating it from a gas.
It can diffuse like a gas while having a density closer to that of a liquid.
solutions.answer: A supercritical fluid exists above its critical temperature and pressure and has properties of both liquids and gases.

steps: Molecules of both gases and liquids have translational, rotational and vibrational motions.

solutions.answer: Gaseous and liquid molecules have translational, rotational and vibrational motions.

solutions.question: Differentiate between the areas which are studied under inorganic and organic chemistry.
steps: Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the study of hydrocarbons and their derivatives.
Inorganic chemistry deals with the study of all elements and their compounds, except organic compounds.
solutions.answer: Organic chemistry studies hydrocarbons and their derivatives, whereas inorganic chemistry studies all elements and their compounds except organic compounds.

solutions.question: Preparation of solutions leads to an important process in chemistry which enables us to purify a compound through crystallization. Describe a process in which potassium nitrate is purified by crystallizing it in water.
steps: Dissolve the impure potassium nitrate in the minimum amount of hot water.
Filter the hot solution to remove insoluble impurities.
Allow the clear filtrate to cool. Potassium nitrate crystals form as the solution cools because its solubility decreases.
Separate the crystals by filtration and dry them.
solutions.answer: Impure potassium nitrate is dissolved in hot water, filtered, cooled to form crystals, and then the crystals are filtered and dried.

solutions.answer: Graphene’s excellent electrical conductivity makes it very useful in electronics.

definitions.text: Chemistry is the branch of science which deals with the properties, composition and the structure of substances. It also deals with the physical and chemical changes in matter and the laws or principles which govern these changes.

This branch investigates how substances behave at atomic and molecular levels. It provides clear explanation as to how fundamental physical laws governing our world cause atoms and molecules to show specific characteristics and in turn react to give huge structures related to life. Physical chemistry is also used to predict and change the rates of reactions and thus optimize the conditions to carry out the reactions on industrial scale.
It is the study of the synthesis, composition, properties and structure of elements and compounds that contain little or no carbon.
It is the branch of chemistry that deals with the carbon compounds (hydrocarbons and their derivatives) other than its simple salts like carbonates, bicarbonates, oxides and carbides.
It is the scientific study of the chemical and biochemical phenomena that occur in this planet.
This branch of chemistry deals with the analysis of different substances. It involves separation, identification and determination of the concentration of the components present in material things.
It is the branch of chemistry in which we understand life through chemical processes. It is the study of chemical substances and vital processes occurring in living organisms.
Nuclear chemistry deals with the reactions taking place in the nucleus of an atom. It deals with radioactivity, nuclear processes and transformation in the nuclei of atoms.
Anything other than energy which carries weight and occupies volume is called matter.
A state of matter is one of the many distinct forms in which matter can exist.
Plasma can be considered as a partially ionized gas containing electrons, ions, photons, etc.
The solubility of a solute is the amount of solute which can dissolve in 100g of a solvent at a particular temperature.

fullMarks: For a question asking you to name a branch, write the branch first, then give a brief reason linked to the topic: reaction rate—physical chemistry; digestion—biochemistry; ecosystem—environmental chemistry; wavelength absorption measurement—analytical chemistry.
For organic versus inorganic chemistry, compare the kinds of compounds studied: carbon compounds in organic chemistry and elements or compounds containing little or no carbon in inorganic chemistry.
For organic chemistry versus biochemistry, make the distinction clear: organic chemistry focuses on carbon compounds; biochemistry focuses on chemical substances and processes in living organisms.
For a plasma answer, state that it is a partially ionized gas and include examples or particles from the text, such as electrons, ions and photons, where relevant.

For a crystallization answer, describe the steps in order: dissolve potassium nitrate in hot water, cool the solution so crystals form, separate the crystals, and dry them. Link the process to the increased solubility of solids in hot water.
When describing solubility, include the amount, the solvent and the temperature: it is the amount of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a particular temperature.
mistakes: Mixing up physical chemistry and nuclear chemistry. Fix: nuclear chemistry studies reactions in the nucleus; physical chemistry studies the behaviour of substances at atomic and molecular levels.
Calling biochemistry simply the study of all carbon compounds. Fix: say that it studies chemical substances and vital processes in living organisms.
Confusing plasma with an ordinary gas. Fix: describe plasma as a partially ionized gas containing particles such as electrons and ions.

Answering that most material things are elements or compounds when the question asks for the form most material things belong to. Fix: answer mixtures and give examples such as air, soil, milk or tap water.

Mixing up environmental and analytical chemistry. Fix: environmental chemistry studies chemical phenomena in the environment; analytical chemistry separates, identifies and determines components in substances.
Describing crystallization without explaining why crystals form. Fix: mention that a solid such as potassium nitrate is more soluble in hot water and crystals form as the solution cools.

shortTheory.question: Why is Chemistry divided into many branches?
shortTheory.answer: To understand the widely spread complex subject of chemistry and to concentrate on its specific aspects, chemistry is divided into many distinct branches. These branches have distinct areas of study for the scientists to focus on and to achieve breakthroughs and advancements.

shortTheory.answer: Organic chemistry deals with carbon compounds, while biochemistry is the study of chemical substances and vital processes occurring in living organisms.

shortTheory.answer: Environmental chemistry is the scientific study of the chemical and biochemical phenomena that occur in this planet.

explain.title: The atom has a central nucleus
explain.body: The nucleus is a tiny central portion of the atom. It contains protons and neutrons, which are held together by strong nuclear force. Almost all the atom's mass is concentrated in the nucleus.

explain.title: Electrons occupy shells
explain.body: In Bohr's model, electrons can revolve in specific orbits called shells. Each shell has a fixed energy. The first shell is nearest to the nucleus and has the lowest energy; shells farther away have greater energy.

explain.title: The modern view describes probability
explain.body: The modern approach does not give an electron a precisely known path. It describes electrons as charged clouds and tells us the probability of finding an electron in a region.

explain.title: Calculate shell capacity
explain.body: Use the formula 2n², where n is the shell number. For example, for n = 3, 2 × 3² = 18, so the third shell can accommodate at most 18 electrons.

mistakes: Do not put electrons in the nucleus; electrons occupy the extra-nuclear region.
Do not confuse the proton's positive charge with the electron's negative charge.
Do not say all shells have equal energy; shells farther from the nucleus have greater energy.
When using 2n², square n before multiplying by 2.
Do not describe the modern view as giving an electron a precisely known path; it gives a probability of finding the electron.

explain.title: Atomic number
explain.body: The number of protons present in the atoms of an element is always fixed and it is called the atomic number of that element. It is represented by Z. An element is identified by its atomic number.

explain.title: Mass number
explain.body: The total number of protons and neutrons present in an atom almost accounts for the total mass of that atom and hence it is called its nucleon number or mass number. It is represented by A. The mass of electron being very small is not included in the mass number.

explain.title: Reading an atom symbol
explain.body: The atomic number is written as a left subscript while the mass number as a left superscript. For example, ¹⁶₈O has 8 protons and a mass number of 16.

explain.title: Finding neutrons
explain.body: The number of neutrons N present in an atom can be calculated if its atomic number Z and mass number (A) are known. N = A − Z. Since an atom as a whole is electrically neutral, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.

mistakes: Do not mix up the left superscript A (mass number) and left subscript Z (atomic number).
Do not use A + Z to find neutrons; use N = A − Z.
Do not say that the mass number includes electrons; it counts protons and neutrons.
For a neutral atom, do not make the electron count equal to the mass number; it equals the proton count.

explain.title: What are isotopes?
explain.body: “Atoms of the same element having different number of neutrons in their nuclei are called isotopes.” Isotopes have the same atomic number but can have different mass numbers.

explain.title: Why are their properties alike and different?
explain.body: “Since the chemical properties of the elements are determined by the number of electrons, all three isotopes will show almost the same chemical behaviour, although their physical properties may be different.” Their different neutron numbers mean different masses.

explain.title: Radioactivity and radioactive decay
explain.body: “This process of emission of radiation is called radioactivity and the isotope which emits energy is called radioactive isotope.” When a radioactive element emits radiation and changes into another element, the process is called radioactive decay.

explain.title: Uses of radioactive isotopes
explain.body: They are used for medical imaging and diagnosing or treating disease. Carbon-14 is used to estimate the age of organic material. Radioactive isotopes can also be used to test the strength of metals and concrete mixtures.

explain.title: Ionization by radiation
explain.body: Radiation with enough energy can force one or more electrons away from an atom. Since the atom loses negative charge, it becomes a positively charged ion called a cation.

mistakes: Do not confuse atomic number with mass number: neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
Do not say isotopes have different numbers of protons; isotopes of one element have the same atomic number.
Do not claim isotopes have exactly the same physical properties; their masses and physical properties may differ.
Do not call every isotope radioactive; the section says some nuclei are unstable, while others are stable.

explain.title: Why relative atomic mass is useful
explain.body: Atoms of different elements have different masses. A common reference scale lets us compare them and helps us work out the ratios in which reactants combine.

explain.title: The reference unit
explain.body: The relative atomic masses of elements are expressed in atomic mass unit (amu). It is defined as one-twelfth the mass of an atom of carbon-12. One amu is 1.67377 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

explain.title: Isotope abundances make a weighted average
explain.body: An element can have several isotopes, and each isotope has its own natural abundance. The relative atomic mass is calculated by multiplying each relative isotopic mass by its abundance, adding the products, and dividing by 100.

explain.title: Finding an unknown isotope mass
explain.body: If the overall relative atomic mass and isotope abundances are known, put the unknown isotope mass in the formula. Set the expression equal to the given relative atomic mass and solve the equation.

explain.title: The atom and its nucleus
explain.body: An atom has a very small nucleus containing protons and neutrons. Electrons are arranged around the nucleus in shells. Almost all the atom's mass is in the nucleus because electrons have very little mass.

explain.title: Atomic number and neutron number
explain.body: The number of protons is the atomic number and identifies the element. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons. Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

explain.title: Electron shells and energy
explain.body: Electrons in shells farther from the nucleus have greater energy. An atom absorbs energy when an electron moves to a higher energy shell and evolves or releases energy when an electron moves to a lower energy shell.

explain.title: Isotopes and relative atomic mass
explain.body: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Their relative atomic mass is a weighted mean based on the abundance of each isotope.

explain.title: Radioactivity and its uses
explain.body: Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation from an unstable nucleus. Radioactive isotopes have uses such as treating cancer, estimating the age of organic matter, and acting as tracers.

mistakes: Do not confuse mass number with atomic number: neutrons are found by subtracting atomic number from mass number.
Do not say isotopes have different numbers of protons. They have the same proton number and different neutron numbers.
Do not treat the electron as having a mass equal to a proton or neutron; its mass is very small.
When explaining energy absorption, say that the electron moves to a higher energy shell; emission occurs when it moves to a lower energy shell.
For weighted means, do not simply add isotope masses or ignore the abundances.
In descriptive answers, do not list applications of radioisotopes without saying what each application does.
For the mercury data printed here, the listed abundances add to 99.3746%, not 100%; show the total used in your calculation.

solutions.question: Why is it said that almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus?
steps: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, each having a mass of approximately 1 atomic mass unit.
The mass of an electron is very small compared with the mass of a proton or a neutron.
Therefore, the mass of the electrons is negligible compared with the mass of the nucleus.
Hence, almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus.
solutions.answer: Almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus because electrons have negligible mass compared with protons and neutrons.

solutions.question: Why are elements different from one another?
steps: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom is called its atomic number.
Each element has a different atomic number, that is, a different number of protons in its nucleus.
Therefore, elements are different from one another because they have different numbers of protons.
solutions.answer: Elements differ from one another because their atoms have different numbers of protons in the nucleus.

solutions.question: How many neutrons are present in ²¹⁰₈₃Bi?
steps: Given: Mass number, A = 210; atomic number, Z = 83.
Required: Number of neutrons, N.
Formula: N = A − Z.
Substitution: N = 210 − 83.
Working: N = 127.
Result: The number of neutrons in ²¹⁰₈₃Bi is 127.
solutions.answer: 127 neutrons

solutions.question: Why is tritium (³₁H) a radioactive element?
steps: Tritium has one proton and two neutrons in its nucleus.
Its nucleus is unstable.
An unstable nucleus emits radiations to become more stable.
Therefore, tritium is radioactive.
solutions.answer: Tritium is radioactive because its nucleus is unstable and emits radiation.

solutions.question: How can an atom absorb and evolve energy?
steps: An atom absorbs energy when an electron jumps from a lower energy level to a higher energy level.
An atom evolves (emits) energy when an electron jumps from a higher energy level to a lower energy level.
The energy absorbed or emitted is equal to the difference between the two energy levels.
solutions.answer: An atom absorbs energy when an electron moves to a higher energy level and emits energy when it returns to a lower energy level.

solutions.question: Why does the energy of electron increase as we move from first shell to second shell?
steps: The second shell is farther from the nucleus than the first shell.
The attraction of the nucleus for an electron becomes weaker as its distance from the nucleus increases.
An electron in the second shell therefore has greater energy than an electron in the first shell.
solutions.answer: The energy of an electron increases from the first shell to the second shell because the second shell is farther from the nucleus.

solutions.question: Why is it needed to lower the pressure of the gas inside the discharge tube?
steps: The pressure of the gas inside the discharge tube is lowered so that there are fewer gas molecules in the path of the electrons.
The electrons can then travel a longer distance without colliding with gas molecules and gain sufficient energy to ionize them.
This makes the discharge and the production of cathode rays possible.
solutions.answer: The pressure is lowered so electrons can travel farther and gain enough energy to ionize gas molecules, producing cathode rays.

solutions.question: What is the classical concept of an electron? How has this concept changed with time?
steps: According to the classical concept, an electron is a negatively charged particle that revolves around the nucleus in a definite path, like a planet revolving around the Sun.
With the development of modern atomic theory, electrons were found to have wave-like as well as particle-like properties.
It is now understood that an electron does not move in a precisely known fixed path; instead, its position is described in terms of the probability of finding it in a region around the nucleus.
solutions.answer: An electron was classically considered a particle moving in a definite path around the nucleus; modern theory describes its wave-particle nature and probability of position.

solutions.question: Why the nuclei of the radioactive elements are unstable?
steps: The nuclei of radioactive elements have an unstable arrangement of protons and neutrons.
Their neutron-to-proton ratio is unsuitable for stability.
They emit radiation to change into more stable nuclei.
solutions.answer: Radioactive nuclei are unstable because their proton-neutron balance is unsuitable, so they emit radiation to become more stable.

solutions.question: During discharge tube experiments, how did the scientists conclude that the same type of electrons and protons are present in all the elements?
steps: Scientists performed discharge tube experiments using different gases and electrodes.
Cathode rays showed the same properties and the same charge-to-mass ratio regardless of the gas or electrode used.
This showed that electrons are identical particles present in the atoms of all elements.
The positive particles observed in the experiments also led scientists to conclude that atoms contain protons; the hydrogen nucleus was identified as a proton.
Thus, electrons and protons are common constituents of the atoms of all elements.
solutions.answer: The same cathode-ray properties in experiments with different gases showed that identical electrons occur in all elements; experiments with positive rays established the presence of protons.

solutions.question: Explain the structure of a hydrogen atom.
steps: A hydrogen atom has a small, positively charged nucleus containing one proton.
One negatively charged electron is present outside the nucleus.
The most common hydrogen atom, protium, has no neutron in its nucleus.
The electrostatic attraction between the proton and electron holds the atom together.
solutions.answer: A hydrogen atom consists of one proton in its nucleus and one electron outside it; ordinary hydrogen has no neutron.

solutions.question: How does the theory of atomic structure explain the ionization of atoms by a radioactive isotope?
steps: Radioactive isotopes emit energetic radiations, such as alpha particles, beta particles or gamma rays.
When this radiation passes through matter, it transfers energy to atoms and may remove electrons from them.
An atom that loses an electron becomes a positively charged ion; the removed electron is free.
solutions.answer: Radiation from a radioactive isotope can knock electrons out of atoms, forming positive ions and free electrons.

solutions.question: What is radioactivity? Explain any three applications of radioactive isotopes.
steps: Radioactivity is the spontaneous disintegration of an unstable atomic nucleus, accompanied by the emission of radiations.
Cobalt-60 is used in radiotherapy to treat cancer.
Iodine-131 is used to diagnose and treat disorders of the thyroid gland.
Carbon-14 is used to determine the age of ancient organic remains.
solutions.answer: Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation from unstable nuclei; radioactive isotopes are used in cancer treatment, thyroid diagnosis and treatment, and carbon dating.

solutions.question: How can scientists synthesize elements in the laboratory?
steps: Scientists can synthesize new elements in the laboratory by bombarding the nuclei of atoms with high-energy particles.
These nuclear reactions produce new elements, many of which are heavier than uranium.
solutions.answer: New elements are synthesized by bombarding atomic nuclei with high-energy particles.

solutions.question: A system just like our solar system exists in an atom. Comment on this statement.
steps: The statement is partly correct: the nucleus is at the centre of an atom, and electrons move around it, as planets move around the Sun.
However, the resemblance is not exact. The planets are held in their orbits by gravitational force, whereas electrons are attracted to the positively charged nucleus by electrostatic force.
solutions.answer: An atom resembles the solar system in its central nucleus and surrounding electrons, but the forces holding them differ.

definitions.text: The total number of protons and neutrons present in an atom almost accounts for the total mass of that atom and hence it is called its nucleon number or mass number.
Atoms of the same element having different number of neutrons in their nuclei are called isotopes.
The relative atomic mass of an element is thus defined as the mass of an atom of that element relative to the mass of light isotope of carbon taken as 12.
It is defined as one-twelfth the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
Since an atom, as a whole, is electrically neutral, the number of electrons present in an atom will be the same as the number of protons.

formulas.use: Find neutrons in an atom: N, A and Z are particle counts (dimensionless; no SI units).
Find a shell’s maximum electron capacity: n is the shell number and the capacity is a particle count (both dimensionless; no SI units).
Find average relative atomic mass from isotope masses and percentage abundances: m values and p values are dimensionless, so the result is dimensionless (no SI units).

fullMarks: For an atom written as ᴬ_ZX, identify A as the mass number and Z as the atomic number before finding its particles.
For a neutron calculation, write N = A − Z, substitute the values, and state the final number of neutrons.
For a neutral atom, state that the number of electrons equals the number of protons; do not assume this for an ion.
When explaining shell energy, say that the second shell is farther from the nucleus than the first and has greater energy.
For questions about electron models, describe the definite shells in Bohr’s model first, then contrast them with the modern probability-cloud idea.
For a relative atomic mass calculation, show the weighted-abundance formula, substitute every isotope mass and abundance, divide by 100, and give the result clearly. Relative atomic mass has no unit.
When explaining why the nucleus contains almost all the atom’s mass, name both protons and neutrons as the heavy particles and mention the strong nuclear force holds them together.
mistakes: Mistake: Subtracting the atomic number from the wrong value. Fix: Use N = A − Z, where A is the superscript mass number and Z is the subscript atomic number.
Mistake: Saying isotopes have different numbers of protons. Fix: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Mistake: Saying the second shell has less energy because it is farther away. Fix: A shell farther from the nucleus has greater energy.
Mistake: Treating an electron’s exact path and location as predictable in the modern model. Fix: Explain that its location is described by probability, not a precisely mapped path.
Mistake: Leaving out either protons or neutrons when explaining the nucleus’s mass. Fix: Name both as the heavy particles concentrated in the nucleus.

Mistake: Giving a relative atomic mass calculation without weighting by abundance or dividing by 100. Fix: Multiply each isotope mass by its percentage abundance, add the products, then divide by 100.

shortTheory.question: Why is it said that almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus?
shortTheory.answer: It was also discovered that almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus because both the heavy particles i.e. protons and neutrons are found to be present here.

shortTheory.question: Why are elements different from one another?
shortTheory.answer: The difference in the properties of elements is due to the difference in the properties of their constituent atoms.

shortTheory.question: How many neutrons are present in ²¹⁰₈₃Bi?
shortTheory.answer: N = A − Z = 210 − 83 = 127 neutrons.

shortTheory.question: Why does the energy of an electron increase as we move from the first shell to the second shell?
shortTheory.answer: The second shell will also be at a definite distance from the nucleus which will, of course, be greater than the first shell and electron present in it will also possess greater value of energy.

shortTheory.question: What is the classical concept of an electron? How has this concept changed with time?
shortTheory.answer: According to this model the electron can revolve around the nucleus of the atom in specific paths called orbits or shells. According to modern approach, electrons are like charged clouds whose location around the nucleus cannot be predicted with one hundred percent certainty.

shortTheory.question: What holds the protons and neutrons together in the nucleus?
shortTheory.answer: In the nucleus these two particles are held together by a strong nuclear force.

explain.title: Atoms form bonds to become more stable
explain.body: Atoms have a tendency to decrease their energy. They can do this by combining with other atoms. This is a natural phenomenon because it increases the stability of atoms.

explain.title: The duplet and octet rule
explain.body: The textbook says: “having two electrons (for hydrogen and helium which have only the first shell) or eight electrons in the outermost shell meant stability and hence unreactivity as well. This principle was named as Duplet or Octet Rule.”

explain.title: Atoms can take an easier path
explain.body: An atom may lose or gain electrons to complete a duplet or octet. The textbook’s example is sodium: it is easier for sodium to lose one electron than to gain seven.

explain.title: Hydrogen can gain or lose one electron
explain.body: The textbook explains that hydrogen can lose one electron to become H⁺ or gain one electron to become H⁻; gaining one electron completes its duplet.

mistakes: Saying sodium gains seven electrons instead of stating that it loses one electron along the energetically easier path.

yourTurn.question: How covalent bond is different from an ionic bond?
solution: A covalent bond is formed by the mutual sharing of an electron pair provided by the bonded atoms.
An ionic bond is formed by the complete transference of electron or electrons from one atom to another atom.

explain.title: What is a chemical bond?
explain.body: A chemical bond is a force of attraction between atoms which holds them together in the form of a molecule or a compound.

explain.title: Ionic bonds form by electron transfer
explain.body: An ionic bond is formed when atoms lose or gain electron(s) to acquire the electronic configuration of the nearest noble gas. The resulting oppositely charged ions are held together by electrostatic attraction.

explain.title: Covalent bonds form by sharing
explain.body: A covalent bond is a bond formed by the mutual sharing of an electron pair provided by the bonded atoms. One shared pair makes a single bond; two and three shared pairs make double and triple bonds.

explain.title: Coordinate covalent bonds have one donor
explain.body: Coordinate covalent bond is a type of covalent bond in which the shared electron pair is donated by one atom only. The donating species is the donor and the accepting species is the acceptor. An arrow points towards the acceptor.

explain.title: Polar and non-polar covalent bonds
explain.body: When a covalent bond is formed between two identical atoms, the shared pair lies midway between them and the bond is non-polar. Between non-identical atoms, the shared pair bends towards the more electronegative atom, making the bond polar.

mistakes: Do not describe an ionic bond as sharing electrons; it forms by complete transfer of electron(s).
Do not say that the whole ionic compound is one positive or negative ion; it contains oppositely charged ions.
Do not reverse the direction of a coordinate-bond arrow; it points towards the acceptor.
Do not confuse a double bond (=) with a triple bond (≡).
Do not say the two electrons in a coordinate shared pair come from different atoms; both are donated by one atom.
When explaining a polar covalent bond, state that the shared pair bends towards the more electronegative atom.

explain.title: The metallic bond
explain.body: A metallic bond, is therefore a type of chemical bond which has positively charged ions bound together by the mobile electrons. In a metal, the outer electrons move freely between spaces among atoms instead of staying attached to one particular nucleus.

explain.title: The strength of a metallic bond
explain.body: The strength of a metallic bond depends upon two factors: the number of positive charges present on the positive ions and the number of mobile electrons set free by each atom. Magnesium releases two electrons per atom, so its metallic bond is stronger than sodium's, where each atom sets free one electron.

explain.title: Conductivity
explain.body: The presence of freely moving electrons in metals makes them good conductor of heat and electricity. The mobile electrons can move through the metal.

explain.title: Hardness and changing shape
explain.body: In metals, the atoms are strongly held and arranged in the form of rows one above the other. This arrangement makes them hard and heavy. When pressure is applied, the upper rows of atoms slip pass the lower rows, changing the shape of the metal. Metals can therefore be drawn into wires and sheets.

mistakes: Do not say that the mobile electrons are attached to just one particular nucleus; the section describes them as moving freely among the atoms.

explain.title: Alkali metals
explain.body: Alkali metals (Na, K) are highly electropositive elements and thus they undergo reactions very easily. Sodium and potassium react vigorously with water and halogens to give their respective hydroxides and halides. They also react with acids to give salts and hydrogen.

explain.title: Alkaline earth metals

explain.title: Aluminium

example.question: Compare the properties of ionic and covalent compounds.
example.answer: Ionic compounds have oppositely charged ions arranged in a crystalline structure and usually have high melting and boiling points. They are generally soluble in polar solvents and conduct electricity when molten or in solution because they have free ions. Covalent compounds mostly exist as discrete neutral molecules, generally have lower melting and boiling points, are usually insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar solvents, and are usually bad conductors.

explain.title: Ionic compounds
explain.body: In ionic compounds oppositely charged ions are properly arranged to give a crystalline structure. As a whole the compound is neutral. There exists a strong electrostatic force between their ions. Ionic compounds are usually solids with high melting and boiling points. They are generally soluble in polar solvents like water and conduct electricity when molten or in solution because free ions are present.

explain.title: Covalent compounds
explain.body: Covalent compounds mostly exist as discrete neutral molecules. There exists a strong electrostatic attraction between the nuclei and the shared electrons. Lower molecular mass covalent compounds are gases or low-boiling liquids, while high molecular mass covalent compounds exist as solids. They generally have lower melting and boiling points, are usually insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar solvents, and are usually bad conductors of electricity.

explain.title: Use the particle explanation
explain.body: When explaining a property, connect it to the particles. For example, ionic compounds conduct electricity in the molten state or in solution because they contain free ions. Do not confuse this with solid ionic compounds, where the ions are held in the crystal arrangement.

mistakes: Saying ionic compounds conduct electricity as solids; the section says they conduct when molten or in solution.

Claiming that every covalent compound is a gas or liquid; high molecular mass covalent compounds can be solids.
Reversing the usual solubility patterns: ionic compounds are generally soluble in polar solvents, while covalent compounds are usually soluble in non-polar solvents.
Writing only one side of a comparison question instead of comparing both ionic and covalent compounds.

example.question: Explain how HCl molecules attract each other by dipole-dipole forces.
example.answer: Chlorine attracts the shared electron pair more strongly than hydrogen, making HCl polar (Hδ⁺ × Clδ⁻). The partial charges cause neighbouring HCl molecules to attract by dipole-dipole forces.

explain.title: What are intermolecular forces?
explain.body: The forces of attraction which are present between the molecules of elements and compounds are named as intermolecular forces of attraction. These attractive forces are generally very weak as compared to the bonding forces present between the atoms of substances. Among the three states of matter, these forces are the weakest among the molecules of the gases and the strongest among the molecules of solids.

explain.title: Why their strength matters
explain.body: Intermolecular forces affect physical properties. The stronger the forces among the molecules of a liquid, the higher its boiling point; stronger intermolecular forces also give a solid a higher melting point.

explain.title: Dipole-dipole forces
explain.body: These attractive forces are present between the molecules of a polar compound like HCl. In HCl, chlorine attracts the shared pair of electrons more strongly than hydrogen, making the bond polar. The partial charges cause HCl molecules to attract each other; these are dipole-dipole forces.

explain.title: Hydrogen bonding
explain.body: Hydrogen bonding is a special case of dipole-dipole attractive forces. When hydrogen is covalent bonded to highly electronegative elements like F, O or N then the large difference of electronegativity values will make the covalent bond highly polar. Strong dipole-dipole attractions are then observed among the molecules. Water molecules form hydrogen bonds, helping explain water's relatively high melting and boiling points.

mistakes: Do not confuse intermolecular forces between molecules with covalent bonds within a molecule.
Do not call every dipole-dipole attraction hydrogen bonding; hydrogen bonding is the special case involving hydrogen bonded to F, O or N.
When explaining a higher boiling point, state that stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to overcome.
Do not say that boiling normally breaks the covalent bonds within the molecules.

explain.title: Ionic solids and their lattice
explain.body: Oppositely charged ions attract strongly and form a crystal lattice. The ions are held in fixed positions, so ionic compounds are stable solids with high melting points. If a force shifts the lattice, it can break, which is why ionic solids are brittle. Because the ions are spherical and can surround one another from all sides, ionic bonds are non-directional.

explain.title: Conductivity and hydration
explain.body: Solid ionic compounds do not conduct electricity because their ions cannot move. When molten, or dissolved in water, the ions can move and carry charge. During hydration, water molecules surround and interact with ions. In aqueous reactions, ions from different compounds can combine to form a new compound, sometimes as a precipitate.

explain.title: Covalent substances and their properties
explain.body: Many low molecular mass covalent substances have weak forces between their molecules, so they are gases or low-boiling liquids. In carbon solids, structure matters: diamond has a rigid network of strongly bonded carbon atoms, while graphite has layers that can slip past one another. Mobile electrons between graphite's layers let it conduct electricity.

explain.title: Water and molecular attractions
explain.body: The section states that liquid water has a high boiling point because strong intermolecular forces are present between its molecules. This is why the strength of attractions between molecules is important when explaining the physical states and boiling points of covalent substances.

mistakes: Saying that solid ionic compounds conduct electricity: in a solid lattice, the ions cannot move.
Forgetting that ionic compounds can conduct when molten or in aqueous solution because their ions are then free to move.
Calling the ionic lattice a molecule instead of an arrangement of ions.
Explaining graphite's conductivity only by saying it has layers; include its mobile electrons between the layers.
Confusing the strong covalent bonds within a substance with the intermolecular forces between covalent molecules.
Forgetting to identify the precipitate when describing an aqueous ionic reaction.

example.question: Explain the formation of an ionic bond and a covalent bond.
example.answer: An ionic bond forms by electron transfer and attraction between oppositely charged ions. A covalent bond forms when atoms share electron pair(s).

explain.title: Four kinds of bonding
explain.body: Ionic bonding involves electron transfer and attraction between oppositely charged ions. Covalent bonding involves shared electron pairs. In a coordinate covalent bond, one atom supplies both electrons in the shared pair. Metallic bonding is the attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.

explain.title: Intermolecular forces affect boiling points
explain.body: Small covalent molecules are often gases or low-boiling liquids because the forces between their molecules are weak. Stronger intermolecular attractions need more energy to overcome. Hydrogen bonding helps explain the high boiling points of water and HF.

explain.title: Ionic and covalent substances have different properties
explain.body: Ionic solids have ions arranged in a lattice and usually have high melting points. They conduct electricity when their ions can move, such as when molten or dissolved. Simple covalent molecules generally do not conduct electricity and often have low melting and boiling points.

explain.title: Metals and graphite conduct electricity
explain.body: Metals conduct because their delocalised electrons can move through the structure. In graphite, each carbon atom bonds to three others, leaving electrons free to move along the layers and carry charge.

explain.title: Structures can be simple molecules or giant networks
explain.body: NaCl forms a regular ionic lattice, while silica (SiO₂) forms a giant covalent network. Graphite is made of layers of covalently bonded carbon atoms. These large-scale arrangements help explain hardness, conductivity and melting behaviour.

mistakes: Do not confuse the bonds within a molecule with forces between molecules; boiling a simple molecular substance usually separates molecules, not atoms within them.
Do not say that an ionic solid conducts electricity while its ions are fixed in place; mobile ions are needed for conduction.
Do not say covalent compounds are always insoluble or that every ionic compound is soluble; use the general trend asked for in the question.
When explaining metallic properties, mention the role of mobile electrons and the non-directional metallic bond, not just that metals are strong.
For a precipitate reaction, identify the insoluble product and state the observation clearly.
In a comparison, discuss both substances and use the same property for each side.

solutions.question: What type of elements lose their outer electron easily and what type of elements gain electron easily?
steps: Metals lose their outermost electrons easily.
Non-metals gain electrons easily.
solutions.answer: Metals lose outer electrons easily, while non-metals gain electrons easily.

solutions.question: Why do lower molecular mass covalent compounds exist as gases or low boiling liquids.
steps: Lower molecular mass covalent compounds have weak forces of attraction between their molecules.
Only a small amount of energy is needed to overcome these forces, so they exist as gases or low-boiling liquids.
solutions.answer: Weak intermolecular forces make lower molecular mass covalent compounds gases or low-boiling liquids.

solutions.question: Give one example of an element which exists as a crystalline solid and it has covalent bonds between its atoms.
steps: Diamond is an element that exists as a crystalline solid.
Its carbon atoms are joined by covalent bonds.
solutions.answer: Diamond is a crystalline solid with covalent bonds between its carbon atoms.

solutions.question: Which property of metals makes them malleable and ductile?
steps: The layers of metal atoms can slide over one another when a force is applied.
This property makes metals malleable and ductile.
solutions.answer: The ability of layers of metal atoms to slide over one another makes metals malleable and ductile.

solutions.question: Is coordinate covalent bond a strong bond?
steps: Yes. A coordinate covalent bond, once formed, is as strong as an ordinary covalent bond.
solutions.answer: Yes, a coordinate covalent bond is as strong as an ordinary covalent bond.

solutions.question: Write down dot and cross formula of HNO₃.
steps: Draw nitrogen as the central atom, joined to three oxygen atoms; join one of these oxygen atoms to hydrogen.
Show one N=O double bond and single bonds from N to the other two oxygen atoms.
Use dots for oxygen electrons and crosses for nitrogen and hydrogen electrons. Show each covalent bond as a shared (×•) pair.
Show two lone pairs on the oxygen in O—H, two lone pairs on the double-bonded oxygen, and three lone pairs on the singly bonded oxygen.
Mark the central nitrogen N⁺ and the singly bonded terminal oxygen O⁻.
solutions.answer: Dot-and-cross formula of HNO₃ shown in the figure.
solutions.figure:
Key: • = electron from oxygen; × = electron from nitrogen or hydrogen. Each (×•) is a shared pair.

                     O(••)(••)
                    (×•)(×•)
                         ║
H—(×•)—O(••)(••)—(×•)—N⁺—(×•)—O⁻(••)(••)(••)

This shows HNO₃ with one N=O double bond, one N—O—H bond and one N—O⁻ bond. The double bond may be shown on either of the two oxygen atoms not bonded to hydrogen (resonance).

solutions.question: Why HF is a liquid while HCl is a gas?
steps: HF molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another because fluorine is highly electronegative.
These intermolecular attractions are strong, so more energy is needed to separate HF molecules.
HCl molecules do not form hydrogen bonds and have weaker intermolecular attractions; therefore, HCl is a gas while HF is a liquid.
solutions.answer: Hydrogen bonding between HF molecules makes HF a liquid, while HCl has weaker intermolecular forces and is a gas.

solutions.question: Why covalent compounds are generally not soluble in water?
steps: Water is a polar solvent, whereas most covalent compounds are non-polar.
Because of this difference, most covalent compounds do not dissolve in water.
solutions.answer: Most covalent compounds are non-polar, so they are generally not soluble in polar water.

solutions.question: How do metals conduct heat?
steps: Metals contain free electrons that can move throughout the metal.
When heated, these electrons gain energy and transfer it rapidly to other electrons and metal particles.
In this way, heat travels through the metal.
solutions.answer: Metals conduct heat through the movement of free electrons.

solutions.question: How many oxides does nitrogen form. Write down the formulae of oxides?
steps: Nitrogen forms five oxides.
Their formulae are N₂O, NO, N₂O₃, NO₂ and N₂O₅.
solutions.answer: Nitrogen forms five oxides: N₂O, NO, N₂O₃, NO₂ and N₂O₅.

solutions.question: What will happen if NaBr is treated with AgNO₃ in water?
steps: A double displacement reaction takes place when aqueous sodium bromide is treated with aqueous silver nitrate.
Silver bromide is formed as a pale yellow precipitate, while sodium nitrate remains in solution.
NaBr(aq) + AgNO₃(aq) → AgBr(s) ↓ + NaNO₃(aq)
solutions.answer: A pale yellow precipitate of AgBr forms.

solutions.question: Why does iodine exist as a solid while Cl₂ exist as a gas?
steps: Iodine molecules (I₂) are larger and have more electrons than chlorine molecules (Cl₂).
The forces of attraction between iodine molecules are stronger than those between chlorine molecules.
More energy is needed to overcome these forces in iodine, so iodine is a solid at room temperature, whereas chlorine is a gas.
solutions.answer: Iodine is solid because its larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces than Cl₂ molecules.

solutions.question: Explain the formation of an ionic bond and a covalent bond.
steps: An ionic bond is formed by the complete transfer of one or more electrons from one atom to another.
The atom that loses electrons forms a positive ion, while the atom that gains electrons forms a negative ion.
The electrostatic force of attraction between these oppositely charged ions is called an ionic bond. For example, sodium transfers an electron to chlorine to form Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in NaCl.
A covalent bond is formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
For example, two chlorine atoms share a pair of electrons to form a Cl₂ molecule.
solutions.answer: An ionic bond forms by electron transfer and attraction between oppositely charged ions; a covalent bond forms by sharing electron pairs.

solutions.question: How do ions arrange themselve to form NaCl crystal.
steps: NaCl crystal consists of a regular, three-dimensional arrangement of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
The ions alternate so that each Na⁺ ion is surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions and each Cl⁻ ion is surrounded by six Na⁺ ions.
The oppositely charged ions are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction.
solutions.answer: In a NaCl crystal, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are arranged alternately in a three-dimensional lattice, with each ion surrounded by six ions of opposite charge.
solutions.figure: Draw a regular arrangement of alternating Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in a three-dimensional cubic lattice. Show each Na⁺ ion surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions and each Cl⁻ ion surrounded by six Na⁺ ions. Label the ions and indicate that the oppositely charged ions are held together by electrostatic attraction.

solutions.question: Explain the properties of metals keeping in view the nature of metallic bond.
steps: Metals consist of positive metal ions arranged in a regular pattern, surrounded by a sea of mobile, delocalised electrons.
The strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons is called the metallic bond.
A large amount of energy is needed to overcome these strong metallic bonds; therefore, metals generally have high melting and boiling points.
The mobile electrons carry charge through the metal, so metals conduct electricity.
The mobile electrons also transfer thermal energy, so metals conduct heat.
When layers of positive ions slide past one another, the sea of electrons continues to hold the ions together; therefore, metals are malleable and ductile.
Metals are lustrous because their mobile electrons reflect light.
solutions.answer: Metallic bonding gives metals high melting and boiling points, electrical and thermal conductivity, malleability, ductility and lustre.

solutions.question: Compare the properties of ionic and covalent compounds.
steps: Ionic compounds consist of positive and negative ions held together by strong electrostatic forces; covalent compounds consist of molecules in which atoms share electron pairs.
Ionic compounds are usually crystalline solids with high melting and boiling points; covalent compounds generally have lower melting and boiling points and may be gases, liquids or solids.
Ionic compounds are generally soluble in water and insoluble in organic solvents; covalent compounds are generally insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.
Ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, but not in the solid state because their ions cannot move freely.
Covalent compounds generally do not conduct electricity because they do not contain mobile ions or free electrons.
solutions.answer: Ionic compounds have ionic lattices, usually high melting points, and conduct electricity when molten or in solution; covalent compounds consist of molecules, usually have lower melting points, and generally do not conduct electricity.

solutions.question: How will you explain the electrical conductivity of graphite crystals?
steps: In graphite, each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three other carbon atoms in flat layers.
The fourth valence electron of each carbon atom is free to move through the layers.
These mobile electrons carry electric charge, so graphite conducts electricity.
solutions.answer: Graphite conducts electricity because it has mobile electrons that can carry electric charge.

solutions.question: Why are metals usually hard and heavy?
steps: Metal atoms are closely packed together in a regular arrangement.
The strong forces of attraction between the metal ions and the sea of mobile electrons hold the atoms firmly together, making metals usually hard.
The close packing of their particles gives metals high density, so they are usually heavy.
solutions.answer: Metals are usually hard and heavy because their particles are closely packed and held together by strong metallic bonding.

solutions.question: The formula of AlCl₃ in vapour phase is Al₂Cl₆ which means it exists as a dimer. Explain the bonding between its two molecules?
steps: In AlCl₃, the aluminium atom is electron-deficient and can accept a lone pair of electrons.
A chlorine atom of one AlCl₃ molecule donates a lone pair to the aluminium atom of another AlCl₃ molecule.
This forms a coordinate covalent bond; two chlorine atoms form such bonds between the molecules.
Thus, two AlCl₃ molecules join to form the dimer Al₂Cl₆.
solutions.answer: Two AlCl₃ molecules form Al₂Cl₆ by coordinate covalent bonds in which chlorine atoms donate lone pairs to electron-deficient aluminium atoms.

solutions.question: Explain the structure of sand (SiO₂).
steps: Draw a silicon atom in the centre of a tetrahedral arrangement, surrounded by four oxygen atoms.
Join each silicon atom to its four oxygen atoms with covalent bonds.
Show each oxygen atom also bonded to another silicon atom, linking neighbouring tetrahedra throughout the structure.
Continue the pattern in all directions to represent the giant covalent structure of sand (SiO₂).
solutions.answer: Sand (SiO₂) has a giant three-dimensional covalent structure in which each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms, and each oxygen atom links two silicon atoms.
solutions.figure: A giant three-dimensional network of silicon and oxygen atoms, with each silicon atom bonded to four oxygen atoms and each oxygen atom linking two silicon atoms.

definitions.text: This gave rise to a principle that having two electrons (for hydrogen and helium which have only the first shell) or eight electrons in the outermost shell meant stability and hence unreactivity as well. This principle was named as Duplet or Octet Rule.
A chemical bond is a force of attraction between atoms which holds them together in the form of a molecule or a compound.

These oppositely charged ions are then held together by the electrostatic force of attraction. The chemical bond, thus formed, is called an Ionic or an Electrovalent Bond and the compounds having such a bond are called ionic compounds.
An ionic bond is therefore a bond which is formed by the complete transference of electron or electrons from one atom to another atom.
A covalent bond is therefore a bond formed by the mutual sharing of an electron pair provided by the bonded atoms. This is called a single covalent bond.
Coordinate covalent bond is a type of covalent bond in which the shared electron pair is donated by one atom only.
A metallic bond, is therefore a type of chemical bond which has positively charged ions bound together by the mobile electrons.
Metals generally have a tendency to lose electrons to form positive ions called cations. This property is called the electropositive character of metals.
Non-metals have an affinity towards electrons. They tend to gain electrons and become negatively charged ions called anions. They are therefore, named as electronegative elements.
The forces of attraction which are present between the molecules of elements and compounds are named as intermolecular forces of attraction.
Due to these partial charges the molecules of HCl start attracting each other. These forces of attraction are called dipole-dipole forces.
This attractive force present between the molecules of water is called Hydrogen Bonding.
