explain.title: Carbon compounds are numerous
explain.body: Carbon forms strong covalent bonds with itself and other elements. It can make chains, branches and rings, so a very large number of organic compounds exist.

explain.title: Alkanes and their reactions
explain.body: Alkanes have carbon–carbon single bonds. They are relatively unreactive, but undergo combustion, substitution (such as halogenation) and cracking. They do not normally undergo addition.

explain.title: Combustion and safety
explain.body: Complete combustion of hydrocarbons produces carbon dioxide and water and releases heat. Natural gas mixed with air can be explosive if ignited, so leaks need immediate safe attention.

explain.title: Names and properties
explain.body: For an alkane name, select the longest chain, number it from the nearer end to a branch, and name the substituents. As alkane size generally increases, melting and boiling points rise; among isomers, branching usually lowers boiling point.

mistakes: Do not say that addition is a normal reaction of alkanes; addition is characteristic of unsaturated hydrocarbons.
Do not confuse cracking, which breaks hydrocarbons into smaller molecules, with halogenation.
When naming a branched alkane, number from the end nearest the substituent and include its position number.
For complete combustion of propane, do not leave the oxygen coefficient unbalanced: it is 5O₂.
Do not claim organic compounds are all soluble in water; most are generally non-polar and do not dissolve well in polar water.
When comparing n-butane and iso-butane, remember that n-butane has the higher boiling point.

recap.question: What are the two important reactions of alkanes described in this section?
recap.answer: Combustion forms carbon dioxide and water, and releases heat.

recap.question: Why do alkanes show little chemical reactivity towards many laboratory reagents?
recap.answer: The carbon–hydrogen bonds are almost non-polar.

solutions.question: Differentiate between an organic and an inorganic compound.
steps: Organic compounds are compounds of carbon, usually containing carbon–hydrogen bonds; examples are methane (CH₄) and ethanol (C₂H₅OH).
Inorganic compounds are compounds that generally do not contain carbon–hydrogen bonds; examples include water (H₂O) and sodium chloride (NaCl).
Some carbon compounds, such as carbon dioxide, carbonates and carbides, are classified as inorganic compounds.
solutions.answer: Organic compounds usually contain carbon–hydrogen bonds, whereas inorganic compounds generally do not.

solutions.question: Why are organic compounds found in large numbers?
steps: Carbon atoms bond strongly with one another, forming long chains, branched chains and rings. This property is called catenation.
Carbon is tetravalent and forms stable covalent bonds with many other elements, including hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and halogens.
Carbon atoms can form single, double and triple bonds, and many compounds show isomerism.
These properties enable carbon to form a very large number of different compounds.
solutions.answer: Catenation, tetravalency, multiple bonding and isomerism enable carbon to form a large number of organic compounds.

solutions.question: Name the products which are obtained when natural gas is oxidized under controlled conditions.
steps: Under controlled oxidation, natural gas (mainly methane) can produce methanol, formaldehyde and formic acid.
solutions.answer: Methanol, formaldehyde and formic acid.

solutions.question: How naphtha fraction is decomposed to give lower hydrocarbons?
steps: Naphtha is heated strongly, usually in the presence of a catalyst, so that its larger hydrocarbon molecules break into smaller molecules.
This process is called cracking and produces lower hydrocarbons, including alkanes and alkenes.
solutions.answer: Naphtha is cracked by strong heating, usually with a catalyst, to form lower hydrocarbons.

solutions.question: Write down the molecular formula, structural formula and the condensed structural formula for iso-butane.
steps: Molecular formula: C₄H₁₀.
Structural formula:
CH₃
CH₃—CH—CH₃
Condensed structural formula: (CH₃)₃CH.
solutions.answer: Molecular formula: C₄H₁₀; structural formula: CH₃—CH(CH₃)—CH₃; condensed structural formula: (CH₃)₃CH.

solutions.question: How are organic compounds useful for us?
steps: Organic compounds are useful as food and fuels.
They are used to make clothing fibres, medicines, plastics, dyes and perfumes.
They are also used in making many household and industrial products.
solutions.answer: Organic compounds are used in food, fuels, clothing, medicines and many everyday products.

solutions.question: Write down the names of five such organic compounds which exist naturally?
steps: Five naturally occurring organic compounds are glucose, starch, cellulose, proteins and fats.
solutions.answer: Glucose, starch, cellulose, proteins and fats.

solutions.question: Give IUPAC name to the following compound: CH₃—CH(CH₃)—CH₂—CH₃.
steps: The longest continuous carbon chain has four carbon atoms, so the parent name is butane.
Number the chain from the end nearest the branch; the methyl group is attached to carbon 2.
The IUPAC name is 2-methylbutane.
solutions.answer: 2-methylbutane.

solutions.question: How do the melting and boiling points of alkanes change when we move from lower members to higher members?
steps: The melting and boiling points of alkanes increase as we move from lower members to higher members.
Higher alkanes have greater molecular mass and stronger intermolecular forces.
solutions.answer: The melting and boiling points of alkanes generally increase from lower members to higher members.

solutions.question: Why do alkanes show little reactivity towards the other reagents?
steps: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons containing strong covalent bonds between carbon and hydrogen atoms.
They are non-polar and have no reactive functional group, so they show little reactivity towards other reagents.
solutions.answer: Alkanes are relatively unreactive because they contain strong covalent bonds and have no reactive functional group.

solutions.question: Why does a mixture of natural gas and air explode?
steps: Natural gas mixes with oxygen in air to form a combustible mixture.
When ignited, the mixture burns very rapidly and releases a large amount of heat.
The rapid expansion of hot gases causes an explosion.
solutions.answer: A mixture of natural gas and air explodes because it burns rapidly, releasing heat and expanding gases.

solutions.question: How do you compare the melting and boiling points of inorganic and organic compounds?
steps: Inorganic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points because many are ionic and have strong forces between their ions.
Organic compounds generally have low melting and boiling points because most are molecular covalent compounds with weak intermolecular forces.
solutions.answer: Inorganic compounds generally have higher melting and boiling points than organic compounds.

solutions.question: Reactions of alkanes with chlorine takes place in the presence of sunlight. What is the role of sunlight in the reaction?
steps: Sunlight provides energy to break chlorine molecules into chlorine atoms.
These chlorine atoms initiate the substitution reaction with alkanes.
solutions.answer: Sunlight initiates the reaction by breaking chlorine molecules into chlorine atoms.

solutions.question: How do you compare the boiling point of n – butane with that of iso – butane?
steps: The boiling point of n-butane is higher than that of iso-butane.
The straight-chain molecules of n-butane have a larger surface area of contact than the branched molecules of iso-butane.
Therefore, the intermolecular forces between n-butane molecules are stronger.
solutions.answer: n-Butane has a higher boiling point than iso-butane.

solutions.question: Why are organic compounds not generally soluble in water?
steps: Most organic compounds are non-polar, whereas water is a polar solvent.
Organic compounds do not form strong attractions or hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
Therefore, they are generally not soluble in water.
solutions.answer: Organic compounds are generally insoluble in water because they are non-polar, while water is polar.

solutions.question: Describe the importance of organic compounds in daily life.
steps: Organic compounds are essential for life; carbohydrates, proteins, fats and vitamins are important components of living organisms and food.
They are used as fuels, for example natural gas, petrol and diesel.
They are used to make medicines, plastics, synthetic fibres, detergents, dyes, paints and cosmetics.
Many materials used for clothing, shelter and other daily needs are made from organic compounds.
solutions.answer: Organic compounds are important in food, fuels, medicines and many materials used in daily life.

solutions.question: Why is carbon so important as an element that the whole branch of chemistry is based on it?
steps: Carbon is important because it forms a very large number of compounds.
A carbon atom is tetravalent, so it can form four covalent bonds with other atoms.
Carbon atoms also form strong bonds with one another, making chains, branched chains and rings. This property is called catenation.
Because of these properties, carbon compounds are numerous and are studied in the branch of chemistry called organic chemistry.
solutions.answer: Carbon’s tetravalency and catenation enable it to form a vast number of compounds, which are studied in organic chemistry.

solutions.question: A carbon–carbon single bond (C – C) in alkanes does not behave as a functional group but a carbon carbon double bond (C = C) in alkenes does. Explain.
steps: A carbon–carbon single bond is relatively less reactive and is present in saturated hydrocarbons called alkanes.
The C–C single bond does not usually take part in characteristic reactions, so it is not considered a functional group.
A carbon–carbon double bond is more reactive and is present in unsaturated hydrocarbons called alkenes.
The double bond takes part in characteristic addition reactions and determines the chemical properties of alkenes; therefore, it is a functional group.
solutions.answer: The reactive C=C bond gives alkenes their characteristic reactions, whereas the less reactive C–C bond in alkanes does not act as a functional group.

solutions.question: Explain IUPAC system of nomenclature for alkanes.
How combustion reaction of alkanes is useful for us?
steps: Alkanes burn in oxygen and produce carbon dioxide and water, releasing heat and light energy.
This energy is used for cooking, heating and running engines and industrial processes.
For example: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + heat.
solutions.answer: Combustion of alkanes releases useful heat energy, so alkanes are used as fuels.

solutions.question: When natural gas valve is kept open in the kitchen, the gas spreads through the whole kitchen. This may cause an explosion. What is the reason of this explosion and how can you avoid it?
steps: Natural gas mixes with air and spreads through the kitchen when a valve is left open.
The gas–air mixture is highly inflammable; a spark or flame can ignite it and cause an explosion.
To avoid this, close the gas valve immediately and open doors and windows to ventilate the kitchen.
Do not light a match or operate electrical switches until the gas has dispersed.
solutions.answer: Gas mixed with air can explode if ignited; close the valve, ventilate the kitchen and avoid flames or electrical switches.

solutions.question: “Neem” is a common tree grown throughout our country. Comment on the medicinal benefits of this tree.
steps: Neem is a medicinal tree whose different parts are used in traditional remedies.
Neem leaves and bark are used for their antiseptic properties and in treating skin problems.
Neem is also used in products for dental care, and neem oil is used to help repel insects.
solutions.answer: Neem leaves, bark and oil are used in traditional remedies, antiseptic preparations, dental care and insect repellents.

solutions.question: Name a few popular medicines which are, in fact, organic compounds?
steps: Many medicines are organic compounds.
Examples include aspirin, paracetamol, penicillin, quinine and morphine.
solutions.answer: Examples of medicines that are organic compounds are aspirin, paracetamol, penicillin, quinine and morphine.

definitions.text: This fact has led us to define organic chemistry as the chemistry of carbon compounds.
The self-linking property of carbon is called catenation and due to this it forms long, straight and branched chains and rings.
Compounds in which carbon forms single bond with other atoms are called saturated compounds.
A structural formula thus shows the symbols for the atoms present in the compounds connected by short lines which represent the bonds present in them.
The family of hydrocarbons constitutes a very large number of simple organic compounds containing carbon and hydrogen only.
Alkanes are the simplest family of hydrocarbons with only carbon – carbon and carbon – hydrogen single bond.
The International Union of Pure & Applied Chemistry has devised a systematic way of naming organic compounds called IUPAC nomenclature.
Cracking is the name of a process in which hydrocarbons with higher molecular masses (which are lesser in demand) are broken up into smaller hydrocarbons which are more in demand.
An addition reaction occurs when hydrogen (H₂) is added to an unsaturated compound.
The reactions which involve the replacement of hydrogen of alkanes by an atom or a group of atoms like halogen are called substitution reactions.
Since these substitution reactions are carried out in the presence of UV light, these are called photochemical substitution reactions.
Alkanes burn in oxygen or air to form CO₂ and H₂O with the evolution of large amount of heat. The reaction is called combustion.

fullMarks: For an explanation, begin with the key definition or main idea, then give the reason in a clear sequence—for example, explain the nearly equal sharing of electrons before concluding that alkane bonds are almost non-polar.

For IUPAC naming, identify the longest continuous carbon chain first, choose its root, identify the class and suffix, name any branch as a prefix, and number the chain from the end nearest the branch.
For preparation and reaction questions, write the complete equation, balance it, and show required conditions above or below the arrow, such as Ni and heat or UV light.
For substitution questions, state that a hydrogen atom is replaced, name the product, and mention UV light when the reaction is photochemical.
For combustion questions, show that the products are CO₂ and H₂O and include heat; check that the numbers of each type of atom balance on both sides.
When asked for molecular, structural, and condensed structural formulas, label each one separately and draw every bond and branch clearly.
In comparison or usefulness questions, answer every part of the prompt and give specific examples from the chapter, such as fuels, plastics, medicines, synthetic fibres, or biomolecules.
mistakes: Mistake: Calling every carbon compound organic. Fix: Remember that carbonates, cyanides, carbides, cyanates, and oxides of carbon are classified as inorganic in this chapter.
Mistake: Describing alkanes as unsaturated. Fix: Alkanes have only single carbon–carbon and carbon–hydrogen bonds, so they are saturated hydrocarbons.
Mistake: Numbering a branched alkane from the end farthest from its branch. Fix: Number the longest chain from the end closest to the branch.
Mistake: Forgetting the UV-light condition in methane chlorination. Fix: Show hν or state that the substitution is carried out in UV light.
Mistake: Writing unbalanced combustion or hydrogenation equations. Fix: Count each type of atom on both sides and balance the equation before finishing.
Mistake: Saying cracking simply burns naphtha. Fix: State that high temperature and zeolite break larger hydrocarbons into smaller hydrocarbons.
Mistake: Giving only one formula when asked for all three forms of iso-butane. Fix: Label its molecular formula, structural formula, and condensed structural formula separately.

shortTheory.question: Define alkanes.
shortTheory.answer: Alkanes are the simplest family of hydrocarbons with only carbon – carbon and carbon – hydrogen single bond.

shortTheory.question: What is cracking?
shortTheory.answer: Cracking is the name of a process in which hydrocarbons with higher molecular masses (which are lesser in demand) are broken up into smaller hydrocarbons which are more in demand.

shortTheory.question: What is a substitution reaction?
shortTheory.answer: The reactions which involve the replacement of hydrogen of alkanes by an atom or a group of atoms like halogen are called substitution reactions.

shortTheory.question: What is an addition reaction?
shortTheory.answer: An addition reaction occurs when hydrogen (H₂) is added to an unsaturated compound.

shortTheory.question: Why do alkanes show little reactivity towards other reagents?
shortTheory.answer: The unreactivity of alkanes may be explained on the basis of the non-polarity of the bonds present in them. The electronegativity values of carbon (2.6) and hydrogen (2.1) do not differ appreciably and the bonding electrons between C – H and C – C bonds, are almost equally shared. This fact makes alkanes almost non-polar.

shortTheory.question: What is combustion?
shortTheory.answer: Alkanes burn in oxygen or air to form CO₂ and H₂O with the evolution of large amount of heat. The reaction is called combustion.

Their units are interrelated, so one unit can be derived from other units without conversion factors.
Therefore, SI units make scientific communication easier.

explain.title: Why scientists use SI units
explain.body: SI units are standard units used internationally. They make it easier for scientists to share, compare and verify measurements. The system is based on 10, so conversions are convenient.

explain.title: Five base units used in chemistry
explain.body: The five are metre (m) for length, second (s) for time, mole (mol) for amount of substance, kilogram (kg) for mass and kelvin (K) for temperature.

explain.title: Derived units and prefixes
explain.body: Derived units are formed from base units. The section lists volume in m³, density in kg m⁻³ and area in m². Prefixes show multiples or fractions of a unit: kilo means 10³, deci 10⁻¹ and milli 10⁻³.

explain.title: Practical laboratory units
explain.body: Chemistry often deals with small quantities, so grams are manageable for mass and cubic centimetres (cm³) are practical for small volumes. Celsius is often convenient for temperature; the section gives K = °C + 273 for conversion to kelvin.

mistakes: Writing Kg or KG instead of kg; symbols have the correct capitalisation and are not pluralised.
Mixing up base units and derived units, such as calling m³ a base unit.
Using kilogram or cubic metre automatically for small laboratory quantities instead of explaining why grams and cm³ are practical.
Giving a prefix's name but the wrong power of ten, especially confusing milli (10⁻³), micro (10⁻⁶), nano (10⁻⁹) and pico (10⁻¹²).
For Celsius-to-kelvin conversion, forgetting to add 273 or giving the answer without the unit K.

explain.title: Error in measurement
explain.body: An error may be defined as the difference between the measured value and the actual value. Errors can happen because an instrument has limitations or because of the skill of the person measuring.

explain.title: Systematic error
explain.body: “Systematic errors may be removed by adding or subtracting a constant adjustment given to each measurement.” These errors affect accuracy. For example, an instrument may deliver a volume slightly different from the volume shown by its graduations.

explain.title: Random error
explain.body: “Random error causes one measurement to differ slightly from the next measurement.” It comes from unpredictable changes, such as environmental factors or slight changes in procedure, and often determines precision.

explain.title: The goal of measurement
explain.body: Experiments aim to produce results that are both accurate and precise. Accuracy concerns the actual value; precision concerns the consistency of repeated measurements.

mistakes: Do not confuse accuracy with precision: accuracy relates to the actual value, while precision relates to agreement among repeated measurements.
Do not say that random error is removed by a constant adjustment; the section gives that correction for systematic error.
Do not describe a random error as a fixed shift; it makes one measurement differ slightly from the next.
When asked for reasons for random error, include unpredictable changes, instrument limitations, environmental factors or slight variation in procedure.

They are imprecise if they are far from one another.

explain.title: Accuracy
explain.body: Accuracy measures how close results are to the true or known value. Compare a reading with the true value to judge accuracy.

explain.title: Precision
explain.body: The closeness of two or more measurements to each other is called precision. Compare repeated readings with one another to judge precision.

explain.title: They are independent
explain.body: Precision is independent of accuracy. Repeated results may agree closely but still be far from the true value; a set of results may also be near the true value but spread apart.

explain.title: Classifying measurements
explain.body: Check two things separately: how close the readings are to the true value, and how close the readings are to each other. Then name accuracy and precision separately.

mistakes: Do not call repeated identical readings accurate unless they are also close to the true or known value.
Do not mix up the meanings: accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness among measurements.
Do not assume that an accurate result must also be precise, or that a precise result must also be accurate.
When classifying a set of readings, state both properties rather than only saying “good measurements.”

explain.title: SI is a shared measurement system
explain.body: SI units provide a common way to measure and communicate quantities. Their decimal prefixes make conversions straightforward. In Chemistry, litre and smaller units are often practical for liquid volumes and small samples.

explain.title: Base and derived units
explain.body: Basic SI units include metre (m) for length, kilogram (kg) for mass, second (s) for time, kelvin (K) for temperature and mole (mol) for amount of substance. Derived units are made by combining base units: area may be measured in m², volume in m³, and density in kg/m³.

explain.title: Accuracy and precision are different
explain.body: Accuracy tells how close a result is to the true value. Precision tells how close repeated measurements are to one another. A result can be precise without being accurate.

explain.title: Measurement errors
explain.body: A systematic error shifts results consistently, often because of instrument bias or a faulty method, and it affects accuracy. A random error varies unpredictably between readings. Calibration, checking zero and using a suitable technique can reduce systematic errors.

explain.title: Standard units support reliable work
explain.body: Using the same units helps people compare results, share measurements and avoid confusion. In daily life and space exploration, unit misunderstandings or conversion errors can cause serious problems.

mistakes: Do not confuse accuracy (closeness to the true value) with precision (agreement among repeated readings).
Use the correct symbol and letter case: kilogram is kg, kelvin is K, and kilo as a prefix is k.
In scientific notation, the first number must be at least 1 and less than 10; 0.000840 = 8.40 × 10⁻⁴.
Do not omit the unit from a numerical answer. Celsius-to-kelvin answers must be given in K.
Do not claim systematic errors are random: systematic errors shift readings consistently, while random errors vary unpredictably.
When explaining the benefit of SI, give a reason such as easier comparison, communication, conversion or fewer mistakes.

recap.question: A true mass is 10 g. A student gets 11.2 g every time. Are the readings precise, accurate, both, or neither?

solutions.question: What is consistency of results?
steps: The closeness of repeated measurements to one another is called consistency of results.
solutions.answer: Consistency of results means that repeated measurements are close to one another.

solutions.question: Why SI units are user friendly?
steps: SI units are based on the decimal system.
Their multiples and submultiples are expressed using powers of ten, so converting from one unit to another is easy.
solutions.answer: SI units are user friendly because their decimal system makes unit conversions easy.

solutions.question: Define systematic error and random error.
steps: A systematic error is an error that affects measurements in the same direction each time, making them consistently too high or too low.
A random error is an error that causes measurements to vary unpredictably from one measurement to another.
solutions.answer: Systematic errors affect measurements consistently in one direction, while random errors cause unpredictable variations.

solutions.question: What is reason behind a random error?
steps: Random errors are caused by unpredictable changes in measuring conditions or by limitations in the observer’s ability to make measurements.
solutions.answer: Random errors result from unpredictable variations in measuring conditions or observation.

solutions.question: Does systematic error affect the accuracy?
steps: Yes. A systematic error makes measurements consistently higher or lower than the true value, so it affects accuracy.
solutions.answer: Yes, a systematic error affects accuracy by shifting measurements away from the true value.

solutions.question: Which other systems of measurements are used apart from SI units?
steps: The other systems of measurement used are the CGS system (centimetre, gram and second) and the British Engineering system (foot, pound and second).
solutions.answer: The CGS and British Engineering systems are also used.

solutions.question: Define metre.
steps: The metre is the distance travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.
solutions.answer: One metre is the distance travelled by light in vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.

solutions.question: Mention two benefits scientists get by using SI units.
steps: SI units provide scientists throughout the world with a common, internationally accepted system of measurement.
They make it easier for scientists to communicate and compare their results without confusion.
solutions.answer: SI units give scientists a common system and make communication and comparison of results easier.

solutions.question: Compare the units in SI system with those in MKS system?
steps: MKS is a system of units based on metre for length, kilogram for mass and second for time.
SI (International System of Units) is the internationally accepted system of measurement.
SI includes the MKS units and additional base units, such as ampere, kelvin, mole and candela.
solutions.answer: MKS uses metre, kilogram and second as its basic units; SI is the international system and includes these units along with additional basic units.

solutions.question: What are five basic SI units which are used in Chemistry?
steps: The five basic SI units commonly used in Chemistry are:
Length — metre (m).
Mass — kilogram (kg).
Time — second (s).
Temperature — kelvin (K).
Amount of substance — mole (mol).
solutions.answer: The five basic SI units commonly used in Chemistry are metre, kilogram, second, kelvin and mole.

solutions.question: Explain the three units derived for the basic SI units.
steps: Area is a derived quantity: area = length × breadth; its SI unit is square metre (m²).
Volume is a derived quantity: volume = length × breadth × height; its SI unit is cubic metre (m³).
Density is a derived quantity: density = mass ÷ volume; its SI unit is kilogram per cubic metre (kg/m³).
solutions.answer: Area, volume and density have derived SI units: m², m³ and kg/m³, respectively.

solutions.question: Explain why do we prefer to use smaller units of mass and volume in Chemistry?
steps: In Chemistry, the masses and volumes of substances used in the laboratory are usually small.
Using the kilogram and cubic metre for these quantities would give inconveniently small numerical values.
Therefore, smaller units such as gram (g), milligram (mg), cubic centimetre (cm³) and millilitre (mL) are more convenient.
solutions.answer: Smaller units are preferred because the masses and volumes commonly measured in Chemistry are small and are more conveniently expressed in units such as grams and millilitres.

solutions.question: What difficulties we expect to encounter if we use different units of measurement in daily life.
steps: Using different units for the same quantity makes measurements difficult to compare.
It makes communication and the exchange of measurement results confusing.
Conversions between different units can cause mistakes and lead to incorrect results.
solutions.answer: Different units make measurements difficult to compare and communicate, and increase the chance of conversion errors.

solutions.question: What are our indigenous units of measurement of mass, volume and length?
steps: Traditional units of mass include tola, seer and maund.
Traditional units of volume include seer and pail.
Traditional units of length include inch, foot, yard and gaz.
solutions.answer: Examples of traditional units are tola, seer and maund for mass; seer and pail for volume; and inch, foot, yard and gaz for length.

solutions.question: Elaborate the difference between precision and accuracy.
steps: Accuracy is the closeness of a measured value to the true or accepted value.
Precision is the closeness of repeated measurements to one another.
A measurement may be precise without being accurate, and accurate without being highly precise.
solutions.answer: Accuracy describes closeness to the true value, whereas precision describes closeness among repeated measurements.

solutions.question: How can you avoid systematic errors in your measurements?
steps: Use a properly calibrated instrument and check it for zero error before taking a measurement.
Use the instrument correctly and read its scale at eye level to avoid parallax error.
Where possible, compare the measurement with a standard instrument or reference.
solutions.answer: Systematic errors can be reduced by calibrating instruments, checking for zero error and using and reading the instrument correctly.

solutions.question: How do taking measurements in SI units ensure safety and reliability?
steps: Using SI units provides a common, internationally accepted system of measurement.
Standard units prevent confusion and errors when measurements are recorded, communicated, or used in calculations.
Accurate and consistent measurements help people make reliable decisions and avoid accidents, especially in science, engineering, and medicine.
solutions.answer: SI units provide standard, clear measurements that reduce confusion and errors, making results more reliable and helping ensure safety.

solutions.question: Can a student be both inaccurate and imprecise in his measurements?
steps: Yes. A measurement can be both inaccurate and imprecise.
It is inaccurate when it is far from the true value.
It is imprecise when repeated measurements differ greatly from one another.
solutions.answer: Yes; measurements may be far from the true value and also vary greatly when repeated.

solutions.question: Elaborate the importance of using SI units in space exploration.
steps: Space exploration involves scientists and engineers in different countries working together.
Using the same SI units allows them to communicate measurements and use data consistently.
Consistent units are essential for calculations involving spacecraft, distances, speeds, masses, and forces.
Using SI units helps prevent conversion mistakes that could cause a spacecraft to follow the wrong path or a mission to fail.
solutions.answer: SI units provide a common measurement system for space missions, enabling consistent calculations and communication while reducing dangerous errors.

definitions.text: For the reasons mentioned above scientists have agreed to adopt standard and user-friendly units called SI or System International Units.
It is the standard unit of length. Symbol m is used for metre. Metre is the distance travelled by light in vacuum in about 300 millionth of a second.
Its symbol is kg and it is the standard unit of mass. A block is kept in France which is taken as a standard unit of mass. It is also defined as the mass of 1000 cm³ of water.
It is the standard unit of time with a symbol s. It is the time that elapses during 9,192,631,770 cycles of the radiation produced by the transition between two levels of the cesium-133 atom.

It is represented by K and it is the standard unit of temperature. It is 1/273rd of the thermodynamic temperature of the triple point of water. It is a point at which all the states of water exist at the same time.
It is the base unit of the amount of pure substance and it is denoted by mol. It is defined as having exactly 6.022 × 10²³ particles of a substance.
An error may be defined as the difference between the measured value and the actual value.

In fact, they have errors that naturally occur and these errors are called systematic errors. Systematic errors may be removed by adding or subtracting a constant adjustment given to each measurement. Systematic error affect the accuracy of the measurement.

Another type of error which a student commits during measurement is called a random error. Random error causes one measurement to differ slightly from the next measurement. It comes from unpredictable changes during an experiment.
Accuracy measures how close results are to the true or known value.
The closeness of two or more measurements to each other is called precision.
Apart from these base units, there are other quantities that are mathematically derived from these base units.

formulas.formula: Volume: m³; area: m²; density: kg m⁻³
formulas.use: Recall the SI derived units listed for volume, area and density (volume in m³; area in m²; density in kg m⁻³).
Use the kilo, deci, centi and milli prefixes to express multiples or fractions of a unit; the powers of ten are dimensionless.

fullMarks: For a question about SI, state the relevant benefit clearly: standard units make communication and data sharing easier and reduce conversions.

When listing the five chemistry base units, give each quantity with its correct unit and symbol: length—metre (m), time—second (s), amount of substance—mole (mol), mass—kilogram (kg), temperature—kelvin (K).
For a derived-unit question, show the quantity and its unit together: volume—m³, density—kg m⁻³, area—m².
For temperature conversion, write the formula first, substitute the Celsius value, and give the final answer in K. Use the textbook conversion K = °C + 273.

For an error question, distinguish the types: systematic error affects accuracy and can be adjusted by adding or subtracting a constant; random error varies between measurements and can come from unpredictable changes.

For accuracy and precision, define each separately. Accuracy is closeness to the true or known value; precision is closeness of measurements to one another. State that one does not guarantee the other.
Write unit symbols correctly and do not pluralize them: use kg, m, s and cm³, not kgs, ms or cm³s.
mistakes: Mixing up accuracy and precision. Fix: accuracy means closeness to the true value; precision means closeness of repeated measurements to one another.
Saying random errors are constant or affect every reading in the same way. Fix: random errors make readings differ unpredictably.
Saying systematic error affects precision only. Fix: systematic error affects accuracy and may be corrected by a constant adjustment.
Writing the Celsius-to-kelvin conversion backwards or giving the answer in °C. Fix: use K = °C + 273 and label the answer K.
Using the wrong base-unit symbol, such as K for kilogram or k for kelvin. Fix: kilogram is kg; kelvin is K.
Pluralizing unit symbols or changing their case. Fix: symbols stay unchanged in plural forms; write 100 mm, not 100 mms.
Listing volume, area and density with incorrect powers or units. Fix: use m³, m² and kg m⁻³ respectively.

shortTheory.question: Q12.2. Why SI units are user friendly?
shortTheory.answer: SI units use base 10, just like our number system. So, it is much easier to learn, remember and convert these units.

shortTheory.question: Q12.3. Define systematic error and random error.
shortTheory.answer: Systematic errors may be removed by adding or subtracting a constant adjustment given to each measurement. Systematic error affect the accuracy of the measurement. Another type of error which a student commits during measurement is called a random error. Random error causes one measurement to differ slightly from the next measurement.

shortTheory.question: Q12.4. What is reason behind a random error?
shortTheory.answer: It comes from unpredictable changes during an experiment. The main reasons for random errors are limitations of instruments, environmental factors and slight variation in procedure.

shortTheory.question: Q12.5. Does systematic error affect the accuracy?
shortTheory.answer: Systematic error affect the accuracy of the measurement.

shortTheory.question: Q12.7. Define metre.
shortTheory.answer: It is the standard unit of length. Symbol m is used for metre. Metre is the distance travelled by light in vacuum in about 300 millionth of a second.

shortTheory.question: Q12.8. Mention two benefits scientists get by using SI units.
shortTheory.answer: The adoption of SI units is important in all branches of science because it makes communication easy worldwide. It allows scientists to share data easily.

explain.title: Explosive and flammable hazards
explain.body: Chemicals that release pressure, gas and heat suddenly when they experience sudden shock are called explosive chemicals. Flammable chemicals or mixtures have a flashpoint around room temperature. Do not move a container you suspect may explode; keep flammable compounds away from heat.

explain.title: Corrosive hazards
explain.body: Corrosive chemicals attack living tissues. They can harm the skin, eyes and respiratory tract. Use a fume cupboard for corrosive vapours, wear splash goggles and a face shield, and add acid slowly to water when mixing concentrated acid with water.

explain.title: Toxic and reactive hazards
explain.body: A toxic chemical is a poisonous material which is capable of causing serious health problems. Work with toxic chemicals in a fume hood, keep the area well ventilated, wear protective devices, and do not work alone. Reactive chemicals can cause fires, explosions or dangerous gases if reactions are not properly performed; handle them carefully and store them separately.

explain.title: Radiation and asphyxiation hazards
explain.body: Radiation can damage tissues and organs. Keep radioactive sources shielded and avoid prolonged exposure. An asphyxiation hazard is a gas or vapour that can cause unconsciousness or death through suffocation. Use asphyxiant chemicals in well-ventilated areas and get trained help if someone inhales such a chemical.

explain.title: General laboratory care
explain.body: Know the laboratory layout and the hazards before starting work. Follow instructions, use appropriate protective equipment, do not taste chemicals, and never work alone. Waste must be disposed of according to its hazard; acids and bases are neutralized before sewer disposal.

mistakes: Adding water to concentrated acid instead of adding acid slowly to water.
Trying to move a container suspected of holding an explosive chemical.
Confusing corrosive chemicals, which attack living tissues, with toxic chemicals, which are poisonous.
Forgetting to mention the fume hood when discussing corrosive or toxic vapours.
Giving only one safety instruction when a question asks for two or more.
Saying that all laboratory waste can be poured down the drain; hazardous waste needs proper disposal.

explain.title: Laboratory safety is shared
explain.body: Everyone in the laboratory has a role in preventing accidents. Follow instructions, use common sense and tell the responsible person about hazards.

explain.title: Recognise chemical hazards
explain.body: Corrosive chemicals can destroy living tissue on contact. Toxic chemicals can poison people. Explosive and shock-sensitive substances can cause blasts, while asphyxiants can cause suffocation.

explain.title: Use warning signs and safe procedures
explain.body: Signs and bottle labels warn users about hazards and help them choose the correct precautions. Read labels before handling chemicals and keep chemicals properly stored.

explain.title: Control exposure
explain.body: Carry out reactions that produce harmful gases or vapours in a fume cupboard. Follow specific precautions for hazards such as radiation, and avoid contact with chemicals.

explain.title: Respond safely to emergencies
explain.body: Raise the alarm, alert the teacher or lab incharge, keep people away from danger and follow the emergency plan. Do not attempt a dangerous cleanup yourself.

solutions.question: Name some corrosive chemicals.
steps: Corrosive chemicals damage or burn living tissues and corrode materials.
Examples include sulphuric acid, hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide.
solutions.answer: Examples of corrosive chemicals are sulphuric acid, hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide.

solutions.question: What type of safety precautions are adopted to avoid damage due to explosive chemicals?
steps: Keep explosive chemicals away from heat, sparks and open flames.
Handle and store them carefully, following the instructions on their containers.
Use only small quantities and keep the containers properly closed.
solutions.answer: Keep explosive chemicals away from heat and flames, and handle and store them carefully according to safety instructions.

solutions.question: What type of damages can reactive chemicals cause?
steps: Reactive chemicals may react violently with other substances, water or air.
They can produce heat, fire or explosions and may release harmful gases.
These reactions can cause burns, injuries and damage to property.
solutions.answer: Reactive chemicals can cause fires, explosions, burns and injuries, and may release harmful gases.

solutions.question: Indicate two such safety instructions which are required to avoid radiation.
steps: Reduce exposure to radiation by spending as little time as possible near its source.
Use proper shielding, such as a lead screen or lead apron, and keep a safe distance from the source.
solutions.answer: Minimize the time spent near a radiation source and use proper shielding, such as lead.

solutions.question: Which chemicals can cause suffocation?
steps: Toxic or asphyxiating gases can cause suffocation.
Examples include carbon monoxide, chlorine and hydrogen sulphide.
solutions.answer: Toxic gases such as carbon monoxide, chlorine and hydrogen sulphide can cause suffocation.

solutions.question: Why signs and symbols are posted on lab. and chemical bottles?
steps: Signs and symbols identify the hazards of chemicals in the laboratory and on chemical bottles.
They warn people about the risks and indicate the precautions needed for safe handling and storage.
solutions.answer: Signs and symbols warn about chemical hazards and show the precautions needed for safe handling and storage.

solutions.question: How fire caused by chemicals should be handled?
steps: Use the correct fire extinguisher or dry sand to put out a fire caused by chemicals.
Do not use water if the burning chemical reacts with water or if the fire involves an electrical source.
Raise the alarm and follow the laboratory emergency procedure.
solutions.answer: Handle a chemical fire with a suitable fire extinguisher or dry sand, and do not use water if it is unsafe.

solutions.question: Why emergency drills are important to face emergency situations?
steps: Emergency drills teach people how to respond quickly and correctly during an emergency.
They help people follow evacuation procedures, reduce panic and prevent injuries and loss of life.
solutions.answer: Emergency drills prepare people to act safely and promptly, reducing panic and injuries during emergencies.

solutions.question: How will you handle an emergency situation caused by fire due to short circuiting?
steps: Immediately switch off the main electric supply, if it is safe to do so.
Raise the alarm and inform the teacher or laboratory attendant at once.
Use a suitable carbon dioxide or dry-powder fire extinguisher; never throw water on a fire involving electrical equipment.
Leave the laboratory by the nearest safe exit if the fire cannot be controlled.
solutions.answer: Switch off the electricity, alert the teacher, and use a suitable extinguisher; never use water on an electrical fire.

solutions.question: What type of reactions should be carried out in fume cupboard?
steps: Reactions that produce poisonous, irritating, or harmful gases and vapours should be carried out in a fume cupboard.
The fume cupboard removes these gases and vapours from the working area.
solutions.answer: Carry out reactions producing poisonous or harmful gases and vapours in a fume cupboard.

solutions.question: Put forward at least two suggestions to improve safety in the lab.
steps: Keep the laboratory clean and uncluttered, and keep aisles and exits clear.
Clearly label all chemicals and store them safely.
Wear safety goggles and a laboratory coat when required.
Keep fire-fighting equipment and first-aid supplies accessible.
solutions.answer: Keep the laboratory tidy, label and store chemicals safely, use protective equipment, and keep safety equipment accessible.

solutions.question: Can you identify warning symbols posted for radiation and asphyxiant chemicals?
steps: The radiation warning symbol is a trefoil: three black blades around a central circle, usually shown on a yellow background.
The asphyxiant warning symbol is a gas cylinder. It warns that a gas may displace oxygen and cause suffocation.
solutions.answer: Radiation: trefoil symbol; asphyxiant: gas-cylinder symbol.

solutions.question: Why sudden shock can cause some chemicals to explode?
steps: Some explosive chemicals are sensitive to shock or sudden impact.
The shock can initiate a rapid chemical reaction or decomposition.
The reaction may release heat and a large volume of gas suddenly, causing an explosion.
solutions.answer: A sudden shock can trigger rapid decomposition of a shock-sensitive explosive, releasing heat and gases and causing an explosion.

solutions.question: Explain hazards due to explosive and toxic chemicals.
steps: Explosive chemicals may explode when exposed to heat, flame, friction, or sudden shock, causing injury and damage.
Toxic chemicals can enter the body by inhalation, swallowing, or contact with the skin.
They may cause poisoning, illness, or death; toxic fumes can also harm people who breathe them.
solutions.answer: Explosive chemicals can cause damaging explosions, while toxic chemicals can poison or seriously harm the body.

solutions.question: Write down five such common safety instructions which are used to avoid all types of hazards.
steps: Read the label and warning signs before using a chemical.
Wear suitable protective equipment, such as safety goggles and a laboratory coat.
Never taste chemicals or directly smell them; waft vapours towards the nose only when instructed.
Do not eat or drink in the laboratory, and never pipette chemicals by mouth.
Keep chemicals properly labelled and follow the teacher’s instructions for handling and disposal.
solutions.answer: Read labels, wear protective equipment, do not taste or directly smell chemicals, never eat or drink in the lab, and follow instructions.

solutions.question: Explain the importance of warning signs and symbols to avoid any accident in the lab.
steps: Warning signs and symbols give information about the hazards of chemicals and equipment.
They alert students to dangers such as fire, explosion, toxicity, radiation, and suffocation.
By recognising and following these warnings, students can take suitable precautions and avoid accidents.
solutions.answer: Warning signs and symbols identify hazards and help students take precautions to prevent laboratory accidents.

solutions.question: Name some toxic chemicals. Describe the effects of spreading toxic gas in the lab.
steps: Examples of toxic chemicals are chlorine, carbon monoxide, ammonia, hydrogen sulphide, mercury compounds and cyanides.
If a toxic gas spreads in the laboratory, it may irritate the eyes and respiratory system and cause coughing and difficulty in breathing.
A high concentration of toxic gas may cause suffocation, unconsciousness or even death.
People and animals in the affected area may be seriously harmed or killed.
solutions.answer: Toxic chemicals include chlorine and carbon monoxide; toxic gases can cause irritation, breathing difficulty, suffocation and death.

solutions.question: A student has spilled over a corrosive and explosive chemical due to an accident. Which emergency measures you will take to tackle the situation.
steps: Immediately warn the teacher or laboratory in-charge and raise the alarm.
Keep everyone away from the spill and evacuate the laboratory if necessary.
Do not touch or try to clean up the chemical yourself.
Keep flames, sparks and other sources of ignition away from the spill because the chemical is explosive.
Do not add water or another chemical to the spill unless directed by trained staff.
If the chemical has contacted skin or eyes, use the safety shower or eyewash immediately and seek medical help.
Allow trained staff wearing suitable protective equipment to deal with the spill using the correct spill-control procedure.
solutions.answer: Warn the laboratory in-charge, keep people and ignition sources away, evacuate if needed, and let trained staff handle the spill; rinse any exposed skin or eyes and seek medical help.

solutions.question: A few decades ago, a tanker carrying poisonous chlorine gas leaked and the gas spread over a large area in Lahore. The accident killed a few persons as well as animals. Give some concrete proposals to avoid such an accident in future.
steps: Tanker vehicles carrying chlorine should be properly designed, leak-proof and regularly inspected and maintained.
Chlorine tanks, valves and pipelines should be tested before transport and secured properly.
Only trained and licensed drivers and trained personnel should handle the tanker.
The tanker should carry clear warning signs and emergency information, and suitable leak-detection and safety equipment should be provided.
Transport routes should be planned to avoid densely populated areas, and unnecessary stops should be avoided.
Authorities should enforce transport safety rules and prepare an emergency plan for prompt warning, evacuation and control of a leak.
solutions.answer: Use well-maintained, leak-proof tankers and enforce safe transport by trained personnel, with suitable routes, warning systems and emergency plans.

definitions.text: Warning signs are displayed when unusual hazards, hazardous materials, hazardous equipment or special conditions are expected.
Chemicals that cause a sudden release of pressure, gas and heat when they experience sudden shock are called explosive chemicals.
Flammable chemicals or mixtures are those which have a flashpoint around room temperature.
Corrosive chemicals attack living tissues when they come in contact with them.
A toxic chemical is a poisonous material which is capable of causing serious health problems.
When a person is exposed to a high dose of radiation, it can damage the functioning of tissues and organs and can cause vomiting, radiation burns, hair loss and radiation syndrome.
It is a type of hazard in which a gas or vapours can cause unconscience or death through suffocation.
While mixing concentrated acids with water, always add acid slowly to water and not vice versa.

fullMarks: Write the hazard’s exact definition first, then give suitable examples from the chapter.
For a question asking for precautions, give separate, numbered actions that directly address the hazard.
For an emergency response, write the steps in a clear order: stay calm, alert people, take the relevant safety action, and call or assist emergency staff.
When explaining a hazard sign, state what danger it warns about and what precaution the sign calls for.
For acid dilution, state the rule clearly: add acid slowly to water, never water to acid.
There are no numerical calculations or formulas in this chapter; do not add irrelevant working or units.
The supplied 2027 paper pattern lists Units 1–11 and gives no examinable exercise references for this unit, so confirm whether this chapter is included before prioritising it for the exam.
mistakes: Writing that water should be added to concentrated acid. Fix: write that acid is added slowly to water, not vice versa.
Giving only one precaution when a question asks for several. Fix: list distinct, relevant precautions in numbered points.
Confusing corrosive and toxic hazards. Fix: corrosive chemicals attack living tissues on contact; toxic chemicals are poisonous and can cause serious health problems.
Saying that all radiation exposure has the same effect. Fix: name the listed effects of high-dose exposure, such as radiation burns and damage to tissues and organs.
Forgetting to mention ventilation when describing precautions for toxic or asphyxiant chemicals. Fix: include a well-ventilated area or a fume hood where relevant.
Giving an incomplete emergency response by describing only the fire. Fix: include alerting people, using the extinguisher where appropriate, and calling or assisting emergency staff.

shortTheory.question: Define explosive chemicals.
shortTheory.answer: Chemicals that cause a sudden release of pressure, gas and heat when they experience sudden shock are called explosive chemicals.

shortTheory.question: What are flammable chemicals or mixtures?
shortTheory.answer: Flammable chemicals or mixtures are those which have a flashpoint around room temperature.

shortTheory.question: What are corrosive chemicals?
shortTheory.answer: Corrosive chemicals attack living tissues when they come in contact with them.

shortTheory.question: What is a toxic chemical?
shortTheory.answer: A toxic chemical is a poisonous material which is capable of causing serious health problems.

shortTheory.question: What is an asphyxiation hazard?
shortTheory.answer: It is a type of hazard in which a gas or vapours can cause unconscience or death through suffocation.

shortTheory.question: How should concentrated acid be mixed with water?
shortTheory.answer: While mixing concentrated acids with water, always add acid slowly to water and not vice versa.

practicals.label: Activity 7.1
practicals.bookText:
The following compounds are provided in the form of liquid or in the
form of their aqueous solutions. Use blue and red litmus paper strips to show
whether these substances are acidic or basic in their aqueous solutions.
| Substance | Acidic | Basic |
|---|---|---|
| Tap water | | |
| Battery water | | |
| Rain water | | |
| Soap solution | | |
| Tooth paste | | |
| Shampoo | | |
| Bleach | | |
EXERCISE (in-text)
In what ways are mineral acids useful for us?
procedure: Take small samples of the provided substances in separate, labelled containers.
Test each sample with a clean blue litmus paper strip and a clean red litmus paper strip.
Observe and record any colour change for each strip, then identify the substance as acidic or basic.
practicals.aim: To use blue and red litmus paper strips to determine whether the provided substances are acidic or basic in aqueous solution.

viva.question: What happens to blue litmus in an acidic solution?
What happens to red litmus in a basic solution?
What do you conclude if neither litmus strip changes colour?
viva.answer: The sample is neutral, or its acidity or basicity is too weak to show a change with litmus.

viva.question: Why should a fresh strip be used for each sample?
viva.answer: To prevent one sample from contaminating another.

viva.question: What may happen when red litmus is placed in bleach?
viva.answer: It may turn blue at first and then lose its colour as the bleach acts on the dye.

apparatus: Provided liquid samples or aqueous solutions

rows: Usually remains blue at first; may fade
May turn blue briefly, then fade or bleach

practicals.title: Testing substances with litmus paper
precautions: Use a clean dropper and separate labelled containers for the samples.
Use a fresh strip for each test and avoid touching the test area with fingers.
Do not taste or directly smell any sample.
Avoid contact with battery water and bleach; rinse any splashes on skin immediately with plenty of water.
Do not mix the samples with one another.
practicals.result: Battery water, rain water and shampoo showed acidic behaviour, while soap solution, toothpaste and bleach showed basic behaviour. Tap water showed no change with either litmus strip.

Take a few granules of zinc in a clean test tube. Add dilute H₂SO₄ in it and heat it gently. Identify the gas evolved in this reaction by taking a burning match stick near the mouth of test tube. Note the observations in your notebook.

procedure: Take a few granules of zinc in a clean test tube.

Note the observations in your notebook.

viva.question: Which gas is evolved when zinc reacts with dilute sulfuric acid?
What observation identifies hydrogen gas?
viva.answer: It burns with a characteristic ‘pop’ sound when tested with a burning match stick.

viva.question: What type of reaction occurs between zinc and dilute sulfuric acid?
What salt is formed in this reaction?
Why should the test tube be heated gently?
viva.answer: To avoid rapid reaction and splashing of the acid.

rows: Effervescence; gas burns with a ‘pop’ sound
Bubbles form; gas burns with a ‘pop’ sound

practicals.title: Identification of hydrogen from zinc and dilute sulfuric acid
precautions: Use only a few zinc granules and dilute sulfuric acid.
Hold the test tube with a holder and keep its mouth pointed away from yourself and others.
Keep the burning match stick near the mouth of the test tube, not inside it.
Wear safety goggles and avoid contact with the acid.
practicals.result: Zinc reacts with dilute sulfuric acid to evolve hydrogen gas, which burns with a ‘pop’ sound.

practicals.label: Activity 7.3
practicals.bookText:
How to clean a blocked drain?
Blocked drains are one of the most common problems that we face every other day. Different blockages require different chemicals to remove them.
One of the ways to clean the drain is to pour half a cup of sodium bicarbonate solution into the drain followed by half a cup of vinegar. Cover the drain and wait for thirty minutes. Pour boiling water down the drain.
Caustic chemical drain cleaners are capable of dissolving grease, hair, food and other common blockages. Pour down the caustic cleaner into your drain. Wait for half an hour and then flush your drain with water.
procedure: For the bicarbonate-and-vinegar method, pour half a cup of sodium bicarbonate solution into the blocked drain, followed by half a cup of vinegar.
Cover the drain and wait for thirty minutes.
Pour boiling water down the drain.
Alternatively, pour caustic chemical drain cleaner down the drain, following its label and using it only with adult supervision.
Wait for half an hour and then flush the drain with water.
Do not use the caustic cleaner together with vinegar or any other cleaner.
practicals.aim: To describe how different chemicals can be used to help clear a blocked drain.

viva.question: What gas is produced when sodium bicarbonate reacts with vinegar?
What is vinegar’s main acidic component?
What kind of substance is sodium bicarbonate?
Why should a caustic drain cleaner be handled carefully?
viva.answer: It is corrosive and can cause severe burns.

viva.question: Why should different drain cleaners not be mixed?
viva.answer: They may react dangerously and produce heat or harmful substances.

practicals.title: Cleaning a blocked drain
precautions: Wear protective gloves and eye protection when handling drain cleaners.
Use caustic drain cleaner only with adult supervision and follow its label.
Never mix caustic drain cleaner with vinegar or any other cleaner.
Keep boiling water and chemicals away from skin and eyes; pour carefully.
Keep the area well ventilated and keep children away from the drain.
practicals.result: Sodium bicarbonate solution and vinegar react to produce carbon dioxide, which may help loosen a blockage. Caustic drain cleaner may dissolve some common blockage materials, but it must be handled with great care.

notes.title: What is Chemistry and why are there branches?
notes.answer: Chemistry studies substances, their properties, composition and structure, and changes in matter. Its branches focus on different aspects of this wide subject.
notes.explanation: Chemistry has several branches so scientists can focus on different kinds of substances and questions. For example, analytical chemistry identifies and measures components in a sample, while environmental chemistry studies chemical effects in air, soil and water. Nuclear chemistry focuses on changes in atomic nuclei.
notes.simple: Different chemistry branches are like different study areas: each one focuses on a particular kind of chemical question.
examples: Finding the components of a lunar sample: analytical chemistry.
Studying pollution caused by chemicals: environmental chemistry.
steps: Read what is being studied or measured.
Match it to the branch that focuses on that subject.
For a sample's components or concentrations, choose analytical chemistry.
notes.checkQuestion: Which branch deals with the separation, identification and measurement of components in a material?
notes.checkAnswer: Analytical chemistry.

notes.title: States of Matter
notes.answer: Matter can exist as a solid, liquid, gas or plasma, as well as in less commonly encountered states.
notes.explanation: Matter occurs in different states. The particle arrangement, distance between particles and strength of attractions explain how solids, liquids, gases and plasma behave.
notes.simple: Think of particles as tiny pieces. In a solid they are tightly packed, in a liquid they stay close but move around, and in a gas they are far apart.
examples: Ice is a solid: its particles are closely packed and stay around fixed positions.
Air is a gas: its particles are far apart, so it is easy to compress.
steps: Compare how close the particles are.
Compare how freely the particles can move.
Use the particle arrangement and attractions to explain the state’s properties.
notes.checkQuestion: Why are gases easily compressible?
notes.checkAnswer: Gases have particles that are very widely apart, no order whatsoever and very weak intermolecular forces.

notes.title: Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
notes.answer: An element has one kind of atom; a compound has different elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio; a mixture contains more than one type of element or compound mixed in any ratio.
notes.explanation: Matter may be an element, a compound, or a mixture. An element has one kind of atom; a compound contains different elements chemically joined in a fixed ratio; a mixture contains substances mixed in any ratio.
notes.simple: Think of the three types this way: an element has one kind of atom, a compound has different elements chemically joined, and a mixture has substances physically mixed together.
examples: Salt water is a homogeneous mixture because its concentration is uniform throughout.
A sample of rock is a heterogeneous mixture because its constituents are not present in the same concentration throughout.
steps: Check whether the sample contains one kind of atom, different elements chemically combined, or substances mixed together.
For a mixture, check whether its composition is uniform throughout.
Call a mixture homogeneous if uniform, and heterogeneous if not uniform.
notes.checkQuestion: What makes a compound different from a mixture?
notes.checkAnswer: A compound is a pure substance made up of two or more different elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio.

notes.title: Allotropic Forms of Substances
notes.answer: Allotropic forms are different structural forms of the same element.
notes.explanation: Allotropy is when an element exists in different structural forms. The forms can have different properties. Carbon has diamond, graphite and Buckminster fullerene as its main allotropic forms; sulphur has rhombic and monoclinic forms.
notes.simple: One element can have different forms because its atoms are arranged differently. These forms may behave differently.
examples: Oxygen: O₂ and O₃
Carbon: diamond, graphite and Buckminster fullerene
steps: Identify the element.
Name the different structural forms in which it exists.
Remember that these forms may have different properties.
notes.checkQuestion: Name the three main allotropic forms of carbon.
notes.checkAnswer: Diamond, graphite and Buckminster fullerene.

notes.title: Elements, compounds and mixtures
notes.answer: A compound has chemically combined elements in a fixed ratio; a mixture has components that are not chemically bound together.
notes.explanation: Elements, compounds and mixtures differ in what they contain and whether their particles are chemically joined. Elements contain one kind of atom; compounds contain elements chemically combined in fixed ratios; mixtures contain substances mixed without chemical bonding.
notes.simple: An element has one kind of atom. A compound has different elements chemically joined. A mixture has substances together but not chemically joined.
examples: Water (H₂O) is a compound: hydrogen and oxygen are chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
Salt water is a mixture: salt and water are mixed, and the salt can be separated by physical methods.
steps: Check whether the sample contains one kind of atom or more than one substance.
If different elements are chemically combined in a fixed ratio, it is a compound.
If substances are mixed without chemical bonding and can be separated physically, it is a mixture.
notes.checkQuestion: What is one key difference between a compound and a mixture?
notes.checkAnswer: A compound contains elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio; a mixture contains components that are not chemically bound together.

notes.title: Telling solutions, colloids and suspensions apart
notes.answer: A true solution has particles that are not visible and pass through filter paper. A colloid has particles that do not settle and pass through filter paper. A suspension has visible particles that settle and are caught by filter paper.
notes.explanation: A true solution has solute particles completely mixed into the solvent. Colloidal particles are bigger than true-solution particles, but are too small to see with the naked eye. Suspension particles can be seen, settle if left standing, and are caught by filter paper.
notes.simple: Think about what happens when you leave a mixture standing or pour it through a filter. These clues help you tell the three mixtures apart.
examples: Starch solution is a colloidal solution.
A mixture of chalk in water is a suspension.
steps: Check whether the particles can be seen with the naked eye.
Leave the mixture standing: suspension particles settle, but colloidal particles do not.
Filter it: true-solution and colloidal particles pass through filter paper; suspension particles are left as residue.
notes.checkQuestion: Which kind of mixture has particles that settle on standing and can be collected on filter paper?
notes.checkAnswer: A suspension: its particles can be seen, settle on standing, and are caught by filter paper.

notes.title: Unsaturated and Saturated Solutions
notes.answer: An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute; a saturated solution contains the maximum amount that can dissolve at that temperature.
notes.explanation: A solution is unsaturated if it can still dissolve more solute at a particular temperature. It is saturated when it has dissolved the maximum amount of solute possible in a particular amount of solvent at that temperature.
notes.simple: Unsaturated means more solute can dissolve. Saturated means no more can dissolve at that temperature.
examples: Sugar dissolves in water, and more sugar can still dissolve: the solution is unsaturated.
At 20°C, 36 g of sodium chloride dissolves in 100 g of water to make a saturated solution.
steps: Check whether more solute can dissolve at the same temperature.
If more can dissolve, the solution is unsaturated.
If the maximum amount has dissolved, the solution is saturated.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the difference between an unsaturated solution and a saturated solution?
notes.checkAnswer: An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute at that temperature; a saturated solution has dissolved the maximum amount.

notes.title: Temperature and solubility
notes.answer: The solubility of a gas in water generally decreases when the temperature increases.
notes.explanation: Temperature affects different solutes in different ways. Many solids dissolve better in warmer water, but some substances change very little or become less soluble. Gases generally become less soluble as water gets warmer.
notes.simple: Heating often lets water dissolve more solid, but not always. It usually makes water hold less gas.
examples: KNO₃ becomes much more soluble as temperature increases.
NaCl solubility changes very little with temperature.
steps: Remember the definition: solubility is measured for 100g of solvent at a particular temperature.
Check the substance: different solutes respond differently to temperature.
For many solids, heating increases solubility; for some, it changes little or decreases.
For gases, solubility in water generally decreases as temperature increases.
notes.checkQuestion: What usually happens to the solubility of a gas in water when the temperature increases?
notes.checkAnswer: Most solid solutes become more soluble as temperature rises, but this is not a rule for every substance. Gases generally become less soluble.

notes.title: States of Matter and Phase Changes
notes.answer: Matter in the Sun exists in the plasma state.
notes.explanation: Matter can be classified by its physical state and by whether it is a pure substance or a mixture. Chemistry is divided into branches so different kinds of substances, reactions and problems can be studied more easily. Temperature affects the solubility of many substances, and cooling a hot saturated solution can produce crystals.
notes.simple: Chemistry studies matter and its changes. Different branches focus on different kinds of matter and questions. Substances can have different structures and properties, and solubility often changes when temperature changes.
examples: A fluorescent tube contains plasma.
Cooling a hot saturated potassium nitrate solution can produce potassium nitrate crystals.
steps: Identify the type of matter or process in the question.
Recall the relevant definition or property.
Apply it to the substance or example given.
For crystallization, dissolve the substance in hot solvent, then cool the solution.
notes.checkQuestion: In which state does matter exist in the Sun?
notes.checkAnswer: Plasma.

notes.title: Structure of the Atom
notes.answer: An atom has a nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in shells.
notes.explanation: Atoms have a tiny central nucleus containing protons and neutrons. Electrons occupy shells around the nucleus. A shell farther from the nucleus has greater energy. Modern science describes electron locations in terms of probability, rather than exact paths.
notes.simple: An atom is like a very tiny centre with electrons around it: the centre is the nucleus, and the electrons occupy energy shells.
examples: A proton has a positive charge, an electron has a negative charge, and a neutron has no charge.
For the third shell, n = 3, so the maximum number of electrons is 2 × 3² = 18.
steps: Identify the shell number n.
Use the formula 2n² to find the shell's maximum number of electrons.
Substitute the value of n and calculate.
notes.checkQuestion: What particles are found in the nucleus, and what holds them together?
notes.checkAnswer: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, held together by strong nuclear force.

notes.title: Atomic Number and Mass Number
notes.answer: Atomic number Z is the number of protons. Mass number A is the total number of protons and neutrons. Neutrons N = A − Z; electrons equal protons in a neutral atom.
notes.explanation: An element is identified by its atomic number, Z, which tells us how many protons its atoms have. The mass number, A, is the total number of protons and neutrons. Subtract Z from A to find the number of neutrons. In a neutral atom, electrons equal protons. For example, ¹⁶₈O has 8 protons, 8 electrons and 8 neutrons; ³²₁₆S has 16 neutrons.
notes.simple: The atomic number gives the protons. The mass number gives protons plus neutrons. Subtract to find neutrons; in a neutral atom, electrons equal protons.
examples: For ¹⁶₈O: protons = 8, electrons = 8, neutrons = 16 − 8 = 8.
For ³²₁₆S: neutrons = 32 − 16 = 16.
steps: Read the left subscript: Z = number of protons.
For a neutral atom, set the number of electrons equal to the number of protons.
Read the left superscript: A = mass number.
Calculate neutrons using N = A − Z.
notes.checkQuestion: How many neutrons are in ²³₁₁Na?
notes.checkAnswer: A neutral atom of ²³₁₁Na has 11 protons, 11 electrons and 12 neutrons.

notes.title: Isotopes, radioactivity and their uses
notes.answer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. Their chemical properties are almost the same, while their physical properties may differ.
notes.explanation: Isotopes have the same number of protons and electrons but different numbers of neutrons. Their electron arrangements are the same, so their chemical behaviour is almost the same; their different masses can give them different physical properties.
notes.simple: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. They react almost alike, but their different masses can make some physical properties different.
examples: ¹²₆C and ¹⁴₆C are isotopes of carbon: each has 6 protons, but they have 6 and 8 neutrons respectively.
Tritium, ³₁H, is radioactive; hydrogen, ¹₁H, and deuterium, ²₁H, are stable.
steps: Find the element's atomic number: this gives the number of protons.
For a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
Find neutrons by subtracting the atomic number from the mass number.
For a relative atomic mass, multiply each isotope's mass by its percentage abundance, add the results, and divide by 100 when the abundances are percentages.
notes.checkQuestion: Why can isotopes of the same element have different masses?
notes.checkAnswer: Isotopes have the same number of electrons, so they show almost the same chemical behaviour. Their different numbers of neutrons give them different masses and physical properties.

notes.title: Calculating Relative Atomic Mass
notes.explanation: An element’s relative atomic mass is the weighted average of the masses of its isotopes, using their percentage abundances.
notes.simple: Multiply each isotope’s mass by its percentage abundance, add the results, then divide by 100.
examples: For krypton, the relative atomic mass is 83.7.
For chlorine, the relative atomic mass of the light isotope is 34.95.
steps: Multiply each isotope mass by its percentage abundance.
Add all the products.
Divide the total by 100.
notes.checkQuestion: Lead has isotopes ²⁰⁴Pb, ²⁰⁶Pb, ²⁰⁷Pb and ²⁰⁸Pb with abundances 2%, 24%, 22% and 52%. What is its relative atomic mass?

notes.title: Atomic structure, isotopes and radioactivity
notes.answer: 127 neutrons
notes.explanation: Atomic structure explains how protons, neutrons and electrons are arranged, why elements differ, and how isotopes and radioactivity behave.
notes.simple: An atom has a tiny nucleus containing protons and neutrons, with electrons arranged around it. The number of protons identifies the element.
examples: A neutral oxygen-16 atom has 8 protons, 8 electrons and 8 neutrons.
A neutral bismuth-210 atom has 210 − 83 = 127 neutrons.
steps: Read the atomic number: it gives the number of protons.
For a neutral atom, set the number of electrons equal to the number of protons.
Subtract the atomic number from the mass number to find neutrons.
For relative atomic mass, multiply each isotope mass by its abundance and find the weighted mean.
notes.checkQuestion: How many neutrons are present in ²¹⁰₈₃Bi?
notes.checkAnswer: A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons; its neutron number is mass number minus atomic number.

notes.title: Why atoms form bonds
notes.answer: Atoms form bonds to lower their energy and increase their stability.
notes.explanation: Atoms form bonds because combining can lower their energy and make them more stable. For example, sodium can lose one electron more easily than gain seven, while hydrogen can gain one electron to complete a duplet.
notes.simple: Atoms join with other atoms when doing so helps them become more stable.
examples: Sodium loses one electron rather than gaining seven to complete its octet.
Hydrogen can gain one electron to complete its duplet.
steps: Atoms can lower their energy by combining with other atoms.
A full outer shell is associated with stability: 2 electrons for a duplet or 8 for an octet.
Atoms may lose or gain electrons along an energetically easier path to reach this stable arrangement.
notes.checkQuestion: How many outer-shell electrons correspond to a duplet and an octet?
notes.checkAnswer: A duplet has 2 outer-shell electrons; an octet has 8.

notes.title: How atoms form chemical bonds
notes.answer: Atoms form chemical bonds by transferring or sharing electrons, or by one atom donating a shared pair.
notes.explanation: A chemical bond is the force of attraction that holds atoms together. Atoms can form bonds by transferring electrons, sharing electrons, or sharing a pair of electrons donated by one atom.
notes.simple: Atoms stick together because they attract each other. They may transfer electrons or share them to make a bond.
examples: Sodium transfers one electron to chlorine, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻; their attraction forms an ionic bond.
Two hydrogen atoms share an electron pair to form H—H, a single covalent bond.
steps: Identify whether electrons are transferred or shared.
For an ionic bond, show the electron transfer and the ions formed.
For a covalent bond, show the shared electron pair or bond line.
For a coordinate covalent bond, identify the donor, acceptor and direction of the arrow.
notes.checkQuestion: What is a covalent bond?
notes.checkAnswer: A covalent bond is formed by mutual sharing of an electron pair provided by the bonded atoms.

notes.title: Metallic Bond
