rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the retained-properties distinction.

rubric.why: Mixture components can be separated by physical methods, whereas the elements in a compound require chemical methods of separation.
rubric.description: (a) States that the components of a mixture can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct separation method or general statement.

rubric.why: A colloid is heterogeneous, even though it may appear homogeneous.
rubric.description: (b) Nature of a colloid
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a colloid is actually a heterogeneous mixture.

rubric.why: Colloidal particles scatter a beam of light, producing the Tyndall effect.
rubric.description: (b) Scattering of light
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that colloids scatter light or show the Tyndall effect.

rubric.why: Colloidal particles remain dispersed instead of settling on standing.
rubric.description: (b) Stability on standing
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that colloidal particles do not settle on standing.

rubric.why: Colloidal particles pass through ordinary filter paper.
rubric.description: (b) Filtration
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that colloidal particles pass through ordinary filter paper or cannot be separated by ordinary filtration.

written.text:
(a) Define any five Branches of Chemistry.
(b) Write down any four differences between Compound and Mixture.
modelAnswer: (a) Physical chemistry deals with the physical properties of matter and the energy changes involved in chemical reactions.
Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that studies carbon compounds.
Inorganic chemistry deals with the properties and reactions of elements and their compounds, generally excluding most carbon compounds.
Biochemistry studies the chemical substances and processes that occur in living organisms.
Industrial chemistry deals with the manufacture of chemical substances and products on an industrial scale.
(b) A compound has a fixed composition; a mixture can have a variable composition.
The elements in a compound are chemically combined; the substances in a mixture are physically mixed.
A compound has properties different from those of its constituent elements; substances in a mixture retain their properties.
A compound can be separated into its elements by chemical methods; a mixture can be separated by physical methods.
written.followUp: Define any five branches of chemistry other than those listed here.

rubric.why: Physical chemistry concerns physical properties of matter and energy changes in chemical processes.
rubric.description: (a) Defines physical chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition of physical chemistry.

rubric.why: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds.
rubric.description: (a) Defines organic chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition of organic chemistry.

rubric.why: Inorganic chemistry studies elements and their compounds, generally excluding most carbon compounds.
rubric.description: (a) Defines inorganic chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition of inorganic chemistry.

rubric.why: Biochemistry studies chemical substances or processes in living organisms.
rubric.description: (a) Defines biochemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition of biochemistry.

rubric.why: Industrial chemistry concerns the manufacture of chemicals and products on an industrial scale.
rubric.description: (a) Defines industrial chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition of industrial chemistry.

rubric.why: A compound has a fixed composition, whereas a mixture can have variable proportions.
rubric.description: (b) Compares composition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the fixed-versus-variable composition difference.

rubric.why: The substances in a compound are chemically combined; those in a mixture are physically mixed.
rubric.description: (b) Compares how the substances are combined.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the chemical-combination versus physical-mixing difference.

rubric.why: A compound has properties different from its constituent elements, while mixture components retain their properties.
rubric.description: (b) Compares the properties of the constituents.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct difference in properties.

rubric.why: Compounds are separated chemically, while mixtures can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.description: (b) Compares methods of separation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the chemical-versus-physical separation difference.

mcqs.stem: One amu (Atomic Mass Unit) is equivalent to:
rationales: This is incorrect because one amu is about 1.66 × 10⁻²¹ mg.
This is correct because one amu is approximately 1.66 × 10⁻²⁴ g.
This is incorrect because one amu is approximately 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
This is incorrect because the exponent should be −24, not −23.

mcqs.stem: Which one of the following shell consists of three subshells?
rationales: The O shell has eight subshells, not three.
The N shell has four subshells, not three.
The L shell has two subshells, not three.
The M shell has three subshells: s, p, and d.

mcqs.stem: The P subshell has:
rationales: A p subshell does not have one orbital.
A p subshell does not have two orbitals.
A p subshell has three orbitals.
A p subshell does not have four orbitals.

mcqs.stem: The concept of Orbit was used by:
rationales: Thomson proposed the plum-pudding model, not electron orbits.
Rutherford proposed the nuclear model, while Bohr introduced fixed electron orbits.
Bohr used fixed orbits to describe electrons around the nucleus.
Planck developed quantum theory but did not introduce the atomic orbit model.

mcqs.stem: The Removal of Electrons from an Atom gives:
rationales: Removing electrons leaves a negatively charged anion, not a positively charged ion.
Electron removal alone does not necessarily form a molecule.
A molecular ion is a charged molecule, not the general result of removing electrons from an atom.
Removing negatively charged electrons leaves the atom positively charged, forming a cation.

mcqs.stem: The nature of charge on canal rays is.
rationales: Canal rays consist of positively charged ions.
Canal rays are not negatively charged.
Canal rays carry charge rather than being neutral.
Canal rays carry full positive charge, not partial negative charge.

mcqs.stem: Electronic configuration of Na is
rationales: [He] 2s¹ is the configuration of lithium, not sodium.
Sodium has the configuration [Ne] 3s¹.
[Ar] 4s¹ is the configuration of potassium.
[Kr] 5s¹ is the configuration of rubidium.

mcqs.stem: K shell can accommodate:
rationales: The K shell is the first shell and can hold a maximum of 2 electrons.
Eight electrons is the maximum capacity of the L shell.
Eighteen electrons is the maximum capacity of the M shell.
Thirty-two electrons is the maximum capacity of the N shell.

mcqs.stem: From the following scientists _____ discovered the proton.
rationales: Goldstein discovered canal rays, not the proton.
J. J. Thomson discovered the electron.
Niels Bohr proposed a model of the atom, not the discovery of the proton.
Rutherford is credited with discovering the proton.

mcqs.stem: Mass of an electron is:
rationales: This value is approximately the mass of a proton, not an electron.
This is not the accepted mass of an electron.
This is not the accepted mass of an electron.
The electron’s mass is approximately 9.11 × 10⁻²⁸ g, so this is the closest listed value.

mcqs.stem: The father of nuclear science is:
rationales: Ernest Rutherford is widely known as the father of nuclear science.
Bohr developed a model of the atom but is not known by this title.
Thomson discovered the electron and proposed an atomic model.
Crookes studied cathode rays but is not known by this title.

mcqs.stem: The “p” subshell has number of orbitals:
rationales: An s subshell has one orbital, not a p subshell.
A p subshell has three orbitals, not two.
A p subshell contains three orbitals.
A d subshell has five orbitals; a p subshell does not have four.

written.text: Define Electronic Configuration.
modelAnswer: Electronic configuration is the distribution of electrons in the shells around the nucleus of an atom.
written.followUp: Write the electronic configuration of an atom having 12 electrons.

rubric.why: Electronic configuration describes how electrons are distributed among shells.
rubric.description: Identifies the distribution of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning the arrangement or distribution of electrons.

rubric.why: The electrons are arranged in shells around the nucleus.
rubric.description: Specifies that the electron arrangement is in shells around the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons are arranged in shells around the nucleus.

written.text: What are the defects of Ruther Ford's Atomic Model?
modelAnswer: Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability: revolving electrons should radiate energy and fall into the nucleus.
It also could not explain the line spectra of atoms.
written.followUp: State one major limitation of Rutherford’s atomic model.

rubric.why: According to classical physics, revolving electrons should radiate energy and fall into the nucleus, so the model could not explain atomic stability.
rubric.description: Explains that Rutherford’s model could not account for atomic stability.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it could not explain why electrons do not lose energy and fall into the nucleus.

rubric.why: The model did not explain the discrete line spectra of atoms.
rubric.description: Identifies the failure to explain atomic spectra.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the model could not explain the line spectra of atoms.

written.text: Differentiate between atomic number and mass number.
modelAnswer: Atomic number (Z) is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
Mass number (A) is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
written.followUp: Define atomic number and mass number, and state how each is determined for an atom.

rubric.why: Atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
rubric.description: Defines atomic number.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying atomic number as the number of protons in the nucleus.

rubric.why: Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
rubric.description: Defines mass number.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying mass number as the sum of the numbers of protons and neutrons.

written.text: Differentiate between atom and ion.
modelAnswer: An atom is electrically neutral because it has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
An ion is a charged particle formed when an atom gains or loses electrons.
written.followUp: Differentiate between a cation and an anion.

rubric.why: An atom is neutral because it has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
rubric.description: Atom is neutral
rubric.how: Look for the idea that an atom has no net charge.

rubric.why: An ion is charged and is formed when an atom gains or loses electrons.
rubric.description: Ion is charged due to electron gain or loss
rubric.how: Look for both the charged nature of an ion and its formation by electron gain or loss.

written.text: Write two observations of Rutherford's Experiment.
modelAnswer: Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without being deflected.
Some alpha particles were deflected, and a very small number bounced back.
written.followUp: State two observations made in Rutherford’s alpha-particle experiment.

rubric.why: Most alpha particles travelled through the foil without deflection.
rubric.description: States that most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without being deflected.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the observation that most particles passed straight through or were undeflected.

rubric.why: A small number of alpha particles were deflected, and a very small number were reflected backwards.
rubric.description: States that some alpha particles were deflected; a very small number bounced back.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either deflection or backward reflection, provided the response identifies it as an observation.

written.text: Write two properties of neutron.
modelAnswer: A neutron has no electrical charge; it is neutral.
Its mass is approximately 1 amu (1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).
written.followUp: State two properties of a proton.

rubric.why: A neutron has no electrical charge.
rubric.description: States that a neutron is electrically neutral.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that its charge is zero.

rubric.why: A neutron has a mass of approximately one atomic mass unit.
rubric.description: States the approximate mass of a neutron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving a mass of about 1 amu or 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

written.text: What is the nature of charge on Cathode rays?
modelAnswer: Cathode rays consist of electrons.
Since electrons are negatively charged, cathode rays carry a negative charge.
written.followUp: What is the nature of charge on protons?

rubric.why: Identifies cathode rays as a stream of electrons.
rubric.description: Cathode rays consist of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that cathode rays consist of electrons.

rubric.why: States the charge carried by cathode rays.
rubric.description: Electrons carry a negative charge, so cathode rays are negatively charged.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that cathode rays carry a negative charge.

written.text: Write down the observations of Rutherford's experiment.
modelAnswer: Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without any deflection.
Some alpha particles were deflected, while a very few bounced back.
written.followUp: State the main conclusions drawn from Rutherford’s alpha-particle scattering experiment.

rubric.why: Most alpha particles passed through the foil without deflection.
rubric.description: States that most alpha particles passed straight through the foil.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this observation.

rubric.why: A small number of alpha particles changed direction, and a very few were reflected backwards.
rubric.description: States that some alpha particles were deflected and very few bounced back.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either deflection or backward scattering.

written.text: Write down Two Properties of Neutron.
modelAnswer: A neutron has no electrical charge; it is electrically neutral.
Its mass is approximately 1 atomic mass unit (amu).
written.followUp: State two properties of a proton.

rubric.why: A neutron has no electrical charge.
rubric.description: States that a neutron is electrically neutral.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the charge property.

rubric.why: A neutron has a mass of approximately one atomic mass unit.
rubric.description: States that a neutron has approximately 1 amu of mass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the mass property.

written.text:
(a) Write down any five properties of cathode rays
(b) Describe postulates of Bohr's Atomic Theory.
modelAnswer: (a) Cathode rays travel in straight lines.
They consist of negatively charged particles called electrons.
They are deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
They produce fluorescence when they strike certain substances.
Their nature is independent of the gas in the discharge tube and the material of the electrodes.
(b) Electrons revolve around the nucleus in definite circular orbits or shells, each having a fixed energy.
An electron does not radiate or absorb energy while it remains in a stationary orbit.
An electron absorbs energy to jump to a higher energy level and releases energy when it falls to a lower level.
The energy absorbed or emitted is equal to the difference between the two energy levels.
written.followUp: Write any five properties of electrons.

rubric.why: Cathode rays travel in straight lines.
rubric.description: (a) States that cathode rays travel in straight lines.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Cathode rays consist of negatively charged particles.
rubric.description: (a) Identifies the negative charge or electron nature of cathode rays.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they are negatively charged or consist of electrons.

rubric.why: Cathode rays are deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
rubric.description: (a) States that cathode rays are deflected by a field.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming an electric or magnetic field and stating that the rays are deflected.

rubric.why: Cathode rays produce fluorescence when they strike certain substances.
rubric.description: (a) States that cathode rays produce fluorescence or a glow.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Their nature does not depend on the gas in the tube or the material of the electrodes.
rubric.description: (a) States that cathode-ray properties are independent of the gas or electrode material.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either independence.

rubric.why: States that electrons occupy specified energy levels around the nucleus.
rubric.description: (b) States that electrons revolve around the nucleus in definite orbits or shells, each with a fixed energy.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning definite electron orbits or shells with fixed energy.

rubric.why: Describes the energy behaviour of electrons while they remain in an allowed orbit.
rubric.description: (b) States that an electron does not radiate or absorb energy while in a stationary orbit.
rubric.how: Award for stating that energy is not exchanged while the electron remains in its orbit.

rubric.why: Explains that an electron changes energy by moving between allowed orbits.
rubric.description: (b) States that an electron absorbs or releases energy when it jumps between energy levels.
rubric.how: Award for explaining energy absorption or release during a transition between shells.

rubric.why: Relates the energy exchanged to the separation between the levels.
rubric.description: (b) States that the absorbed or emitted energy equals the difference between the two energy levels.
rubric.how: Award for linking the energy of the transition to the difference between the levels.

written.text:
(a) How are Cathode Rays produced? What are their four major characteristics?
(b) Explain Bohr’s atomic model.
modelAnswer: (a) Cathode rays are produced in a discharge tube containing gas at low pressure when a high voltage is applied between its electrodes.
They travel in straight lines.
They carry a negative charge.
They are deflected towards the positive plate in an electric field.
They produce fluorescence when they strike certain substances.
(b) An atom has a small, positively charged nucleus at its centre, and electrons move around it.
Electrons can move only in certain fixed orbits, or shells, each having a definite energy.
An electron does not radiate energy while it remains in one of these permitted orbits.
An electron absorbs energy to move to a higher-energy orbit and emits energy when it falls to a lower-energy orbit.
written.followUp: How are anode rays produced? State four of their characteristics.

rubric.why: Describes the conditions under which cathode rays are produced.
rubric.description: (a) States that cathode rays are produced in a discharge tube containing gas at low pressure when a high voltage is applied.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the production method and conditions.

rubric.why: Includes a fundamental observed property of cathode rays.
rubric.description: (a) States that cathode rays travel in straight lines.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this characteristic.

rubric.why: Identifies the electrical nature of cathode rays.
rubric.description: (a) States that cathode rays carry a negative charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this characteristic.

rubric.why: Shows how cathode rays respond to an electric field.
rubric.description: (a) States that cathode rays are deflected towards the positive plate in an electric field.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this characteristic.

rubric.why: Includes another characteristic observed when cathode rays strike certain materials.
rubric.description: (a) States that cathode rays produce fluorescence when they strike certain substances.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this characteristic.

rubric.why: This identifies the atom’s central structure and the particles around it.
rubric.description: (b) States that an atom has a central nucleus with electrons around it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying both the nucleus and electrons.

rubric.why: Bohr’s model allows electrons to occupy only particular orbits or energy levels.
rubric.description: (b) States that electrons occupy fixed orbits or shells with definite energies.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for fixed orbits, shells or definite energy levels.

rubric.why: Electrons in permitted stationary orbits do not lose energy by radiation.
rubric.description: (b) States that an electron does not radiate energy while it remains in a permitted orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons in stationary orbits do not radiate energy.

rubric.why: An electron changes energy when it moves between permitted orbits.
rubric.description: (b) States that an electron absorbs energy to move to a higher orbit or emits energy when it moves to a lower orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing either transition with its energy change.

written.text:
(a) Explain five postulates of Bohr's atomic model.
(b) Write four results of Experiment of Rutherford's Atomic Model.
modelAnswer: (a) Electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed circular orbits called energy levels or shells.
An electron in a permitted orbit does not radiate or absorb energy; its energy remains constant.
Only certain orbits are allowed, and the electron’s angular momentum is quantized: mvr = nh/2π.
The energy of an orbit increases as its distance from the nucleus increases.
An electron absorbs or emits a definite amount of energy when it jumps between orbits; ΔE = hν.
(b) Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without any deflection.
Some alpha particles were deflected through small angles.
Very few alpha particles were deflected through large angles or turned back.
These results showed that most of the atom is empty space and that its positive charge is concentrated in a small, dense nucleus.
written.followUp: State four postulates of Dalton’s atomic theory.

rubric.why: Bohr proposed that electrons occupy definite permitted orbits around the nucleus.
rubric.description: (a) States that electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed orbits or energy levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the permitted fixed orbits or energy levels.

rubric.why: Electrons in permitted stationary orbits do not continuously lose or gain energy.
rubric.description: (a) States that an electron in a permitted orbit does not radiate or absorb energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this stationary-orbit property.

rubric.why: Only certain orbits are allowed, as expressed by the quantization of angular momentum.
rubric.description: (a) States that angular momentum is quantized, or gives the corresponding relation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the quantization rule or giving mvr = nh/2π.

rubric.why: The energy of permitted orbits increases with their distance from the nucleus.
rubric.description: (a) States that orbit energy increases with distance from the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship between orbit distance and energy.

rubric.why: An electron exchanges a definite amount of energy when it transitions between permitted orbits.
rubric.description: (a) Explains that an electron absorbs or emits energy during a transition between orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing absorption or emission during a transition, or giving ΔE = hν.

rubric.why: Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil without deflection.
rubric.description: (b) States that most alpha particles passed through the foil without deflection.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this observation.

rubric.why: Some alpha particles were deflected through small angles.
rubric.description: (b) States that some alpha particles were slightly deflected.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this observation.

rubric.why: Very few alpha particles were sharply deflected or turned back.
rubric.description: (b) States that very few alpha particles were deflected through large angles or turned back.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this observation.

rubric.why: The scattering results showed that the atom is mostly empty space and that its positive charge is concentrated in a small, dense nucleus.
rubric.description: (b) Gives a conclusion drawn from the experiment.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying that the atom is mostly empty space or that positive charge is concentrated in a small, dense nucleus.

mcqs.stem: A bond formed between two non-metals is expected to be:
rationales: Non-metal atoms generally form covalent bonds by sharing electrons.
Ionic bonds usually form between a metal and a non-metal.
A coordinate covalent bond is a particular type of covalent bond, not the general expected answer here.
Metallic bonds occur between metal atoms.

mcqs.stem: Transfer of Electrons between Atoms results in:
rationales: Metallic bonding involves attraction between metal ions and delocalized electrons, not electron transfer between atoms.
Electron transfer between atoms forms an ionic bond.
Covalent bonding involves sharing electrons rather than transferring them.
Coordinate covalent bonding involves a shared pair donated by one atom rather than electron transfer.

mcqs.stem: Which pair has polar covalent bond?
rationales: O₂ and Cl₂ have nonpolar bonds between identical atoms.
N₂ has a nonpolar bond, so this pair does not both have polar covalent bonds.
H₂O has polar bonds, but C₂H₂ is not a clear example of a polar covalent molecule.
Both H₂O and HCl contain polar covalent bonds.

mcqs.stem: A Bond formed between two Non Metals is expected to be:
rationales: Ionic bonds typically form through electron transfer, often between a metal and a nonmetal.
Two nonmetals generally share electrons and form a covalent bond.
A coordinate covalent bond is a particular covalent bond formed when one atom supplies both shared electrons, not the general expected answer.
Metallic bonding occurs among metal atoms, not between two nonmetals.

mcqs.stem: One is a Polar Molecule:
rationales: O₂ is nonpolar because it consists of identical atoms.
Cl₂ is nonpolar because it consists of identical atoms.
HCl is polar because its atoms have different electronegativities.
H₂ is nonpolar because it consists of identical atoms.

mcqs.stem: A bond pair in Covalent Molecules usually has:
rationales: A covalent bond pair contains more than one electron.
A covalent bond pair consists of two shared electrons.
Three electrons do not constitute a bond pair.
Four electrons are not the number in a single covalent bond pair.

mcqs.stem: Hydrogen bonding is represented by:
rationales: A dotted or dashed line conventionally represents a hydrogen bond.
A single line represents a covalent bond, not a hydrogen bond.
A double line represents a double covalent bond.
A triple line represents a triple covalent bond.

mcqs.stem: Which one is a polar molecule?
rationales: O₂ is nonpolar because it consists of identical atoms sharing electrons equally.
Cl₂ is nonpolar because it consists of identical atoms sharing electrons equally.
HCl is polar because chlorine attracts the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen.
H₂ is nonpolar because its identical atoms share electrons equally.

mcqs.stem: The valence electrons which are involved in chemical bonding are termed as:
rationales: Attractive forces are not the name for valence electrons involved in bonding.
Repulsive forces are not the name for valence electrons involved in bonding.
Valence electrons that participate in chemical bonds are called bonding electrons.

written.text:
(a) What is a molecule? Describe any four types of molecules with examples.
(b) Calculate the number of moles and molecules in 6 gm of water (H₂O).
modelAnswer: (a) A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and retain its chemical properties.
A monoatomic molecule contains one atom; for example, helium (He).
A diatomic molecule contains two atoms; for example, oxygen (O₂).
A triatomic molecule contains three atoms; for example, ozone (O₃).
A polyatomic molecule contains more than three atoms; for example, phosphorus (P₄).
(b) Given: m = 6 g = 0.006 kg; M(H₂O) = 18 g mol⁻¹ = 0.018 kg mol⁻¹.
Formula: n = m/M.
Substitution: n = 0.006 kg ÷ 0.018 kg mol⁻¹ = 0.333 mol.
Formula: number of molecules = n × Nₐ.
Substitution: number of molecules = 0.333 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
Answer: 0.333 mol of water contains approximately 2.01 × 10²³ molecules.

mcqs.stem: The following reaction is an exothermic reaction. H₂ + Cl₂ \(\xrightarrow{Sunlight}\) 2HCl From where does the energy come to break the bonds of H₂ and Cl₂?

rationales: Ordinary molecular collisions do not supply the specific initiating energy in this photochemical reaction.
Sunlight supplies the energy needed to initiate bond breaking in H₂ and Cl₂.
The surroundings are not the stated source of the initiating energy.
Collisions with the container walls do not provide the initiating energy specified for this reaction.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following reactions has the least value of activation energy?
rationales: The reaction of hydrogen with oxygen requires energy to overcome a substantial activation barrier.
Combustion of solid carbon requires overcoming a significant activation barrier.
The ions in solution can react readily to form insoluble AgCl, so this precipitation reaction has the least activation energy.
The reaction involving solid iodine and hydrogen requires overcoming a comparatively larger activation barrier.

mcqs.stem: Formation of which hydrogen halide from the elements is an endothermic reaction?
rationales: Formation of HCl from its elements is exothermic.
Formation of HF from its elements is exothermic.
Formation of HBr from its elements is exothermic.
Formation of HI from its elements is endothermic because breaking the reactant bonds requires slightly more energy than forming the HI bonds releases.

mcqs.stem: What are the products of anaerobic respiration?
rationales: ATP, CO₂, and H₂O are associated with aerobic respiration, not anaerobic respiration.
CO₂ and H₂O alone do not describe the products of anaerobic respiration.
This is the intended choice because anaerobic fermentation releases ATP and forms ethanol, although the usual yeast equation lists CO₂ rather than H₂O.
Ethanol alone omits the energy captured as ATP; the listed water is also not the usual coproduct in yeast fermentation.

mcqs.stem: Which reaction do you expect to be a reversible reaction?
options: [FIGURE: (a) Energy versus Path of Reaction graph; A + B starts at a higher energy level than C + D, with a red curve rising to a peak and then falling to C + D.]
[FIGURE: (b) Energy versus Path of Reaction graph; A + B and C + D are at the same energy level, with a red curve rising to a peak and then falling to C + D.]
[FIGURE (c): Energy vs Path of Reaction graph. The curve starts at A + B, rises to a peak, and ends at C + D at a higher energy level.]
[FIGURE (d): Energy vs Path of Reaction graph. The curve starts at A + B, rises to a peak, and ends at C + D at a higher energy level.]
rationales: The products are at a lower energy than the reactants, so this graph is not the textbook-expected balanced energy profile for a reversible reaction.
The reactants and products are at the same energy level, making this the textbook-expected choice for a reversible reaction.
The products are at a higher energy than the reactants, so this graph does not show equal-energy endpoints.
As described, the products are at a higher energy than the reactants, so this graph does not show equal-energy endpoints.

mcqs.stem: What does it show when a chemical reaction is exothermic?
options: It shows the bonds which break are weaker than those are formed.
It shows the bond which break are stronger than those are formed.
Exothermic nature of the reaction is not concerned with bond formation or bond breakage.
It shows that the reactants are more stable than the products.
rationales: In an exothermic reaction, forming stronger bonds releases more energy than is needed to break the weaker reactant bonds.
Exothermicity indicates that the bonds formed are stronger overall than the bonds broken, not the reverse.
Exothermicity is directly related to the relative energies of bonds broken and bonds formed.
Exothermic reactions generally produce more stable products, rather than showing that the reactants are more stable.

mcqs.stem: When NaOH and HCl are mixed the temperature increases. The reaction is:
options: endothermic with a positive enthalpy change.
endothermic with a negative enthalpy change.
exothermic with a positive enthalpy change.
exothermic with a negative enthalpy change.
rationales: A temperature increase indicates heat release, not an endothermic reaction.
A temperature increase indicates heat release, not an endothermic reaction.
The reaction is exothermic, but exothermic reactions have a negative enthalpy change.
The temperature increase shows that the reaction releases heat, so it is exothermic with a negative enthalpy change.

mcqs.stem: The average bond dissociation energy for the C-H bond is 412 kJ mol⁻¹. Which of the following process will have enthalpy change close to 412 kJ mol⁻¹?
rationales: This process breaks multiple C–H bonds and also changes the carbon and hydrogen products, so its enthalpy is not close to one average C–H bond energy.
This process involves breaking multiple C–H bonds and forming solid carbon, so its enthalpy is not close to one C–H bond energy.
This process breaks all four C–H bonds, giving an enthalpy change much larger than the energy for one bond.
This process breaks just one C–H bond, so its enthalpy change is close to the average bond dissociation energy of 412 kJ mol⁻¹.

mcqs.stem: Why does the following exothermic reaction not occur? C (Diamond) → C (Graphite) ΔH= -3kJ mol⁻¹
options: Structure of diamond is more stable than that of graphite.
Diamond has strong covalent bonds than does the graphite.
The change from diamond to graphite has high activation energy.
Density of graphite is less then that of diamond.
rationales: Graphite is more stable than diamond under ordinary conditions, so this is not the reason the conversion fails to occur readily.
The conversion is not prevented because diamond’s covalent bonds are stronger than graphite’s; its main obstacle is the reaction pathway.
The conversion is thermodynamically favorable but does not occur readily because it has a high activation energy.
Graphite’s lower density than diamond does not explain why the conversion is kinetically slow.

mcqs.stem: A student is studying water as it boils in a beaker. Which is the system?
options: The water and everything around it
rationales: Correct: the water is the part being studied, so it is the system.
Incorrect: the beaker and burner are examples of the surrounding.

Incorrect: reactants are part of the system being studied.

mcqs.stem: Which energy transfer describes an endothermic change?
options: The system absorbs energy from the surrounding
The system transfers energy to the surrounding
The surrounding absorbs energy from the system
rationales: Correct: in an endothermic change, energy moves from the surrounding into the system.
Incorrect: energy moving from the system to the surrounding describes an exothermic change.
Incorrect: an endothermic change involves energy transfer into the system.
Incorrect: this describes energy leaving the system, so it is exothermic.

mcqs.stem: What will happen if the rates of forward and reverse reactions are very high?
options: The equilibrium point will reach very soon.
The equilibrium point will reach very late.
The reaction will not attain the state of dynamic equilibrium.
The reaction will be practically irreversible.
rationales: High forward and reverse rates make the equilibrium composition establish quickly.
High reaction rates do not make equilibrium take longer to establish.
A reversible reaction can still reach dynamic equilibrium when both rates are high.
High rates alone do not make a reversible reaction practically irreversible.

mcqs.stem: Predict which components of the atmosphere react in the presence of lightning.
rationales: Lightning does not primarily drive a reaction between nitrogen and water vapour.
Oxygen and water vapour are not the main atmospheric components reacting to form nitrogen oxides during lightning.
Carbon dioxide and oxygen are not the principal pair involved in this lightning reaction.
Lightning provides enough energy for nitrogen and oxygen to react and form nitrogen oxides.

mcqs.stem: An inorganic chemist places one mole of PCl₃ in a container A and one mole of each Cl₂ and PCl₃ in container B. Both the containers were sealed and heated to the same temperature to reach the state of equilibrium. Guess about the composition of mixtures in both the containers.
options: Both the containers will have the same composition of mixtures.
Container A will have more concentration of PCl₃ than B.
Container A will have less concentration of PCl₃ than B.
Both the containers will have zero concentration of its reactants.
rationales: The mixtures will differ because the containers start with different amounts of the reacting substances.
In container B, some PCl₃ reacts with Cl₂ to form PCl₅, leaving less PCl₃ than in container A.
Container A does not have less PCl₃; it starts without Cl₂ to consume it in forming PCl₅.
The reactants will not necessarily be completely consumed because the reaction reaches a dynamic equilibrium.

mcqs.stem: CaO or lime is used extensively in steel, glass and paper industries. It is produced in an exothermic reversible reaction by the decomposition of lime (CaCO₃). Choose the conditions to produce maximum amount of lime.
options: Heating at high temperature in a closed vessel
Heating at high temperature in an open vessel
Cooling it in a closed vessel
Cooling it in an open vessel
rationales: A closed vessel allows CO₂ to accumulate, which opposes further CaCO₃ decomposition.
High temperature promotes decomposition, and an open vessel lets CO₂ escape, shifting the reaction toward CaO.
Cooling opposes the decomposition needed to produce CaO.
Cooling opposes decomposition, and opening the vessel does not compensate for the low temperature.

mcqs.stem: What condition should be met for the reversible reaction to achieve the state of equilibrium?
options: All the reactants should be converted into the products.
50% of the reactants should be converted into products.
The concentrations of all the reactants and the products should become constant.
One of the products should be removed from the reaction mixture.
rationales: Equilibrium does not require complete conversion of reactants into products.
Equilibrium does not require a fixed 50% conversion of the reactants.
At equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant because the forward and reverse rates are equal.
Removing a product disturbs the equilibrium rather than being a condition required to attain it.

mcqs.stem: Why the gas starts coming out when you open a can of fizzy drink?
options: Because the solubility of the gas increases
Because the gas is insoluble in water
Because the gas is dissolved under pressure hence it comes out when pressure is decreased
Because the solubility of the gas decreases at high pressure
rationales: Opening the can lowers the pressure, so the gas’s solubility decreases rather than increases.
The gas is dissolved in the drink before the can is opened, so it is not simply insoluble in water.
The gas is dissolved under pressure and escapes when opening the can reduces that pressure.
High pressure increases the gas’s solubility in the drink rather than decreasing it.

mcqs.stem: The following reaction is performed in a closed vessel. CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) How the equilibrium will be affected if you increase the pressure?
options: The forward reaction will be favoured
The backward reaction will be favoured
No effect on forward or backward reaction
rationales: The forward reaction produces a gas, so increased pressure does not favour it.
The backward reaction consumes gaseous CO₂, so increased pressure favours that side, which has fewer gas molecules.
The backward reaction is affected because it consumes the gaseous CO₂.
The pressure change shifts the equilibrium toward the side with fewer gas molecules.

mcqs.stem: When a reaction will become a reversible one?
options: If the activation energy of the forward reaction is comparable to that of backward reaction
If the activation energy of the forward reaction is higher than that of backward reaction
If the activation energy of the forward reaction is lower than that of backward reaction
If the enthalpy change of both the reactions is zero.
rationales: When the forward and backward activation energies are comparable, both directions can proceed at appreciable rates, allowing reversibility.
A much higher forward activation energy would hinder the forward reaction rather than explain a readily reversible reaction.
A much lower forward activation energy would make the forward direction easier but does not by itself establish reversibility.
Zero enthalpy change is not a requirement for a reaction to be reversible.

mcqs.stem: Is reversible reaction useful for preparing compounds on large scale?
options: They are useful only when equilibrium lies far to the right side
They are useful only when equilibrium lies far to the left side
rationales: Reversible reactions can be useful for large-scale preparation when conditions are chosen to favour the desired product.
Reversible reactions can be used industrially by adjusting conditions to obtain a useful yield of the desired compound.
A reaction need not have equilibrium far to the right to be useful, since products can sometimes be separated or conditions adjusted.
An equilibrium far to the left is not the only circumstance in which a reversible reaction can be useful.

mcqs.stem: What will happen to the concentrations of the products if a reversible reaction at equilibrium is not disturbed?
options: They will remain constant for some time and then start decreasing
rationales: At equilibrium, product concentrations remain constant as the forward and reverse reactions proceed at equal rates.
Products do not keep increasing when the system is undisturbed at equilibrium.
Products do not keep decreasing when the system is undisturbed at equilibrium.
The product concentrations remain constant rather than changing after some interval.

mcqs.stem: Which description best identifies a reversible reaction?
options: Reactants form products, and products can form reactants under the same conditions.
All reactants are completely changed into products.
The reaction proceeds only when a product is removed.
The reaction can occur only in an open container.
rationales: This is correct because a reversible reaction can proceed forwards and backwards under the same conditions.
This describes a reaction going to completion, not the usual behaviour of a reversible reaction.
Removing a product can drive a reversible reaction to completion, but it does not define a reversible reaction.
A reversible reaction can occur in a closed container; it does not require an open container.

mcqs.stem: Which symbol does your textbook use to show a reversible reaction?
rationales: This arrow shows a reaction proceeding in one direction, not the reversible symbol.
This is correct because its two half arrowheads point in opposite directions.
This symbol can indicate a gas being produced, but it does not show a reversible reaction.
This symbol can indicate a decrease, but it does not show a reversible reaction.

written.text: Why are combustion reactions generally irreversible?

written.text: Define dynamic equilibrium.
modelAnswer: Dynamic equilibrium is the state in a reversible reaction in which the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates.
As a result, the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.

rubric.why: Identifies the opposing reactions and the equal rates required at dynamic equilibrium.
rubric.description: In a reversible reaction, the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that both reactions continue in a reversible reaction at equal rates.

rubric.why: States the consequence of the equal forward and reverse rates.
rubric.description: The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant, so there is no overall change.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that concentrations remain constant or that there is no overall change.

written.text: What is dynamic equilibrium?
modelAnswer: Dynamic equilibrium is the state in a closed system where the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates.
The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.
written.followUp: What happens to the forward and reverse reaction rates when a reversible reaction reaches dynamic equilibrium?

rubric.why: Equal forward and reverse reaction rates are essential to dynamic equilibrium.
rubric.description: States that the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explicitly stating that the two rates are equal.

rubric.why: At equilibrium, equal rates mean there is no net change in the concentrations of reactants and products.
rubric.description: States that reactant and product concentrations remain constant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that concentrations remain constant at equilibrium.

written.text: What is meant by Dynamic Equilibrium?
modelAnswer: Dynamic equilibrium is the state in a reversible reaction in a closed system when the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal.
Both reactions continue, but the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.
written.followUp: What happens to the forward and reverse reaction rates at dynamic equilibrium?

rubric.why: States the defining rate condition for dynamic equilibrium.
rubric.description: The forward and reverse reaction rates are equal.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the two reaction rates become equal.

rubric.why: Explains why equilibrium is dynamic while observable amounts remain unchanged.
rubric.description: Both reactions continue, while the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.
rubric.how: Award for stating that concentrations remain constant or that both reactions continue.

written.text: How is dynamic equilibrium different from the static equilibrium?
modelAnswer: In dynamic equilibrium, forward and backward changes continue at equal rates.
In static equilibrium, there is no change or movement.
written.followUp: Study the effect of heat on hydrated copper sulphate. Why does this salt look coloured and why does it lose colour upon heating?

rubric.description: States that forward and backward changes continue at equal rates in dynamic equilibrium.
rubric.why: The key feature of dynamic equilibrium is that opposing changes continue at equal rates.
rubric.how: Mention both directions and that their rates are equal.

rubric.description: Contrasts this with no change or movement in static equilibrium.
rubric.why: This distinguishes static equilibrium from continuing dynamic changes.
rubric.how: State that static equilibrium has no continuing change or movement.

written.text: How is dynamic equilibrium different from the static equilibrium?
modelAnswer: In dynamic equilibrium, the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates.
In static equilibrium, no change or movement is taking place.
written.followUp: Elaborate an example of dynamic equilibrium which exists in this world between the three physical states of water.

rubric.description: States that both reactions continue at equal rates.
rubric.why: This states what makes dynamic equilibrium dynamic.
rubric.how: Mention the continuing forward and backward reactions and that their rates are equal.

rubric.description: States that static equilibrium has no change or movement.
rubric.why: This clearly contrasts dynamic equilibrium with a static state.
rubric.how: Explain that a static state has no continuing reaction or movement.

written.text: How can you decrease the time to attain the position of equilibrium in a reversible reaction?
modelAnswer: Use a catalyst and suitable conditions to make the reaction rates faster.
For example, the formation and decomposition of ammonia are reasonably fast at around 400°C in the presence of a catalyst, so equilibrium is reached within minutes.
written.followUp: Elaborate an example of dynamic equilibrium which exists in this world between the three physical states of water.

rubric.description: Names a catalyst as a way to decrease the time.
rubric.why: A catalyst can make the reaction reach equilibrium sooner.
rubric.how: State that a catalyst should be used.

rubric.description: Links faster reaction rates or the textbook ammonia example to shorter time.
rubric.why: The reaction reaches equilibrium sooner when its reactions are reasonably fast.
rubric.how: Explain that rates become faster, or give the ammonia example at around 400°C with a catalyst.

written.text: How is dynamic equilibrium different from the static equilibrium?
modelAnswer: In dynamic equilibrium, the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates.
In static equilibrium, there is no ongoing reaction or movement.
written.followUp: What is the effect of increasing pressure on the following reaction at equilibrium? N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)

rubric.description: State that forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates.
rubric.why: This identifies what continues in dynamic equilibrium.
rubric.how: Mention both continuing reactions and equal rates.

rubric.description: State that static equilibrium has no ongoing reaction or movement.
rubric.why: This distinguishes static equilibrium from dynamic equilibrium.
rubric.how: Contrast dynamic activity with no ongoing change.

written.text: How can you get the maximum yield in a reversible reaction?
modelAnswer: Select suitable temperature and pressure conditions to favour the forward reaction.
Increase the concentration of reactants or remove products as they form.
These changes shift the equilibrium towards the products and increase the yield.
written.followUp: What is the effect of increasing pressure on the following reaction at equilibrium? N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)

rubric.description: State that conditions should favour the forward reaction.
rubric.why: Maximum yield requires equilibrium to favour product formation.
rubric.how: Refer to shifting equilibrium towards the products.

rubric.description: Name suitable changes such as removing product or adjusting pressure, temperature, or concentration.
rubric.why: Give a practical way of adjusting the equilibrium position.
rubric.how: Give at least one relevant condition or product-removal method.

mcqs.stem: A compound which completely ionize in aqueous solution is:
rationales: Acetic acid is a weak acid and only partially ionizes in water.
Sodium hydroxide is a strong base and dissociates essentially completely in aqueous solution.
Benzene is a molecular compound that does not ionize in water.
Sugar dissolves as molecules and does not ionize in water.

mcqs.stem: Out of the following, _____ is a weak electrolyte.
rationales: NaCl dissociates almost completely in water and is a strong electrolyte.
NaOH ionizes almost completely in water and is a strong electrolyte.
H₂SO₄ is a strong electrolyte in water.
CH₃COOH ionizes only partially in water, so it is a weak electrolyte.

mcqs.stem: One of the following, is weak electrolyte
rationales: Correct: acetic acid ionizes only partially in water, making it a weak electrolyte.
Incorrect: sulphuric acid is a strong electrolyte.
Incorrect: sodium chloride dissociates substantially into ions in water.
Incorrect: sodium hydroxide is a strong electrolyte.

mcqs.stem: Example of weak electrolyte is
rationales: NaCl is a strong electrolyte because it dissociates extensively in water.
NaOH is a strong electrolyte because it dissociates extensively in water.
H₂SO₄ is generally classified as a strong electrolyte.
CH₃COOH is a weak electrolyte because it ionizes only partially in water.

mcqs.stem: Which one of the following is electrolyte?
rationales: Sugar solution does not produce ions and is not an electrolyte.
Benzene is a non-electrolyte because it does not form ions in solution.
An acid solution contains mobile ions and conducts electricity.
Rubber does not contain mobile ions and is not an electrolyte.

mcqs.stem: Which one of the following is weak electrolyte?
rationales: Sodium chloride is a strong electrolyte because it dissociates extensively in water.
Sodium hydroxide is a strong electrolyte.
Acetic acid ionizes only partially in water, so it is a weak electrolyte.
Sulfuric acid is a strong electrolyte.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following is a weak electrolyte?
rationales: NaCl dissociates almost completely in water and is a strong electrolyte.
NaOH dissociates almost completely in water and is a strong electrolyte.
CH₃COOH ionizes only partially in water, so it is a weak electrolyte.
H₂SO₄ is generally classified as a strong electrolyte.

mcqs.stem: Acetic acid is an example of
rationales: Acetic acid ionizes only partially in water, so it is not a strong electrolyte.
Acetic acid is a weak electrolyte because it ionizes only partially in water.
Acetic acid is a weak acid, not a strong acid.
Acetic acid is an acid, not a base.

mcqs.stem: Which one of following solution is non-electrolyte:
rationales: Sulfuric acid solution ionizes and conducts electricity.
Sugar solution does not produce ions and is a non-electrolyte.
Lime solution contains ions and conducts electricity.
Sodium chloride solution contains ions and conducts electricity.

mcqs.stem: Which acid is not used as a food or mixed with food?
rationales: Tartaric acid is used in foods such as baking powders and confectionery.
Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) is used in foods as a nutrient and antioxidant.
Citric acid is commonly added to foods for acidity and flavour.
Formic acid is not ordinarily used as a food or mixed with food because it is corrosive and toxic at sufficient concentrations.

mcqs.stem: While baking, which gas is responsible for raising the bread and making it soft?
rationales: Oxygen does not produce the bubbles that make bread rise during baking.
Carbon dioxide forms bubbles in the dough, causing the bread to rise and become soft.
Nitrogen is not the gas responsible for bread rising during baking.
Carbon monoxide is poisonous and does not raise bread.

mcqs.stem: Predict the main characteristics of the reactions of metals with acids.
options: All the above mentioned characteristics are true
rationales: The metal is consumed or dissolves as it reacts with the acid.
The metal’s atoms form a salt with the acid’s anion.
Hydrogen gas is generally evolved when a reactive metal reacts with an acid.
All three listed features generally occur when a reactive metal reacts with an acid.

written.text: Why is HF a weak acid?
modelAnswer: HF is a weak acid because it ionizes only partially in water, producing relatively few H⁺ ions.
The strong H–F bond resists breaking, which contributes to this incomplete ionization.
written.followUp: Why is acetic acid classified as a weak acid?

rubric.why: Identifies incomplete ionization in water as the reason HF is weak.
rubric.description: HF ionizes only partially in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that HF does not ionize completely in water.

rubric.why: Links HF's strong bond to its incomplete ionization.
rubric.description: The strong H–F bond resists ionization.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for relating HF's strong bond to its weak acidity.

written.text: How does calcium metal react with dilute H₂SO₄?
modelAnswer: Calcium reacts with dilute sulfuric acid to form calcium sulfate and hydrogen gas.
Ca(s) + H2SO4(aq) → CaSO4(s) + H2(g).
The sparingly soluble calcium sulfate forms a coating on the calcium, which can slow or stop the reaction.
written.followUp: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of calcium with dilute hydrochloric acid and state the gas produced.

rubric.why: The equation shows calcium displacing hydrogen from dilute sulfuric acid.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced chemical equation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct balanced equation: Ca + H2SO4 → CaSO4 + H2.

rubric.why: Calcium sulfate forms a coating on calcium, and hydrogen gas is produced.
rubric.description: Identifies the coating effect or the gas produced.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a calcium sulfate coating forms or that hydrogen gas is produced.

written.text: Define strong electrolyte and give an example.
modelAnswer: A strong electrolyte is a substance that ionizes almost completely in aqueous solution or in the molten state.
It conducts electricity well; for example, sodium chloride (NaCl) is a strong electrolyte.
written.followUp: Define a weak electrolyte and give one example.

rubric.why: A strong electrolyte ionizes or dissociates almost completely in aqueous solution or in the molten state.
rubric.description: Defines a strong electrolyte by its near-complete ionization or dissociation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it ionizes or dissociates almost completely.

rubric.why: An appropriate example demonstrates a strong electrolyte; strong electrolytes conduct electricity well.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example of a strong electrolyte.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an example such as sodium chloride (NaCl) or hydrochloric acid (HCl).

written.text: Define weak electrolytes.
modelAnswer: Weak electrolytes ionize or dissociate only partially in water.
They conduct electricity weakly because relatively few ions are present in the solution.
written.followUp: What is a strong electrolyte, and how does it differ from a weak electrolyte in water?

rubric.why: States that weak electrolytes form ions only to a limited extent in water.
rubric.description: Weak electrolytes ionize or dissociate only partially in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating partial ionization or dissociation.

rubric.why: Connects partial ionization to weak electrical conduction.
rubric.description: They conduct electricity weakly because relatively few ions are present in solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relation between few ions and weak conduction.

written.text: Which are weak electrolytes?
modelAnswer: Weak electrolytes ionize only partially in water.
Weak acids and weak bases are weak electrolytes; examples include acetic acid (CH₃COOH) and ammonium hydroxide (NH₄OH).
written.followUp: What is a strong electrolyte? Give one example.

rubric.why: Weak electrolytes ionize only partially in solution; weak acids and weak bases are examples.
rubric.description: Identifies weak electrolytes as partially ionizing substances or as weak acids and bases.
rubric.how: Award for stating partial ionization or identifying weak acids/bases.

rubric.why: These are standard examples of weak electrolytes.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of a weak electrolyte.
rubric.how: Award for at least one correct example.

written.text: What are weak electrolytes? Give one example.
modelAnswer: Weak electrolytes ionize only partially in aqueous solution.
Acetic acid (CH3COOH) is an example.
written.followUp: What are strong electrolytes? Give one example.

rubric.why: Partial ionization in solution is the defining feature of a weak electrolyte.
rubric.description: States that weak electrolytes ionize only partially in aqueous solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that only some of the dissolved substance forms ions.

rubric.why: A valid example completes the response.
rubric.description: Gives one example of a weak electrolyte.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example, such as acetic acid.

written.text: Give any two examples of strong electrolytes.
modelAnswer: Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is a strong electrolyte.
Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) is another example of a strong electrolyte.
written.followUp: What happens to an electrolyte when it dissolves in water?

rubric.why: Hydrochloric acid is a strong electrolyte.
rubric.description: Gives one example of a strong electrolyte.
rubric.how: Award for one correct example, such as HCl.

rubric.why: Sodium hydroxide and sodium chloride are strong electrolytes.
rubric.description: Gives a second example of a strong electrolyte.
rubric.how: Award for a second distinct correct example, such as NaOH or NaCl.

written.text: What is meant by strong electrolytes? Give one example.
modelAnswer: Strong electrolytes ionize completely into ions in aqueous solution.
Example: sodium chloride (NaCl).
written.followUp: What is meant by weak electrolytes? Give one example.

rubric.why: Strong electrolytes produce ions completely in aqueous solution or molten state.
rubric.description: States that strong electrolytes ionize completely to form ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for complete ionization or dissociation.

rubric.why: A suitable example must be a strong electrolyte.
rubric.description: Gives one correct example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

written.text: Define weak electrolyte and give an example.
modelAnswer: A weak electrolyte is a substance that ionizes only partially in aqueous solution.
Example: acetic acid (CH₃COOH).
written.followUp: Define a strong electrolyte and give one example.

rubric.why: A weak electrolyte produces ions only partially in aqueous solution.
rubric.description: Defines a weak electrolyte as one that ionizes or dissociates only partially in solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating partial ionization or dissociation in solution.

rubric.why: Acetic acid and carbonic acid are weak electrolytes.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of a weak electrolyte.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

mcqs.stem: The amount of energy given out when an electron is added to an atom is called:
rationales: Lattice energy is associated with forming an ionic solid from gaseous ions.
Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an electron from an atom.
Electronegativity is an atom’s tendency to attract shared electrons in a bond.
Electron affinity is the energy released when an electron is added to an atom.

mcqs.stem: 4th and 5th period of the long form of periodic table are called
rationales: The fourth and fifth periods are not short periods.
Normal periods refers to the second and third periods.
The fourth and fifth periods are called long periods.
Very long periods refers to the sixth and seventh periods.

mcqs.stem: Which one of the following halogen has lowest electronegativity?
rationales: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity among the halogens listed.
Chlorine is more electronegative than bromine and iodine.
Bromine is more electronegative than iodine.
Electronegativity decreases down the halogen group, making iodine the lowest here.

mcqs.stem: In long form of periodic table horizontal lines are called.
rationales: Groups are the vertical columns of the periodic table.
Blocks are regions classified by the subshell being filled.
Periods are the horizontal rows of the periodic table.
Triads are historical groups of three elements, not the horizontal lines.

mcqs.stem: Along the period which one of the following decreases:
rationales: Atomic radius generally decreases across a period.
Ionization energy generally increases across a period.
Electron affinity generally increases across a period, with some exceptions.
Electronegativity generally increases across a period.

mcqs.stem: In long form of periodic table the horizontal lines are called:
rationales: Groups are the vertical columns of the periodic table.
Blocks classify elements by the subshell being filled.
Periods are the horizontal rows of the periodic table.
Triads are historical groups of three elements, not horizontal rows.

mcqs.stem: Which one of the following Halogens has lowest Electronegativity?
rationales: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity among the halogens listed.
Chlorine is more electronegative than bromine and iodine.
Bromine is more electronegative than iodine.
Iodine has the lowest electronegativity among the halogens listed.

mcqs.stem: Mendeleev Periodic Table was based on:
rationales: Mendeleev did not base his table on electronic configuration.
Mendeleev arranged elements mainly in order of increasing atomic mass.
Atomic number became the basis of the modern periodic table, not Mendeleev’s table.
Completion of subshells was not the basis of Mendeleev’s table.

mcqs.stem: Identify the General Electronic Configuration of Boron Family:
rationales: The boron family does not have an outer configuration of ns¹.
The boron family does not have an outer configuration of ns² alone.
The configuration ns²np² characterizes the carbon family.
Boron-family elements have the general outer configuration ns²np¹.

mcqs.stem: Identify the General Electronic Configuration of Alkaline Earth Metals:
rationales: Alkaline earth metals do not have the general outer configuration ns¹.
The configuration ns²np² is characteristic of the carbon family.
The configuration ns²np¹ is characteristic of the boron family.
Alkaline earth metals have the general outer configuration ns².

mcqs.stem: The symbol of silver is.
rationales: Na is the symbol for sodium.
Ca is the symbol for calcium.
Ag is the symbol for silver.
Si is the symbol for silicon.

mcqs.stem: Vertical columns in modern periodic table are called.
rationales: Periods are the horizontal rows of the modern periodic table.
Groups are the vertical columns of the modern periodic table.
Noble gases are a family of elements, not the name for all vertical columns.
Transition elements are a category of elements, not the name for vertical columns.

written.text: Define Ionization energy.
modelAnswer: Ionization energy is the minimum amount of energy required to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom.
written.followUp: Define electron affinity.

rubric.why: Checks that ionization energy is an energy requirement.
rubric.description: Ionization energy is the minimum energy required.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is the minimum energy required.

rubric.why: Checks what is removed and the state of the atom.
rubric.description: The energy removes an electron from an isolated gaseous atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for specifying the removal of an electron from a gaseous atom.

written.text: Define atomic radius
modelAnswer: Atomic radius is half the distance between the nuclei of two identical bonded atoms; it represents the distance from the nucleus to the outermost shell of an atom.
written.followUp: Define ionic radius.

rubric.why: Atomic radius is commonly defined as half the distance between the nuclei of two identical bonded atoms; it also represents the distance from the nucleus to the outermost shell in the elementary atomic model.
rubric.description: Defines atomic radius using the standard inter-nuclear distance or nucleus-to-outermost-shell description.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for a correct definition; award 1 mark for an incomplete but relevant definition.

written.text: Define electron affinity
modelAnswer: Electron affinity is the energy released when an isolated gaseous atom accepts an electron to form a negative ion.
written.followUp: Define electronegativity.

rubric.why: Includes the energy change associated with electron gain.
rubric.description: States that energy is released when the atom gains an electron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the release of energy.

rubric.why: Specifies the atom’s state when it accepts the electron.
rubric.description: States that a neutral gaseous atom accepts an electron to form a negative ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for specifying the gaseous atom accepting an electron.

written.text: Give the trend of ionization energy in a period.
modelAnswer: Ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
This is because nuclear charge increases and atomic radius generally decreases, so the outer electron is attracted more strongly to the nucleus.
written.followUp: State and explain the trend in ionization energy down a group.

rubric.why: Ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
rubric.description: Gives the direction of the ionization-energy trend across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it increases across the period from left to right.

rubric.why: Increasing nuclear charge and decreasing atomic radius strengthen attraction to the outer electron.
rubric.description: Gives a reason for the increase across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the trend to increasing nuclear attraction, increasing nuclear charge, or decreasing atomic radius.

written.text: What is meant by periodic function?
modelAnswer: A periodic function is a property that repeats at regular intervals.
When elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number, their properties repeat periodically.
written.followUp: State the modern periodic law.

rubric.why: Periodicity means that similar properties recur at intervals.
rubric.description: States that the properties of elements repeat periodically.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that element properties repeat or recur periodically.

rubric.why: The periodic repetition occurs when elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
rubric.description: Relates the periodic repetition of properties to increasing atomic number.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying increasing atomic number as the basis for the periodic repetition.

written.text: State modern periodic law. Who put forward this law?
modelAnswer: Modern periodic law: The properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.
This law was put forward by Henry Moseley.
written.followUp: State the modern periodic law and name the scientist who proposed it.

rubric.why: The modern periodic law relates the periodic properties of elements to their atomic numbers.
rubric.description: States the modern periodic law.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.

rubric.why: Henry Moseley put forward the modern periodic law.
rubric.description: Names the scientist who proposed the law.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Henry Moseley.

written.text: How did Newlands arrange the elements?
modelAnswer: Newlands arranged the elements in order of increasing atomic masses.
He observed that the properties of every eighth element were similar to those of the first, like notes in a musical octave.
written.followUp: State the main idea of the Law of Octaves and name its proposer.

rubric.why: Newlands used increasing atomic mass as the order of arrangement.
rubric.description: States that Newlands arranged elements in order of increasing atomic mass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the increasing atomic mass order.

rubric.why: The similarity of every eighth element is the defining observation in Newlands’ arrangement.
rubric.description: States that every eighth element had properties similar to the first.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the every-eighth similarity.

written.text: Why the Elements are called "S" and "P" Block Elements?
modelAnswer: They are called s-block elements because the last electron enters an s subshell.
They are called p-block elements because the last electron enters a p subshell.
written.followUp: Why are elements in Groups 1 and 17 called s-block and p-block elements, respectively?

rubric.why: The block name depends on the subshell into which the last electron enters.
rubric.description: Explains the name s-block.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the last electron enters an s subshell for s-block elements.

rubric.why: The block name depends on the subshell into which the last electron enters.
rubric.description: Explains the name p-block.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the last electron enters a p subshell for p-block elements.

written.text: Why shielding effect of electrons makes cation formation easy?
modelAnswer: Inner-shell electrons shield the outermost electrons from the full attraction of the nucleus.
The outer electrons are therefore less strongly held and can be removed easily to form a cation.
written.followUp: Explain how shielding affects the removal of an outer-shell electron.

rubric.why: Inner-shell electrons shield outer electrons from the full attraction of the nucleus.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of inner electrons on the nuclear attraction experienced by outer electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that shielding by inner electrons reduces the nuclear attraction on outer electrons.

rubric.why: Reduced attraction makes outer electrons easier to remove, allowing cations to form.
rubric.description: Connects shielding with easy electron removal and cation formation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that shielding makes an outer electron easier to remove or a cation easier to form.

written.text:
(a) Explain the variation in the following properties in the periods giving reasons.
i- Atomic radius ii- Ionization energy
(b) Suppose a new element is discovered. Where would you like to accommodate this element in the periodic table?
modelAnswer: (a) Across a period from left to right, atomic radius decreases.
The nuclear charge increases while added electrons enter the same main shell, so the stronger attraction pulls the electron cloud closer to the nucleus.
Ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
The outer electrons are held more strongly because of the increased nuclear attraction and smaller atomic radius, so more energy is needed to remove an electron.
(b) Find the atomic number of the new element.
Place it in the position that preserves the increasing order of atomic numbers.
Use its electronic configuration to identify the appropriate period.
Place it in a group with elements of similar outermost-shell configuration and chemical properties.
written.followUp: Explain how atomic radius and ionization energy change from left to right across a period.

rubric.why: Atomic radius becomes smaller across a period.
rubric.description: (a) States that atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction of the trend.

rubric.why: Increasing nuclear charge attracts electrons in the same main shell more strongly.
rubric.description: (a) Explains the decrease in radius by increasing nuclear charge while electrons are added to the same shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking increased nuclear charge and the same shell to the smaller radius.

rubric.why: Ionization energy generally rises across a period.
rubric.description: (a) States that ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction of the trend.

rubric.why: Stronger attraction makes the outer electron harder to remove, so more energy is required; both the cause and consequence are needed for these marks.
rubric.description: (a) Links the stronger attraction on outer electrons to the increased energy needed to remove one.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the stronger nuclear attraction and 1 mark for stating that more energy is needed to remove an electron.

rubric.description: (b) Use atomic number to determine its place in the sequence.
rubric.why: The modern table's arrangement is based on atomic number.
rubric.how: State that the new element is placed according to its atomic number.

rubric.description: (b) Show how it fits into the sequence.
rubric.why: Elements must follow the modern table's ascending order.
rubric.how: Say it is placed in the correct position in increasing atomic-number order.

rubric.description: (b) Identify the period using its electronic configuration.
rubric.why: The electronic configuration can help determine its period.
rubric.how: Relate its configuration to the appropriate period.

rubric.description: (b) Identify a suitable group.
rubric.why: A matching group reflects similar chemical properties.
rubric.how: Place it with elements whose properties and outermost-shell configurations are similar.

written.text:
(a) Arrangement of the elements in the form of a periodic table is a remarkable achievement of chemists. Comment on this statement citing the benefits of this table.
(b) Which information is needed to locate the elements in the periodic table if you do not know its atomic number? Is atomic mass helpful for this purpose?
modelAnswer: (a) The periodic table arranges elements in increasing order of atomic number.
Elements with similar properties are placed in the same groups.
The properties of elements repeat after regular intervals, showing periodicity.
This arrangement makes it easier to study and compare elements.
The position of an element can help us predict its properties.
(b) The electronic configuration and properties of the element can help to identify its group and period.
Elements in a group have similar outermost-shell electronic configurations and similar chemical properties.
Atomic mass is not the basis for locating elements in the modern periodic table.
The modern periodic table is based on increasing atomic number.
written.followUp: Why was atomic number chosen to arrange the elements in the periodic table?

rubric.description: (a) State how the table is organised.
rubric.why: The answer should identify the organising principle of the modern table.
rubric.how: Mention arrangement in increasing atomic number.

rubric.description: (a) Explain the benefit of groups.
rubric.why: Grouping related elements is a key benefit of the table.
rubric.how: State that elements with similar properties occur in the same group.

rubric.description: (a) Mention periodicity.
rubric.why: The table displays the regular recurrence of element properties.
rubric.how: Explain that properties repeat after regular intervals.

rubric.description: (a) Give a practical benefit.
rubric.why: The arrangement makes relationships between elements easier to examine.
rubric.how: Say the table helps students study or compare elements.

rubric.description: (a) Give a further use of the table.
rubric.why: The arrangement can help predict the properties of elements.
