written.text:
(a) Explain the variation in the following properties in the periods giving reasons. (a) Atomic radius (b) Ionization energy
(b) The electronic configuration of the outermost shell of an element is s²p³. Find out period number and the group number of the element. In which block will you place this element?
modelAnswer: (a) (a) Atomic radius generally decreases from left to right in a period.
The charge on the nucleus increases across the period and pulls the electrons closer to the nucleus.
(b) Ionization energy generally increases from left to right in a period.
The smaller radius gives stronger attraction between the nucleus and the outer electrons.
Therefore, more energy is needed to remove an outer electron.
(b) The number of outermost electrons = 2 + 3 = 5.
The configuration ns² np³ belongs to group 15.
The p-subshell is being filled, so the element belongs to the p-block.
The shell number is not given in s²p³, so the period cannot be fixed from this information alone.
written.followUp: Atomic radii of boron and aluminum are 88 pm and 125 pm respectively. Which element is expected to lose electron or electrons easily?

rubric.description: (a) State the ionization-energy trend across a period.
rubric.why: The direction of the ionization-energy trend is essential.
rubric.how: State that ionization energy generally increases from left to right.

rubric.description: (a) Explain the change in ionization energy.
rubric.why: The stronger attraction explains why removing an electron needs more energy.
rubric.how: Relate the smaller radius to stronger attraction between the nucleus and outer electrons.

rubric.description: (a) Give the combined final conclusion.
rubric.why: The final statement must correctly summarise both trends.
rubric.how: Conclude that radius decreases while ionization energy increases across a period.

rubric.description: (b) Identify the number of electrons in the stated outermost-shell configuration.
rubric.why: Counting the outermost electrons is the basis for identifying the group.
rubric.how: Add the electrons in s² and p³ to obtain five.

rubric.description: (b) Give the group number.
rubric.why: The group number is a requested part of the answer.
rubric.how: Use the group 15 configuration ns² np³ shown in Table (8.2).

rubric.description: (b) Identify the block.
rubric.why: The question also asks for the element's block.
rubric.how: The outermost configuration includes p electrons, so it belongs to the p-block.

rubric.description: (b) State the limitation in identifying the period from the given shorthand.
rubric.why: The period depends on the number of the shell being filled, which is not shown in s²p³.
rubric.how: Explain that a principal shell number, such as 2 in 2s² 2p³, is needed to fix the period.

written.text: Why are noble gases not reactive?

This stable arrangement means they have little tendency to gain, lose, or share electrons, so they are not reactive.

mcqs.stem: The most abundant gas found in the atmosphere is
rationales: Carbon monoxide is present only in small amounts in the atmosphere.

mcqs.stem: Which gases are responsible for greenhouse effect?
rationales: Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide are air pollutants but are not the principal greenhouse-gas pair among these options.

Carbon dioxide and methane trap outgoing heat and are greenhouse gases.
Oxygen and nitrogen make up most of the atmosphere but are not significant greenhouse gases.

options: Waste gases from digestion of animals
rationales: Decomposing vegetation is not the main source of atmospheric sulfur oxides in this context.

Photochemical smog forms through sunlight-driven reactions and is not the source of atmospheric sulfur.
Burning sulfur-containing fossil fuels releases sulfur oxides into the atmosphere.

mcqs.stem: Concentration of which gas in the atmosphere is decreased by photosynthesis in plants?
rationales: Photosynthesis releases oxygen rather than decreasing its atmospheric concentration.
Photosynthesis does not substantially consume atmospheric nitrogen.

mcqs.stem: People of which age groups are most affected by the air pollution?
rationales: Young adults are generally less vulnerable than children and older people to the effects of air pollution.

Children and aged people are particularly vulnerable to air pollution because of developing or weakened health.

mcqs.stem: In which area there is a greater possibility of acid rain?
rationales: Villages usually have fewer major sources of the pollutants that cause acid rain.
Big cities can have substantial emissions, but industrial areas are the most likely choice because of concentrated pollutant sources.
Industrial emissions of sulfur and nitrogen oxides make acid rain more likely around industrial areas.
Water bodies may be affected by acid rain but are not necessarily where it is most likely to form.

mcqs.stem: Why is smog not felt in summer?
options: Because fog is not present in summer
Because due to heat of the Earth the smoke rises up
Because in summer smoke and fog cannot mix with each other
Because less fossil fuels are burnt in summer
rationales: Fog can occur in summer under suitable conditions, so its absence is not the general explanation.
Warm conditions cause smoke to rise and disperse, making the ground-level smog described here less noticeable.
Smoke and fog can mix; summer warmth and atmospheric conditions, not an inability to mix, explain the effect.
Fossil fuels are still burned in summer, so reduced fuel use is not the general explanation.

rationales: Carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide are not the essential combination identified for photochemical smog formation.

Volatile organic compounds and nitrogen oxides are involved, but sunlight is essential and carbon monoxide is not the defining component.

written.text: What are the harmful effects of carbon monoxide?

written.text:
(a) Describe the harmful effects of the major pollutants present in the air.
(b) Describe harmful effects of the major pollutants present in the air.
modelAnswer: (a) Carbon dioxide: Higher levels increase global warming, which can melt ice caps, warm oceans and raise sea levels; extreme weather may also occur.
Carbon monoxide: It is extremely poisonous and can cause suffocation and death by stopping red blood cells from carrying the oxygen the body needs.
Oxides of nitrogen: They can damage lungs, irritate eyes and damage vegetation; they can also cause acid rain.
Oxides of sulphur: They irritate eyes, cause breathing difficulties and cause acid rain.
Hydrocarbons: They can cause pneumonia, coughing and other breathing and lung diseases; they also cause global warming.
Particulate matter: It irritates eyes, can cause severe breathing problems for people with asthma, makes clothes dirty and reduces visibility.
Ozone: Breathing ozone can cause chest pain, coughing, throat irritation and congestion.
(b) Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin in the blood, reducing its ability to carry oxygen and causing serious health effects.
Sulphur dioxide irritates the respiratory system and can contribute to acid rain.
Nitrogen oxides can cause respiratory problems and contribute to acid rain and photochemical smog; particulate matter can damage the lungs.
Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) damage the ozone layer, while hydrocarbons can contribute to photochemical smog.

rationales: Alkanes undergo substitution reactions, such as halogenation.
Alkanes undergo combustion in oxygen.
Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons and generally do not undergo addition reactions.
Alkanes can undergo cracking to form smaller hydrocarbons.

mcqs.stem: Which hydrocarbon is responsible for explosions in coal mines?
rationales: Butane is not the gas chiefly responsible for coal-mine explosions.
Pentane is not the gas chiefly responsible for coal-mine explosions.
Methane, also called firedamp, can accumulate in coal mines and cause explosions.
Ethene is not the gas chiefly responsible for coal-mine explosions.

mcqs.stem: Which product will be formed when ethyl bromide (CH₃ CH₂ Br) is treated with Zn/HCl
rationales: Reduction replaces bromine with hydrogen without removing a carbon, so methane is not formed.
Reduction of ethyl bromide replaces bromine with hydrogen to form ethane, CH₃—CH₃.
This product has four carbons and would require carbon-chain coupling, not simple reduction.
This product has three carbons and would require carbon-chain extension, not simple reduction.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following is not a process of halogenation of alkanes?
rationales: Cracking breaks larger hydrocarbons into smaller ones and is not a process of alkane halogenation.
Chlorination is halogenation using chlorine.
Bromination is halogenation using bromine.
Iodination is halogenation using iodine.

written.text: Differentiate between an organic and an inorganic compound.

written.text: Why are organic compounds found in large numbers?
modelAnswer: Carbon forms four covalent bonds and forms strong, stable bonds with itself.

This gives rise to a very large number of organic compounds.

written.text:
(a) Why is carbon so important as an element that the whole branch of chemistry is based on it?
(b) Why do alkanes show little reactivity towards the other reagents?
modelAnswer: (a) Carbon is generally unable to gain or lose electrons to form ionic bonds, so it forms four covalent bonds.
Because of its small size, these covalent bonds are short and strong.
Carbon forms strong, stable bonds with itself and with hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen.
The self-linking property of carbon is called catenation.
Catenation enables carbon to form long, straight and branched chains and rings.
These properties allow carbon to form a very large number of compounds.
(b) Alkanes contain only carbon–carbon and carbon–hydrogen single bonds.
They do not have a reactive functional group or a carbon–carbon multiple bond.
Therefore, alkanes show little reactivity towards usual chemical reagents.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following pairs of quantities may be measured in the same unit?
rationales: Heat is energy, while temperature is measured in kelvins or degrees, not units of energy.
Temperature and area are different kinds of quantities and use different units.
Heat and work are both forms of energy, so they may be measured in the same unit, such as joules.
Length and work are different kinds of quantities and use different units.

mcqs.stem: In which unit we usually measure the energy present in the food?
rationales: Kilojoules are used for energy, but the customary unit named in this item for food energy is the calorie.
Megajoules are energy units, but they are not the usual unit for expressing the energy in food here.
The calorie is commonly used to express the energy content of food.
The joule is an SI energy unit, but the customary food-energy unit among these choices is the calorie.

mcqs.stem: What prefix is used for 10⁻¹²?
rationales: Mega represents 10⁶, not 10⁻¹².
Pico represents 10⁻¹².
Giga represents 10⁹, not 10⁻¹².
Tessa is not the SI prefix for 10⁻¹²; the relevant prefix is pico.

mcqs.stem: In SI unit of pressure is expressed in:
rationales: Newton per metre is not a unit of pressure because pressure is force per unit area.
Newton per square metre is equivalent to a pascal, but pascal is the named SI unit requested here.
Joule is the SI unit of energy, not pressure.
Pascal is the named SI unit of pressure.

mcqs.stem: Which symbol is used for kilogram in SI units?
rationales: K is the symbol for kelvin, not kilogram.
A lowercase k is the SI prefix kilo, not the symbol for kilogram by itself.
Kgm is not the SI symbol for kilogram.
kg is the SI symbol for kilogram.

mcqs.stem: What does a mole represent?
rationales: A mole represents a specified number of elementary entities, so it relates to number.
Mass is measured in units such as kilograms or grams, not represented by a mole.
Volume is measured in units such as litres or cubic metres, not represented by a mole.
Length is measured in units such as metres, not represented by a mole.

mcqs.stem: Which unit of volume should usually be used in Chemistry?
rationales: Millilitres are used for small volumes, but the usual general unit in chemistry among these choices is the litre.
The litre is commonly used for measuring volume in chemistry.
Cubic centimetres are useful for small volumes, but the usual general unit among these choices is the litre.
Cubic metres are SI volume units but are generally too large for routine chemistry measurements.

mcqs.stem: Express 0.000840 in scientific notation:
rationales: 840 × 10⁻⁶ equals 0.000840, but its coefficient is not between 1 and 10 as required in normalized scientific notation.
8.40 × 10⁻⁴ equals 0.000840 and has a coefficient between 1 and 10.
84.0 × 10⁻⁵ equals 0.000840, but its coefficient is not between 1 and 10 as required in normalized scientific notation.

mcqs.stem: In SI units prefix nano means:
rationales: Nano means 10⁻⁹.
10⁻⁸ is not the value represented by nano.
10⁻¹¹ is not the value represented by nano.
10⁻¹² is represented by pico, not nano.

mcqs.stem: 65°C is equivalent to:
rationales: 208 K is not the correct conversion; adding 273 to 65 gives 338 K.
65°C is approximately 338 K because kelvin temperature is found by adding 273 to Celsius temperature.
403 K is not the correct conversion of 65°C.
300 K is not the correct conversion; 65°C is approximately 338 K.

mcqs.stem: Which SI-derived unit is used for volume?
rationales: Metre is the base unit of length, not volume.
Square metre is the derived unit of area.
Cubic metre is the derived SI unit of volume.
Kilogram is the base unit of mass.

mcqs.stem: What power of ten does the prefix milli represent?
rationales: 10⁻¹ represents deci.
10⁻² represents centi.
10⁻³ represents milli.
10⁻⁶ represents micro.

mcqs.stem: Safety in the chemistry laboratory is:
options: the responsibility of the students only
the responsibility of the professor only
the responsibility of the lab. incharge only
rationales: Safety is not solely the students’ responsibility; everyone in the laboratory shares it.
The professor has an important role, but is not the only person responsible for safety.
The lab in-charge has safety duties, but responsibility is shared by everyone in the lab.
Correct: everyone in the laboratory shares responsibility for maintaining safety.

mcqs.stem: Accidents often result from:
rationales: Mistakes can contribute to accidents, but they are not the only cause listed.
Failing to use common sense can contribute to accidents, but it is not the only cause listed.
Failing to follow instructions can contribute to accidents, but it is not the only cause listed.
Correct: mistakes, lack of common sense, and failure to follow instructions can all lead to accidents.

mcqs.stem: The label “Warning” on a chemical bottle signifies:
options: that the chemical can cause less serious injury
that the chemical can cause serious injury
that user should be careful when using chemical
that user should open it only in the presence of a teacher
rationales: Correct: in the hazard-label system assumed here, “Warning” indicates a less serious hazard than “Danger.”
This describes a more severe hazard level, typically signaled by “Danger,” rather than “Warning.”
This is general advice, not the specific meaning of the “Warning” label.
A teacher’s presence is not what the “Warning” label signifies.

mcqs.stem: The label “Corrosive” on a chemical bottle indicates:
options: that the material is an oxidizing agent
that the material can degrade rapidly upon exposure
that its contact destroys living tissue
rationales: An oxidizing agent is a distinct hazard category and is not the meaning of “Corrosive.”
Rapid degradation upon exposure describes instability or decomposition, not corrosiveness.
Correct: corrosive substances can destroy living tissue on contact.
The possibility of explosion is a different hazard and is not what “Corrosive” indicates.

mcqs.stem: Example of highly toxic chemical:
rationales: Ethanol is not the highly toxic example among these choices.
Acetic acid can be hazardous, but it is not the highly toxic example among these choices.
Correct: potassium cyanide is highly toxic.
Potassium permanganate is hazardous, but it is not the highly toxic example among these choices.

mcqs.stem: Example of self-reactive chemical:
rationales: Potassium is highly reactive, but it is not the self-reactive example intended here.
Phenol is hazardous, but it is not generally classified as the self-reactive example in this list.
Correct: picric acid can become dangerously unstable, especially when dry, and is the self-reactive example.
n-Hexane is flammable, but it is not the self-reactive example in this list.

mcqs.stem: When diluting an acid with water:
rationales: Adding acid quickly can cause dangerous heating and splashing.
The mixture should be stirred carefully as appropriate; avoiding stirring is not the safe dilution rule.
Correct: add acid slowly to water to reduce the risk of heat-driven splashing.
Adding water to concentrated acid can cause rapid heating and splashing.

mcqs.stem: What should you do in case of a fire drill in the lab.?
options: close gas valves and turn off all equipments
carry chemicals out of the lab.
rationales: A safety shower is for rinsing chemical exposure, not for evacuating during a fire drill.
A fume cupboard is not a safe place to shelter during a fire drill.
Correct: if it is safe to do so, shut gas valves and turn off equipment before evacuating.
Chemicals should not be carried out during a fire drill because this delays evacuation and creates additional risk.

mcqs.stem: What is the safe method for mixing concentrated acid with water?
options: Add water to the concentrated acid
rationales: This is unsafe because the textbook instructs that acid must not be added to water in this direction.
This is correct because the textbook says to add acid slowly to water.
This is unsafe because the textbook gives a specific order and says to add the acid slowly.
This is not the stated safety method and adds an unnecessary hazard.

mcqs.stem: You suspect that a chemical may explode. What should you do with its container?
options: Move the container to a safer place
Open the container to inspect it
Do not try to move the container
Shake it gently to check its contents
rationales: Moving it could cause a shock, which may trigger an explosion.
Opening it is not a safe response and may expose people to the hazard.
This is correct because the textbook says not to attempt to move a suspected explosive container.
Shaking it creates shock and could trigger an explosion.

mcqs.stem: Which precaution is recommended when working with corrosive chemicals that may give off vapours?
options: Store the chemical beside other chemicals
Keep it in an unlabelled container
rationales: This is correct because corrosive chemicals should be used in a fume cupboard to avoid breathing corrosive vapours.
This is not a stated safety precaution and could make safe storage harder.
This is unsafe; the textbook says not to work alone with toxic chemicals and calls for care with hazards.
This is unsafe because the chemical should be identifiable and kept safely.

mcqs.stem: Which action is a suitable precaution when working with toxic chemicals?
options: Wear gloves and a mask or other protective device
Taste a small amount to identify it
Work in a closed, unventilated room
Leave it in a drinking-water bottle
rationales: This is correct because the textbook advises wearing gloves, masks or other protective devices.
This is dangerous; chemicals must never be tasted.
This is unsafe because toxic chemical work areas should be well ventilated and work should be done in a fume hood.
This is unsafe because toxic chemicals should be kept in their original container.

written.text: Why flammable liquids are not stored in refrigerator?
modelAnswer: Flammable liquids can ignite and must be kept away from heat sources.
They are not stored in refrigerators because they may ignite or explode.
written.followUp: Under which circumstances explosive chemicals are likely to explode?

rubric.description: Recognizes that the liquids are flammable.
rubric.why: Identifying the hazard shows why special storage is needed.
rubric.how: State that flammable liquids can ignite and must be kept away from heat sources.

rubric.description: Gives the risk of storing them in a refrigerator.
rubric.why: The danger of ignition or explosion explains the storage precaution.
rubric.how: Explain that they may ignite or explode.

written.text: How will you dispose off acid and alkali waste after the experiment is finished?
modelAnswer: Acids and bases are first neutralized.
They are then disposed of in the sewer.
written.followUp: Under which circumstances explosive chemicals are likely to explode?

rubric.description: States that the acid and alkali are neutralized first.

rubric.how: Write that acids and bases must first be neutralized.

rubric.description: States the disposal step after neutralization.
rubric.why: The textbook gives sewer disposal after neutralization.
rubric.how: Say that the neutralized waste is then disposed of in the sewer.

written.text: Name some corrosive chemicals.
modelAnswer: Examples of corrosive chemicals are mineral acids including HF, caustic alkalies and acetic acid (glacial).
written.followUp: Under which circumstances explosive chemicals are likely to explode?

rubric.description: Names a mineral acid, such as HF.

rubric.how: Give HF or another mineral acid as an example.

rubric.description: Names another corrosive chemical.
rubric.why: A further example completes the requested list.
rubric.how: Give caustic alkalies or glacial acetic acid.

written.text: What type of safety precautions are adopted to avoid damage due to explosive chemicals?
modelAnswer: Obtain prior approval from the teacher, use the smallest quantity and conduct the experiment in a fume hood.
Remove nearby chemicals and apparatus and inform other people working with you.
Wear safety spectacles, gloves and a lab coat, and keep flammable compounds away from heat sources.
Pour flammable liquid carefully and properly dispose of hazardous waste.
written.followUp: Under which circumstances explosive chemicals are likely to explode?

rubric.description: Gives a precaution about approval, quantity or work location.
rubric.why: Planning and minimizing the amount reduce the risk of an incident.
rubric.how: Mention teacher approval, the smallest quantity, or using a fume hood.

rubric.description: Gives another relevant precaution.
rubric.why: Protective equipment and careful handling help reduce harm.
rubric.how: Mention PPE, keeping flammable chemicals away from heat, careful pouring, or proper disposal.

written.text: What type of damages can reactive chemicals cause?
modelAnswer: When reactions with reactive chemicals are not properly performed, they may cause fires and explosions and evolve dangerous gases.
These reactions can cause extreme damage to life and property.
written.followUp: Under which circumstances explosive chemicals are likely to explode?

rubric.description: Names fires or explosions.
rubric.why: These are the direct dangers named in the section.
rubric.how: State that improperly performed reactions may cause fires or explosions.

rubric.description: Mentions dangerous gases or damage to life and property.
rubric.why: This identifies further consequences and the seriousness of the damage.
rubric.how: Add that dangerous gases may evolve and life and property may be harmed.

written.text: Which chemicals can cause suffocation?
modelAnswer: Chemical asphyxiants can cause suffocation.
Examples include hydrogen cyanide, carbon monoxide, nitrogen, argon, helium, methane and carbon dioxide.
written.followUp: Under which circumstances explosive chemicals are likely to explode?

rubric.description: Identifies chemical asphyxiants.
rubric.why: The answer should identify the relevant group of chemicals.
rubric.how: State that chemical asphyxiants can cause suffocation.

rubric.description: Names at least one textbook example.
rubric.why: An example shows that the student can recognize the chemicals in this group.
rubric.how: Give one or more examples such as carbon monoxide or nitrogen.

written.text: What type of reactions should be carried out in fume cupboard?
modelAnswer: Reactions that may form hazardous vapours, including toxic or corrosive vapours, should be carried out in a fume cupboard.
This helps avoid breathing the vapours.
written.followUp: Under which circumstances explosive chemicals are likely to explode?

rubric.description: States that the reaction is done in a fume cupboard.
rubric.why: The answer must identify the required place for the work.
rubric.how: Name the fume cupboard as the place to carry out the work.

rubric.description: Identifies the kind of reaction or vapour hazard.
rubric.why: The reason for using a fume cupboard is to avoid breathing harmful vapours.
rubric.how: Explain that it is for work that may produce hazardous, toxic or corrosive vapours.

written.text: What does warning sign “caution” convey the message?
modelAnswer: The caution sign warns people to be alert and take extra care.
People must follow the precautions required in that area.
written.followUp: What does warning sign “caution” convey the message?

rubric.description: State that the sign warns people to be alert or careful.
rubric.why: The answer must explain the warning conveyed by caution.
rubric.how: Mention being alert, careful or taking extra care.

written.text: Name some explosive chemicals.
modelAnswer: Examples of explosive chemicals include picric acid, nitroglycerin and TNT.
These chemicals must be handled only with appropriate laboratory precautions.
written.followUp: What does warning sign “caution” convey the message?

rubric.description: Give at least one correct example.
rubric.why: The question asks for examples of explosive chemicals.

rubric.description: Give at least one additional correct example.

written.text:
(a) A student has spilled over a corrosive and explosive chemical due to an accident. Which emergency measures you will take to tackle the situation.
(b) Explain hazards due to explosive and toxic chemicals.
modelAnswer: (a) Alert the teacher and other people working nearby.
Keep people away from the spill and do not move or disturb the suspected explosive chemical, because shock may cause an explosion.
Follow the teacher's emergency instructions and do not attempt to handle the spill without appropriate precautions.
Use appropriate protective equipment for the corrosive chemical, such as gloves and splash goggles or a face shield.
If anyone is affected, wash the area with soap and water and seek medical attention.
(b) Explosive chemicals can cause a sudden release of pressure, gas and heat when they experience sudden shock.
They can cause burns and other injuries and damage people, windows and tables.
A toxic chemical is poisonous and is capable of causing serious health problems.
Toxic vapours can form during an experiment, so work in a fume hood and seek immediate medical aid if exposure is suspected.
written.followUp: Under which circumstances explosive chemicals are likely to explode?

rubric.description: (a) Alerts the teacher or people nearby.
rubric.why: Promptly informing responsible people helps others respond safely.
rubric.how: Say to alert the teacher and inform other people working nearby.

rubric.description: (a) Keeps people from disturbing the explosive chemical.
rubric.why: A suspected explosive chemical must not be disturbed because shock may trigger an explosion.
rubric.how: State that the container should not be moved or shocked.

rubric.description: (a) Gives a safe response to the spill area.

rubric.description: (b) Mentions toxic vapours or an appropriate precaution.

written.text:
(a) A few decades ago, a tanker carrying poisonous chlorine gas leaked and the gas spread over a large area in Lahore. The accident killed a few persons as well as animals. Give some concrete proposals to avoid such an accident in future.

modelAnswer: (a) Chlorine should be handled and transported according to safe procedures by trained people.
The tanker, containers and equipment should be checked and maintained to prevent leaks.
Chlorine should be kept in a suitable, clearly identified container.
An emergency plan should be prepared so that people know how to respond to a leak.
If a leak occurs, people should be moved away from the contaminated area and an appropriately trained person should be called.
(b) The radiation symbol identifies a radiation hazard.
The sign marked “Risk of asphyxiation” warns of a suffocation hazard.

rubric.how: Suggest checking the tanker, container or equipment before use and transport.

rubric.description: (a) Proposes safe handling or transport.

rubric.description: (a) Proposes training for workers.

rubric.description: (b) Identify the radiation warning symbol.

rubric.description: (b) Explain that the warning alerts people to the risk of suffocation.
rubric.why: The answer should show that the sign is a warning of a real danger.
rubric.how: Mention the risk warning or lack of oxygen.

(a) A few decades ago, a tanker carrying poisonous chlorine gas leaked and the gas spread over a large area in Lahore. The accident killed a few persons as well as animals. Give some concrete proposals to avoid such an accident in future.
(b) Explain the importance of warning signs and symbols to avoid any accident in the lab.
modelAnswer: (a) Display clear toxic-gas warning signs on tankers and storage areas.

They show which precautions must be followed.
Following these precautions helps people act safely and avoid accidents.

rubric.description: (a) Propose checking and maintaining gas containers.

rubric.how: Mention an emergency response plan or drills.

rubric.description: (b) State the safety benefit.

rubric.how: Explain that following the signs helps people act safely and avoid accidents.

mcqs.stem: Mist is an example of solution.
rationales: Mist consists of tiny liquid droplets dispersed in a gas.
Gas in liquid describes a gas dispersed in a liquid, such as foam.
Solid in gas describes solid particles dispersed in a gas, such as smoke.
Gas in solid describes gas dispersed in a solid.

mcqs.stem: One amu (Atomic Mass Unit) is equivalent to:
rationales: This is incorrect because one amu is about 1.66 × 10⁻²¹ mg.
This is correct because one amu is approximately 1.66 × 10⁻²⁴ g.
This is incorrect because one amu is approximately 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
This is incorrect because the exponent should be −24, not −23.

mcqs.stem: A bond formed between two non-metals is expected to be:
rationales: Non-metal atoms generally form covalent bonds by sharing electrons.
Ionic bonds usually form between a metal and a non-metal.
A coordinate covalent bond is a particular type of covalent bond, not the general expected answer here.
Metallic bonds occur between metal atoms.

mcqs.stem: The mass of one molecule of water is
rationales: One water molecule has a mass of approximately 18 atomic mass units.
18 g is the mass of one mole of water, not one molecule.
18 mg is not the mass of one water molecule.
18 kg is not the mass of one water molecule.

mcqs.stem: The following reaction is an exothermic reaction. H₂ + Cl₂ \(\xrightarrow{Sunlight}\) 2HCl From where does the energy come to break the bonds of H₂ and Cl₂?
options: By collisions of the molecules with the walls of the container
rationales: Ordinary molecular collisions do not supply the specific initiating energy in this photochemical reaction.
Sunlight supplies the energy needed to initiate bond breaking in H₂ and Cl₂.
The surroundings are not the stated source of the initiating energy.
Collisions with the container walls do not provide the initiating energy specified for this reaction.

mcqs.stem: What will happen if the rates of forward and reverse reactions are very high?
options: The equilibrium point will reach very soon.
The equilibrium point will reach very late.
The reaction will not attain the state of dynamic equilibrium.
The reaction will be practically irreversible.
rationales: High forward and reverse rates make the equilibrium composition establish quickly.
High reaction rates do not make equilibrium take longer to establish.
A reversible reaction can still reach dynamic equilibrium when both rates are high.
High rates alone do not make a reversible reaction practically irreversible.

mcqs.stem: A compound which completely ionize in aqueous solution is:
rationales: Acetic acid is a weak acid and only partially ionizes in water.
Sodium hydroxide is a strong base and dissociates essentially completely in aqueous solution.
Benzene is a molecular compound that does not ionize in water.
Sugar dissolves as molecules and does not ionize in water.

mcqs.stem: The amount of energy given out when an electron is added to an atom is called:
rationales: Lattice energy is associated with forming an ionic solid from gaseous ions.
Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an electron from an atom.
Electronegativity is an atom’s tendency to attract shared electrons in a bond.
Electron affinity is the energy released when an electron is added to an atom.

mcqs.stem: Transition elements are:
rationales: Transition elements are not all gases; they are generally solid metals.
Transition elements are not non-metals.
Transition elements are metals.
Transition elements are not metalloids.

mcqs.stem: The development of chemical industry has generated.
rationales: Unemployment is not the intended environmental effect of chemical industry development.
Malnutrition is not the intended effect described here.
Chemical industry development can generate polluted air.
Lack of transport is not the intended effect described here.

mcqs.stem: Which one molecule will evaporate first:
rationales: Hexane has the lowest boiling point of these alkanes and evaporates most readily.
Octane has a higher boiling point than hexane.
Decane has a higher boiling point than octane.
Dodecane has the highest boiling point among these options.

mcqs.stem: Which compound has a triple covalent bond?
rationales: CH₄ contains only single covalent bonds.
C₂H₄ contains a double bond, not a triple bond.
C₂H₂ contains a carbon–carbon triple covalent bond.
C₂H₆ contains only single covalent bonds.

written.text: Why do we stir paints thoroughly before using?
modelAnswer: Paint contains solid pigment particles dispersed in a liquid, and these particles settle on standing.
We stir the paint to redisperse the particles and make the paint uniform before use.
written.followUp: Why should a bottle of paint be shaken or stirred before use?

rubric.why: Identifies what happens to paint when left standing.
rubric.description: Solid pigment particles settle out of the liquid on standing.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the solid particles/pigment settle or sink when paint is left undisturbed.

rubric.why: Explains the purpose of stirring before use.
rubric.description: Stirring redistributes the settled particles to make the paint uniform.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that stirring redistributes or mixes the particles evenly.

written.text: Define Electronic Configuration.
modelAnswer: Electronic configuration is the distribution of electrons in the shells around the nucleus of an atom.
written.followUp: Write the electronic configuration of an atom having 12 electrons.

rubric.why: Electronic configuration describes how electrons are distributed among shells.
rubric.description: Identifies the distribution of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning the arrangement or distribution of electrons.

rubric.why: The electrons are arranged in shells around the nucleus.
rubric.description: Specifies that the electron arrangement is in shells around the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons are arranged in shells around the nucleus.

written.text: What are the defects of Ruther Ford's Atomic Model?
modelAnswer: Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability: revolving electrons should radiate energy and fall into the nucleus.
It also could not explain the line spectra of atoms.
written.followUp: State one major limitation of Rutherford’s atomic model.

rubric.why: According to classical physics, revolving electrons should radiate energy and fall into the nucleus, so the model could not explain atomic stability.
rubric.description: Explains that Rutherford’s model could not account for atomic stability.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it could not explain why electrons do not lose energy and fall into the nucleus.

rubric.why: The model did not explain the discrete line spectra of atoms.
rubric.description: Identifies the failure to explain atomic spectra.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the model could not explain the line spectra of atoms.

written.text: Why does ice float on water?
modelAnswer: In ice, hydrogen bonds hold water molecules in an open cage-like structure.
This makes ice less dense than liquid water, so ice floats on water.
written.followUp: Why is ice less dense than liquid water?

rubric.why: Describes the open arrangement of water molecules in ice.
rubric.description: Hydrogen bonding forms an open cage-like structure in ice.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the open, cage-like structure formed in ice.

rubric.why: Connects the structure to the reason ice floats.
rubric.description: The open structure gives ice a lower density than liquid water, so it floats.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that ice is less dense than water or explaining this by its larger volume for the same mass.

written.text: Differentiate between lone pair and bond pair of electrons
modelAnswer: A lone pair is a pair of valence electrons that is not shared with another atom.
A bond pair is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms to form a covalent bond.
written.followUp: Differentiate between a polar covalent bond and a non-polar covalent bond.

rubric.why: Defines a lone pair as a pair not shared in bonding.
rubric.description: States that a lone pair is a pair of valence electrons not shared with another atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the unshared electron pair.

rubric.why: Defines a bond pair as electrons shared between atoms.
rubric.description: States that a bond pair is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms in a covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the shared electron pair.

written.text: Define redox reaction.
modelAnswer: A redox reaction is a chemical reaction in which oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously.
Oxidation and reduction take place together in the same reaction.
written.followUp: Define oxidation and reduction, and state how they are related in a redox reaction.

rubric.why: A redox reaction involves both oxidation and reduction.
rubric.description: States that oxidation and reduction occur in a redox reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying both processes.

rubric.why: The two processes occur together in the same reaction.
rubric.description: States that oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that both occur at the same time.

written.text: Define Avogadro's number?
modelAnswer: Avogadro's number is the number of particles present in one mole of a substance.
Its value is approximately 6.02 × 10²³.
written.followUp: How many particles are present in one mole of a substance? Give the name and value of this number.

rubric.why: The definition identifies the number of particles in one mole.
rubric.description: Definition
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining Avogadro's number as the number of particles or entities in one mole of a substance.

rubric.why: The value is the key quantitative fact in the definition.
rubric.description: Value
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the value as approximately 6.02 × 10²³.

written.text: Differentiate between molecular mass and formula mass.
modelAnswer: Molecular mass is the sum of the atomic masses of all the atoms in one molecule, usually of a covalent compound.
Formula mass is the sum of the atomic masses of all the atoms or ions represented by one formula unit, usually of an ionic compound.
written.followUp: Differentiate between molecular mass and gram molecular mass.

rubric.why: Molecular mass is the sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule.
rubric.description: Defines molecular mass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly defining molecular mass as the sum of the atomic masses in a molecule.

written.text: Why test tube becomes warm when Li₂SO₄ is dissolved in water?
modelAnswer: Dissolving Li₂SO₄ in water is exothermic, so heat is released and the test tube becomes warm.
The energy released during hydration of the ions is greater than the energy absorbed to separate the ions in the lattice.
written.followUp: Why does a test tube become cold when an endothermic salt dissolves in water?

rubric.why: The observed warming is due to heat released during dissolution.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that heat is released.

rubric.why: The heat of hydration released is greater than the energy absorbed in separating the ionic lattice.
rubric.description: Explain the energy balance that produces the warming.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly comparing hydration and lattice energies.

written.text: Differentiate between spontaneous reaction and non spontaneous reaction.
modelAnswer: A spontaneous reaction occurs on its own under the given conditions without a continuous supply of external energy.
A non-spontaneous reaction does not occur on its own under the given conditions and requires an external energy supply.
written.followUp: Differentiate between exothermic and endothermic reactions.

rubric.why: A spontaneous reaction proceeds on its own under the stated conditions.

rubric.description: Defines a non-spontaneous reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it requires an external energy supply or does not occur on its own under the given conditions.

written.text: What is the difference between enthalpy and enthalpy change?
modelAnswer: Enthalpy (H) is the total heat content of a system; H = U + PV.
Enthalpy change (ΔH) is the difference between the enthalpy of products and reactants, and represents heat absorbed or released at constant pressure.
written.followUp: What is the difference between heat and enthalpy change?

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct description of enthalpy.

rubric.description: Defines enthalpy change as the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct meaning of enthalpy change.

written.text: Why are combustion reactions generally irreversible?
modelAnswer: Combustion forms stable products, usually carbon dioxide and water, and releases energy.
These products do not readily recombine to form the original fuel, so combustion is generally irreversible.
written.followUp: Why is the formation of carbon dioxide and water by burning a fuel difficult to reverse?

rubric.why: Combustion forms stable products, usually carbon dioxide and water.
rubric.description: Identifies the stable products formed in combustion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for referring to stable products or naming carbon dioxide and water.

rubric.why: The products do not readily recombine to form the original fuel, so the reaction does not readily proceed in reverse.
rubric.description: Explains why combustion is generally irreversible.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the products do not readily form the original fuel again.

written.text: Define dynamic equilibrium.
modelAnswer: Dynamic equilibrium is the state in a reversible reaction in which the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates.
As a result, the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.
written.followUp: What conditions are required for dynamic equilibrium in a reversible reaction?

rubric.why: Identifies the opposing reactions and the equal rates required at dynamic equilibrium.
rubric.description: In a reversible reaction, the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that both reactions continue in a reversible reaction at equal rates.

rubric.why: States the consequence of the equal forward and reverse rates.
rubric.description: The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant, so there is no overall change.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that concentrations remain constant or that there is no overall change.

written.text: Why is HF a weak acid?
modelAnswer: HF is a weak acid because it ionizes only partially in water, producing relatively few H⁺ ions.
The strong H–F bond resists breaking, which contributes to this incomplete ionization.
written.followUp: Why is acetic acid classified as a weak acid?

rubric.why: Identifies incomplete ionization in water as the reason HF is weak.
rubric.description: HF ionizes only partially in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that HF does not ionize completely in water.

rubric.why: Links HF's strong bond to its incomplete ionization.
rubric.description: The strong H–F bond resists ionization.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for relating HF's strong bond to its weak acidity.

written.text: Define Ionization energy.
modelAnswer: Ionization energy is the minimum amount of energy required to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom.
written.followUp: Define electron affinity.

rubric.why: Checks that ionization energy is an energy requirement.
rubric.description: Ionization energy is the minimum energy required.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is the minimum energy required.

rubric.description: The energy removes an electron from an isolated gaseous atom.

written.text: Define atomic radius
modelAnswer: Atomic radius is half the distance between the nuclei of two identical bonded atoms; it represents the distance from the nucleus to the outermost shell of an atom.
written.followUp: Define ionic radius.

rubric.why: Atomic radius is commonly defined as half the distance between the nuclei of two identical bonded atoms; it also represents the distance from the nucleus to the outermost shell in the elementary atomic model.
rubric.description: Defines atomic radius using the standard inter-nuclear distance or nucleus-to-outermost-shell description.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for a correct definition; award 1 mark for an incomplete but relevant definition.

written.text: Why are noble gases not reactive?
modelAnswer: Noble gases have complete outermost electron shells (helium has a complete duplet; the others have an octet).
This stable arrangement means they have little tendency to gain, lose, or share electrons, so they are not reactive.
written.followUp: Why are noble gases generally chemically stable?

rubric.why: Noble gases have complete outermost electron shells.
rubric.description: Identifies the complete outermost electron shell of noble gases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that their valence shell is complete.

rubric.why: Their stable electron arrangement gives them little tendency to gain, lose, or share electrons.
rubric.description: Explains how the complete shell results in low reactivity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for connecting the stable arrangement to little or no tendency to gain, lose, or share electrons.

written.text: Write any two uses of sodium.
modelAnswer: Sodium is used in sodium-vapour lamps, including street lamps.
Liquid sodium is used as a coolant or heat-transfer medium in some nuclear reactors.
written.followUp: Write any two uses of potassium.

rubric.why: Sodium is also used as a heat-transfer medium in some nuclear reactors.

written.text: What are transition metals?
modelAnswer: Transition metals are elements that have partially filled d orbitals in their atoms or in one of their ions.

written.text: What are the harmful effects of carbon monoxide?
modelAnswer: Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin in the blood to form carboxyhaemoglobin.
This reduces the blood’s ability to carry oxygen and can cause suffocation, unconsciousness, or death.
written.followUp: Explain how carbon monoxide interferes with oxygen transport in the body.

rubric.description: States that carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin in the blood.

rubric.why: Explains the harmful effect on the body.

written.text: Define environmental Chemistry.
modelAnswer: Environmental chemistry is the branch of chemistry that studies chemical processes occurring in the environment and the effects of pollutants and human activities on it.

written.text: Differentiate between an organic and an inorganic compound.
modelAnswer: Organic compounds generally contain carbon bonded to hydrogen, for example methane (CH₄).
Inorganic compounds are generally mineral compounds and usually do not contain carbon–hydrogen bonds, for example sodium chloride (NaCl).
written.followUp: Give one difference between an organic compound and an inorganic compound, with an example of each.

rubric.description: States that inorganic compounds are generally mineral compounds and usually lack carbon–hydrogen bonds; a suitable example may also be given.

written.text: How are organic compounds useful for us?
modelAnswer: Organic compounds are used as food and as fuels such as petrol and natural gas.
They are also used to make medicines, clothing fibres and plastics.

written.text:
(a) Write differences between elements, compounds and mixtures?
(b) Explain Bohr’s atomic model.
modelAnswer: (a) An element consists of only one kind of atom; a compound contains two or more elements chemically combined; a mixture contains substances physically mixed together.
The elements in a compound are present in a fixed proportion, whereas the components of a mixture may be present in any proportion.
A compound has properties different from those of its constituent elements, while the components of a mixture retain their properties.
A compound can be separated into its elements by chemical means, whereas a mixture can be separated by physical methods.
(b) An atom has a small, positively charged nucleus at its centre, and electrons move around it.
Electrons can move only in certain fixed orbits, or shells, each having a definite energy.
An electron does not radiate energy while it remains in one of these permitted orbits.
An electron absorbs energy to move to a higher-energy orbit and emits energy when it falls to a lower-energy orbit.
written.followUp: Compare elements, compounds and mixtures by their composition and method of separation.

rubric.why: Award for distinguishing the basic composition of all three types of matter.
rubric.description: (a) Identifies an element as one kind of atom, a compound as chemically combined elements, and a mixture as physically combined substances.
rubric.how: Give 2 marks when all three distinctions are stated; give 1 mark if two are correct.

rubric.why: Award for distinguishing the fixed composition of compounds from mixtures.
rubric.description: (a) States that compounds have a fixed ratio of elements, whereas mixture components can be in any proportion.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for both parts of the comparison.

rubric.why: Award for comparing the properties of compounds and mixtures.
rubric.description: (a) States that a compound has properties different from its constituent elements, while mixture components retain their properties.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for both parts of the comparison.

rubric.why: Award for distinguishing how compounds and mixtures can be separated.
rubric.description: (a) States that compounds are separated chemically, while mixtures can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for both methods of separation.

rubric.why: This identifies the atom’s central structure and the particles around it.
rubric.description: (b) States that an atom has a central nucleus with electrons around it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying both the nucleus and electrons.

rubric.why: Bohr’s model allows electrons to occupy only particular orbits or energy levels.
rubric.description: (b) States that electrons occupy fixed orbits or shells with definite energies.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for fixed orbits, shells or definite energy levels.

rubric.why: Electrons in permitted stationary orbits do not lose energy by radiation.
rubric.description: (b) States that an electron does not radiate energy while it remains in a permitted orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons in stationary orbits do not radiate energy.

rubric.why: An electron changes energy when it moves between permitted orbits.
rubric.description: (b) States that an electron absorbs energy to move to a higher orbit or emits energy when it moves to a lower orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing either transition with its energy change.

written.text:
(a) Define ionic bond. Explain it with an example.
(b) Explain Arrhenius concept of acids and bases.
modelAnswer: (a) An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by the transfer of electrons.
For example, a sodium atom transfers its outermost electron to a chlorine atom.
Sodium becomes a positive ion, Na⁺, and chlorine becomes a negative ion, Cl⁻.
The oppositely charged ions attract each other and form the ionic compound sodium chloride, NaCl.
(b) According to the Arrhenius concept, an acid produces H⁺ ions in aqueous solution.
A base produces OH⁻ ions in aqueous solution.
written.followUp: Define a covalent bond and explain its formation in a hydrogen molecule.

rubric.why: Defines ionic bonding as electron transfer followed by attraction between ions.
rubric.description: (a) An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed after electron transfer.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for electron transfer and 1 mark for electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

rubric.why: Explains the electron transfer and resulting ions in the example.
rubric.description: (a) In sodium chloride, sodium transfers one electron to chlorine, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the transfer from sodium to chlorine and 1 mark for correctly identifying the ions.

rubric.why: Connects the ions' attraction to formation of the ionic compound.
rubric.description: (a) The attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ forms the ionic compound NaCl.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the ionic attraction producing sodium chloride.

rubric.description: (b) Defines an Arrhenius acid.
rubric.why: This is the defining Arrhenius behaviour of an acid.
rubric.how: State that an acid increases H⁺ (or H₃O⁺) in aqueous solution.

rubric.description: (b) Defines an Arrhenius base.
rubric.why: This is the defining Arrhenius behaviour of a base.
rubric.how: State that a base produces OH⁻ in water.

rubric.description: (b) Specifies the aqueous condition.
rubric.why: The Arrhenius definitions specifically refer to aqueous solution.
rubric.how: Make clear that the ions are produced in water.

written.text:
(a) Explain the variation in the following properties in the periods giving reasons.
i- Atomic radius ii- Ionization energy
(b) Percentage of CO₂ in air is only 0.04%. Then how does it become harmful for the ecosystem?
modelAnswer: (a) Across a period from left to right, atomic radius decreases.
The nuclear charge increases while added electrons enter the same main shell, so the stronger attraction pulls the electron cloud closer to the nucleus.
Ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
The outer electrons are held more strongly because of the increased nuclear attraction and smaller atomic radius, so more energy is needed to remove an electron.
(b) Higher levels of CO₂ lead to increased global warming.
Global warming can melt ice caps and warm oceans, causing sea levels to rise.
It can also cause extreme weather changes such as heat waves, heavy rains and wild fires.
written.followUp: Explain how atomic radius and ionization energy change from left to right across a period.

rubric.why: Atomic radius becomes smaller across a period.
rubric.description: (a) States that atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction of the trend.

rubric.why: Increasing nuclear charge attracts electrons in the same main shell more strongly.
rubric.description: (a) Explains the decrease in radius by increasing nuclear charge while electrons are added to the same shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking increased nuclear charge and the same shell to the smaller radius.

rubric.why: Ionization energy generally rises across a period.
rubric.description: (a) States that ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction of the trend.

rubric.why: Stronger attraction makes the outer electron harder to remove, so more energy is required; both the cause and consequence are needed for these marks.
rubric.description: (a) Links the stronger attraction on outer electrons to the increased energy needed to remove one.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the stronger nuclear attraction and 1 mark for stating that more energy is needed to remove an electron.

rubric.description: (b) State the main cause-and-effect link.
rubric.why: The answer must connect increased carbon dioxide levels with global warming.
rubric.how: Explain that higher CO₂ levels lead to increased global warming.

rubric.description: (b) Give an effect on ice or oceans.
rubric.why: Melting ice caps or warming oceans are stated consequences.
rubric.how: Mention melting ice caps or warming oceans.

rubric.description: (b) State the effect on sea levels.
rubric.why: Rising sea levels are an important ecosystem consequence named in the section.

rubric.description: (b) Give an example of extreme weather.
rubric.why: The section also links higher CO₂ levels with extreme weather.
rubric.how: Name a heat wave, heavy rain or wild fire.

mcqs.stem: Which one of the following solutions contains more water?
rationales: A 2 M solution has the greatest solute concentration among these choices.
A 1 M solution is more concentrated than the 0.5 M and 0.25 M solutions.
A 0.5 M solution is more concentrated than the 0.25 M solution.
A 0.25 M solution is the most dilute and therefore contains the greatest proportion of water for the same solution volume.

mcqs.stem: Which one of the following shell consists of three subshells?
rationales: The O shell has eight subshells, not three.
The N shell has four subshells, not three.
The L shell has two subshells, not three.
The M shell has three subshells: s, p, and d.

mcqs.stem: Transfer of Electrons between Atoms results in:
rationales: Metallic bonding involves attraction between metal ions and delocalized electrons, not electron transfer between atoms.
Electron transfer between atoms forms an ionic bond.
Covalent bonding involves sharing electrons rather than transferring them.
Coordinate covalent bonding involves a shared pair donated by one atom rather than electron transfer.

mcqs.stem: Empirical formula of benzene is:
rationales: CH₂O is not the empirical formula of benzene.
CHO is not the empirical formula of benzene.
C₂H₂ is the molecular formula of ethyne, not benzene’s empirical formula.
Benzene, C₆H₆, simplifies to the empirical formula CH.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following reactions has the least value of activation energy?
rationales: The reaction of hydrogen with oxygen requires energy to overcome a substantial activation barrier.
Combustion of solid carbon requires overcoming a significant activation barrier.
The ions in solution can react readily to form insoluble AgCl, so this precipitation reaction has the least activation energy.
The reaction involving solid iodine and hydrogen requires overcoming a comparatively larger activation barrier.

mcqs.stem: Predict which components of the atmosphere react in the presence of lightning.
rationales: Lightning does not primarily drive a reaction between nitrogen and water vapour.
Oxygen and water vapour are not the main atmospheric components reacting to form nitrogen oxides during lightning.
Carbon dioxide and oxygen are not the principal pair involved in this lightning reaction.
Lightning provides enough energy for nitrogen and oxygen to react and form nitrogen oxides.

mcqs.stem: Out of the following, _____ is a weak electrolyte.
rationales: NaCl dissociates almost completely in water and is a strong electrolyte.
NaOH ionizes almost completely in water and is a strong electrolyte.
H₂SO₄ is a strong electrolyte in water.
CH₃COOH ionizes only partially in water, so it is a weak electrolyte.

mcqs.stem: 4th and 5th period of the long form of periodic table are called
rationales: The fourth and fifth periods are not short periods.
Normal periods refers to the second and third periods.
The fourth and fifth periods are called long periods.
Very long periods refers to the sixth and seventh periods.

mcqs.stem: Chlorine atom has ______ electrons in the valence shell.
rationales: Chlorine does not have one valence electron.
Chlorine does not have two valence electrons.
Chlorine has seven, not five, valence electrons.
Chlorine has seven valence electrons, so this is correct.

mcqs.stem: The most abundant gas found in the atmosphere is
rationales: Carbon monoxide is present only in small amounts in the atmosphere.
Oxygen is abundant but is less abundant than nitrogen.
Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the atmosphere, the largest share.
Argon is present in much smaller amounts than nitrogen.

mcqs.stem: Molecular formula of Benzene is
rationales: C₆H₁₂O₆ is the molecular formula of glucose.
C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ is the molecular formula of sucrose.
C₆H₆ is the molecular formula of benzene.
CaCO₃ is the formula of calcium carbonate.

mcqs.stem: Which other atom is almost always present along with carbon atom in all organic compounds?
rationales: Oxygen is common in many organic compounds but is not almost always present.
Nitrogen occurs in some organic compounds but is not almost always present.
Hydrogen is almost always bonded to carbon in organic compounds.
Halogens occur only in some organic compounds, not almost always.

written.text:
(a) What is a coordinate covalent bond? Explain it with the help of examples.
(b) Compare Arrhenius and Brønsted – Lowry concepts of acids and bases.
modelAnswer: (a) A coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair are donated by one atom.
The atom donating the pair is the donor; the atom accepting it is the acceptor.
In NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺, nitrogen donates its lone pair to H⁺, forming a coordinate covalent bond.
In H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺, oxygen donates one of its lone pairs to H⁺, forming a coordinate covalent bond.
(b) Arrhenius: an acid produces H⁺ in water, while a base produces OH⁻ in water.
Brønsted–Lowry: an acid donates a proton (H⁺), while a base accepts a proton (H⁺).
The Brønsted–Lowry concept describes proton transfer and is not restricted to aqueous solution.

mcqs.stem: An inorganic chemist places one mole of PCl₃ in a container A and one mole of each Cl₂ and PCl₃ in container B. Both the containers were sealed and heated to the same temperature to reach the state of equilibrium. Guess about the composition of mixtures in both the containers.
options: Both the containers will have the same composition of mixtures.
Container A will have more concentration of PCl₃ than B.
Container A will have less concentration of PCl₃ than B.
Both the containers will have zero concentration of its reactants.
rationales: The mixtures will differ because the containers start with different amounts of the reacting substances.
In container B, some PCl₃ reacts with Cl₂ to form PCl₅, leaving less PCl₃ than in container A.
Container A does not have less PCl₃; it starts without Cl₂ to consume it in forming PCl₅.
The reactants will not necessarily be completely consumed because the reaction reaches a dynamic equilibrium.

written.text: How many molecules are present in 1.5 g H₂O?
modelAnswer: Given: m = 1.5 g = 1.5 × 10⁻³ kg; M(H₂O) = 18 g mol⁻¹ = 18 × 10⁻³ kg mol⁻¹.

Substitution: n = (1.5 × 10⁻³ kg)/(18 × 10⁻³ kg mol⁻¹) = 0.0833 mol.
N = 0.0833 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 5.02 × 10²² molecules.

(b) A strong acid ionizes to a large extent in water.

(b) Q10.2. Percentage of CO₂ in air is only 0.04%. Then how does it become harmful for the ecosystem?
modelAnswer: (a) (a) Atomic radius generally decreases from left to right in a period.
The charge on the nucleus increases across the period and pulls the electrons closer to the nucleus.
(b) Ionization energy generally increases from left to right in a period.
The smaller radius gives stronger attraction between the nucleus and the outer electrons.
Therefore, more energy is needed to remove an outer electron.
(b) Although CO₂ makes up only about 0.04% of air, it absorbs and traps some outgoing heat.
When its concentration increases, the greenhouse effect becomes stronger.
This causes global warming and climate change.
Changes in temperature, rainfall and habitats can disturb ecosystems and harm organisms.

written.text: What is saturated solution and how it is prepared?
modelAnswer: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a specified temperature.

written.text: What is meant by Molarity?
modelAnswer: Molarity is the number of moles of solute dissolved per dm³ (litre) of solution.

written.text: Differentiate between physical and chemical properties.

written.text: Explain how are dilute solution prepared from concentrated solutions?
modelAnswer: Use the dilution formula M1V1 = M2V2 to calculate the volume of concentrated solution required.
Put some distilled water into a volumetric flask.
Measure the calculated volume of concentrated solution with a pipette and transfer it to the flask.
Add distilled water until the bottom of the meniscus reaches the calibration mark.
Stopper the flask and mix the solution thoroughly.
When diluting an acid, add the acid slowly to water, never water to acid.

modelAnswer: Ice floats on water because it is less dense than liquid water.

written.text: Define molecule and describe four types of molecules.
modelAnswer: A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and retain its chemical properties.
A monoatomic molecule contains one atom; for example, helium (He).
A diatomic molecule contains two atoms; for example, hydrogen (H₂).
A triatomic molecule contains three atoms; for example, water (H₂O).
A polyatomic molecule contains more than three atoms; for example, phosphorus (P₄).

written.text: Narrate four characteristics of colloids.
modelAnswer: A colloid is a heterogeneous mixture, although it may appear homogeneous to the naked eye.

A concentrated solution contains a relatively large amount of solute; for example, a large amount of sugar dissolved in water.
A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a solvent at a particular temperature; for example, saturated salt water.
An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute at that temperature; for example, salt water to which more salt can still be added and dissolved.

written.text: Define boiling point. Explain how is it affected by different factors.
modelAnswer: The boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which its vapour pressure becomes equal to the external pressure.
External pressure: Increasing the pressure raises the boiling point; decreasing the pressure lowers it.
Impurities: Dissolved non-volatile impurities generally raise the boiling point.
Nature of the liquid: Stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to overcome and result in a higher boiling point.

written.text: Give comparison between solution and colloid.
modelAnswer: A solution is homogeneous, whereas a colloid is heterogeneous but may appear homogeneous.
Solution particles are smaller than 1 nm; colloidal particles are about 1–1000 nm in size.
A solution does not show the Tyndall effect; a colloid scatters light and shows the Tyndall effect.
Particles of both solutions and colloids pass through ordinary filter paper.
Particles in both mixtures remain dispersed and do not settle on standing.

written.text: Ice floats on water why?

written.text: What is solubility? How temperature effect it. Write in detail
modelAnswer: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a solvent at a specified temperature to form a saturated solution.
It is commonly expressed as the amount of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a specified temperature.
As temperature increases, the solubility of most solid solutes in liquids generally increases.
In contrast, the solubility of gases in liquids generally decreases as temperature increases.

written.text: Explain the factors on which diffusion of liquids depends .
modelAnswer: Diffusion occurs from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
A greater concentration difference (concentration gradient) makes diffusion faster.
Increasing temperature increases the kinetic energy of particles, so diffusion becomes faster.
Smaller particles generally diffuse faster than larger particles.
The nature of the liquid also affects diffusion; it is generally faster in a less viscous liquid.

written.text:
A lunar mission has recently brought samples from the Moon. The following experiments were then carried out on it. Point out the branch of chemistry these experiments are related to. 1. Determining its composition
2. Studying the physical properties of materials it contains
3. Carrying out chemical reactions with usual inorganic reagents
modelAnswer: 1. Determining the sample's composition involves analysis of its components, so it is analytical chemistry.
2. Studying physical properties of materials is related to physical chemistry.
3. Reactions with usual inorganic reagents are related to inorganic chemistry.
Therefore, the branches are analytical chemistry, physical chemistry and inorganic chemistry, respectively.

written.text:
(a) Write down any five properties of cathode rays
(b) Describe postulates of Bohr's Atomic Theory.
modelAnswer: (a) Cathode rays travel in straight lines.
They consist of negatively charged particles called electrons.
They are deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
They produce fluorescence when they strike certain substances.
Their nature is independent of the gas in the discharge tube and the material of the electrodes.
(b) Electrons revolve around the nucleus in definite circular orbits or shells, each having a fixed energy.
An electron does not radiate or absorb energy while it remains in a stationary orbit.
An electron absorbs energy to jump to a higher energy level and releases energy when it falls to a lower level.
The energy absorbed or emitted is equal to the difference between the two energy levels.

written.text:

(b) Explain Bohr’s atomic model.
modelAnswer: (a) Cathode rays are produced in a discharge tube containing gas at low pressure when a high voltage is applied between its electrodes.
They travel in straight lines.
They carry a negative charge.
They are deflected towards the positive plate in an electric field.
They produce fluorescence when they strike certain substances.
(b) An atom has a small, positively charged nucleus at its centre, and electrons move around it.
Electrons can move only in certain fixed orbits, or shells, each having a definite energy.
An electron does not radiate energy while it remains in one of these permitted orbits.
An electron absorbs energy to move to a higher-energy orbit and emits energy when it falls to a lower-energy orbit.

written.text:
(a) Explain five postulates of Bohr's atomic model.
(b) Write four results of Experiment of Rutherford's Atomic Model.
modelAnswer: (a) Electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed circular orbits called energy levels or shells.
An electron in a permitted orbit does not radiate or absorb energy; its energy remains constant.
Only certain orbits are allowed, and the electron’s angular momentum is quantized: mvr = nh/2π.
The energy of an orbit increases as its distance from the nucleus increases.
An electron absorbs or emits a definite amount of energy when it jumps between orbits; ΔE = hν.
(b) Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without any deflection.
Some alpha particles were deflected through small angles.
Very few alpha particles were deflected through large angles or turned back.
These results showed that most of the atom is empty space and that its positive charge is concentrated in a small, dense nucleus.
written.followUp: State four postulates of Dalton’s atomic theory.

written.text: What is a coordinate covalent bond? Explain it with the help of examples.
modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair are donated by one atom.
The atom donating the pair is the donor; the atom accepting it is the acceptor.
In NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺, nitrogen donates its lone pair to H⁺, forming a coordinate covalent bond.
In H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺, oxygen donates one of its lone pairs to H⁺, forming a coordinate covalent bond.

written.text: Define ionic bond and explain it with an example.
modelAnswer: An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by the transfer of electrons from one atom to another.
A sodium atom loses one electron to form a sodium ion: Na → Na+ + e−.
A chlorine atom gains this electron to form a chloride ion: Cl + e− → Cl−.
The oppositely charged Na+ and Cl− ions attract each other and form sodium chloride (NaCl).

written.text: Why does electropositive character increase in a group.
modelAnswer: Down a group, atomic size and shielding effect increase.
The valence electron is farther from the nucleus and is less strongly attracted to it.
It is therefore lost more easily, so electropositive character increases.

rubric.why: The outer electron becomes easier to remove, so the atom more readily forms a positive ion.

written.text: Define coordinate covalent bond and explain it with two examples.
modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair are donated by the same atom.
In the ammonium ion, NH4+, nitrogen in NH3 donates a lone pair to H+ to form a coordinate covalent bond.
In the hydronium ion, H3O+, oxygen in H2O donates a lone pair to H+ to form a coordinate covalent bond.
written.followUp: Define a coordinate covalent bond and explain its formation in the hydronium ion, H3O+.

rubric.why: A coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond formed by sharing an electron pair.

written.text: Define boiling point and explain how it is affected by nature of liquid and intermolecular forces.
modelAnswer: The boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which its vapour pressure becomes equal to the external pressure.
The boiling point depends on the nature of the liquid; different liquids have different boiling points.
A volatile liquid has a relatively low boiling point, while a less volatile liquid has a higher boiling point.
When a liquid boils, its molecules must overcome the intermolecular forces of attraction.
Stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to overcome and therefore give a higher boiling point; weaker forces give a lower boiling point.
written.followUp: Define melting point and explain how intermolecular forces affect it.

rubric.why: Boiling point is defined by the temperature at which a liquid's vapour pressure equals the external pressure.

rubric.why: Different liquids have different boiling points because their nature and volatility differ.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct statement about the effect of liquid nature or volatility.

rubric.description: Relates volatility to boiling point.

rubric.description: Explains the effect of force strength on boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship between force strength and boiling point.

written.text: Define ionic bond and give its example.

written.text: Define electrolyte. Discuss its different types.
modelAnswer: An electrolyte is a substance that produces mobile ions when molten or dissolved in water and therefore conducts electricity.
A strong electrolyte ionises almost completely in aqueous solution and conducts electricity well; examples include hydrochloric acid and sodium chloride.
A weak electrolyte ionises only partially in aqueous solution and conducts electricity weakly; examples include acetic acid and ammonium hydroxide.
written.followUp: Define an electrolyte and distinguish between strong and weak electrolytes with examples.

rubric.description: An electrolyte produces mobile ions and conducts electricity when molten or in aqueous solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a definition linking ions to electrical conduction.

rubric.description: A weak electrolyte ionises only partially in solution and conducts electricity weakly; examples include acetic acid or ammonium hydroxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for partial ionisation and 1 mark for a suitable example or its weak conductivity.

written.text: How an Atom can accommodate 08 Electrons in its Valence Shell. Write two ways.
modelAnswer: An atom can attain eight electrons in its valence shell by gaining or losing electrons (electron transfer).
It can also attain an octet by sharing electrons with another atom.

written.text: Why are Ionic Compounds Solid? Explain.
modelAnswer: Ionic compounds contain oppositely charged ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction.
The ions are held in fixed positions in a crystal lattice, so ionic compounds are solids.

rubric.description: The ions are held in fixed positions in a crystal lattice, making the compound solid.

written.text: Why Atoms do react with each other.
modelAnswer: Atoms react with one another to attain a stable electronic configuration, usually like that of a noble gas.
They do this by losing, gaining, or sharing valence electrons.

written.text: Define ionic compounds and describe their four properties
modelAnswer: Ionic compounds are compounds formed by the transfer of electrons from one atom to another; they consist of oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic forces of attraction.
They are usually crystalline solids.
They generally have high melting and boiling points.
They are usually soluble in water and insoluble in organic solvents.
They do not conduct electricity in the solid state, but conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water.

written.text: Why do the electrons move freely in metals?
modelAnswer: The valence electrons in metals are delocalized and can move freely among the positive metal ions.
When an electric field is applied, these mobile electrons move through the metal and carry electric charge.

written.text: Why does a dipole develop in a molecule?
modelAnswer: A dipole develops when atoms in a molecule have different electronegativities and share electrons unequally.
This creates a partial positive end and a partial negative end in the molecule.

written.text: Define metallic bond and explain it.
modelAnswer: A metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalized electrons.
Metal atoms release their outer electrons, which form a mobile sea of electrons around the positive ions.
The attraction between this electron sea and the positive ions holds the metal lattice together.
